@SecKennedy @HHSGov @HHSResponse @OIGatHHS @TheJusticeDept Please read the following.  I realize you all know this problem exists.  

It's now time for the public to tell you, We the People want this fixed, so that it never happens again.  We've lived it, our tax dollars contributed, and accountability must prevail with justice.

Public Health and Influence: How Policy Gets Shaped

Public-health policy is often presented as a simple process. Scientists study a problem, experts review the evidence, and government acts.

The record is often more complicated.

Across nutrition, tobacco, pharmaceuticals, vaccines, opioids, food fortification, patents, and insurance, the same forces appear again and again: research funding, lobbying, expert influence, political pressure, direct access to government officials, patents, government purchasing, and financial gain after policy decisions are made.

Shaping the Science

In the 1960s, the Sugar Research Foundation paid Harvard researchers to study heart disease.

Industry records later showed that the foundation helped set the research question, supplied studies, and reviewed drafts before publication. The final work focused heavily on fat and cholesterol while downplaying evidence about sugar. The industry's role and funding were not disclosed (Kearns et al., 2016).

That mattered because public-health advice helped shape the American diet.

Diabetes has many causes, including genetics, obesity, inactivity, aging, and diet. Still, the growth has been enormous. Current CDC estimates say about 40 million Americans have diabetes, while more than 100 million adults have prediabetes (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC], 2026a).

The issue is not that sugar alone caused that increase. The issue is that the sugar industry paid for research that shifted attention away from its own product while the public relied on that research for health advice.

Fund the research → shape the question → influence the evidence → shape the public message.

Tobacco: Shape the Science, Then the Law

Tobacco companies went much further.

Internal company records showed that the industry funded scientists, worked with outside experts, supported groups that appeared independent, and promoted doubt about the dangers of smoking and secondhand smoke.

The industry then used lobbyists, experts, and outside groups to fight cigarette taxes, advertising restrictions, clean-air laws, airline smoking rules, and stronger local smoking laws.

The result was not simply confusion. Regulation was delayed or weakened while cigarettes continued to be sold.

Smoking and secondhand smoke have caused millions of deaths in the United States.

Shape the evidence → create outside support → lobby lawmakers → delay regulation → protect the market.

Folic Acid: Direct Pressure on the Regulator

Folic-acid fortification shows influence working in the opposite direction. Instead of trying to stop regulation, outside groups pushed the government to create it.

CDC researcher Godfrey Oakley Jr. later wrote that FDA had decided in May 1995 not to permit or require folic-acid fortification.

That decision did not end the campaign.

March of Dimes president Jennifer Howse and medical director Richard Johnston Jr. gathered support from pediatric, obstetric, and genetics organizations. They collected letters supporting fortification and built a professional coalition.

Johnston then personally carried those letters to FDA Commissioner David Kessler.

Johnston later said Kessler consulted FDA nutrition officials during the meeting and then indicated that the rule would move forward. Oakley later described the Howse-Johnston effort as the “political pressure” that changed the outcome.

FDA issued mandatory fortification rules in March 1996.

CDC estimates that folic-acid fortification prevents roughly 1,300 neural-tube defects each year in the United States (CDC, 2015, 2026b).

At the same time, researchers have continued to study possible problems from population-wide exposure to synthetic folic acid, including unmetabolized folic acid, masking or worsening neurological effects of vitamin B12 deficiency, medication interactions, and possible cancer-related effects at high exposure levels.

Research has also examined 5-MTHF, another form of folate, as an alternative. Recent reviews have found that it can reduce unmetabolized folic acid in the blood, although there is not yet enough evidence to show that it produces better overall clinical outcomes (Frye & Rossignol, 2026).

CDC continues to recommend folic acid and says common MTHFR variants are not a reason to avoid it.

Commercial beneficiaries included vitamin suppliers, food manufacturers, and later companies developing folate-containing products.

Oakley later became a co-inventor of folate-related pharmaceutical technology and disclosed that he was a paid consultant to Ortho-McNeil on folate matters (Oakley & Wald, 2007). The records found so far do not establish when that consulting relationship began.

Agency resistance → professional coalition → direct access to FDA leadership → policy reversal → nationwide mandate.

Opioids: Working Both Sides of Regulation

The opioid crisis showed another form of influence.

A congressional investigation found that at least 22 McKinsey consultants worked for both FDA and opioid manufacturers, including Purdue Pharma, sometimes at the same time (U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, 2022).

The investigation found examples of McKinsey consultants advising Purdue on how to deal with FDA while other McKinsey teams were working inside FDA on drug-safety and regulatory projects.

McKinsey also promoted its government experience to private clients as a source of insight into regulators.

Purdue and other opioid manufacturers made enormous revenue while prescription opioid use expanded.

The public cost was devastating. More than 800,000 Americans died from opioid overdoses between 1999 and 2023, with later deaths pushing that toll still higher (CDC, 2024).

Not every opioid death came from a prescription drug. Heroin and illegal fentanyl later became major drivers of the epidemic. But prescription opioids were the first major wave (CDC, 2024).

Industry seeks an advantage → insiders understand the regulator → strategy is built around the agency → sales continue → public harm grows.

Vaccines: Influence the Experts, Government, and Market

Vaccine policy can be shaped at several stages before and after a product reaches FDA.

Manufacturers fund vaccine research and clinical trials. Experts involved in that research can later take part in federal advisory work under conflict-of-interest rules.

Historical federal reviews have documented vaccine advisers with financial ties involving manufacturer-funded research, consulting, stock ownership, and patents (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General [HHS OIG], 1992).

Industry also lobbies government directly.

PhRMA, BIO, Pfizer, Merck, Moderna, Sanofi, and GSK have all used federal lobbying channels on issues involving research funding, vaccine policy, liability, reimbursement, patents, regulation, and government purchasing.

Government also helps decide which vaccine technologies move forward.

NIH, NIAID, BARDA, HHS, and the Department of Defense can fund research, support trials, finance manufacturing, and commit to buying products before they reach the market.

COVID-19 showed this clearly. Moderna's vaccine was co-developed with NIAID scientists, while BARDA and Operation Warp Speed helped support vaccine development, manufacturing, and advance purchases (National Institutes of Health [NIH], 2020; U.S. Government Accountability Office [GAO], 2020).

The basic chain was:

Industry lobbying and research funding → government priorities and funding → manufacturer develops vaccine → FDA authorizes or licenses it → ACIP recommends use → government and insurers cover or buy it → manufacturer receives revenue.

The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) is important because its recommendations help shape U.S. vaccine policy, insurance coverage, and public purchasing.

In June 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 sitting ACIP members. HHS said the move was meant to address conflicts of interest and rebuild public trust (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services [HHS], 2025).

The decision was opposed by major medical organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, which argued that replacing the panel weakened confidence in the advisory process. These groups were not necessarily the exact same organizations involved in the 1995 folic-acid pressure campaign, although some came from the same professional fields (American Academy of Pediatrics, 2025).

The episode shows how important control of advisory bodies has become. These committees influence recommendations that can affect millions of people and billions of dollars in vaccine sales.

It establishes that companies that profit from vaccine use can fund research, employ experts, lobby government, work with public agencies, and sell products into markets expanded by federal recommendations and government purchasing.

Influence the Experts

Vaccines are part of a larger issue.

FDA and other agencies depend on outside experts.

Those experts can have research grants, consulting contracts, patents, stock ownership, or other financial ties to companies affected by their decisions.

Federal rules sometimes allow participation through disclosure, recusals, waivers, or other authorizations.

Companies can also fund doctors, patient groups, professional organizations, and speakers who participate in regulatory debates.

That creates a basic conflict question: how independent is expert advice when some of the experts or institutions involved also receive money from the industries affected by the decision?

Patent Office: Influence Can Protect the Market

The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) is another important part of the system.

Drug companies, patent lawyers, and trade groups lobby Congress and communicate directly with USPTO through hearings, public comments, and industry meetings.

Patents matter because they can protect profitable drugs from competition.

The FTC challenged more than 100 Orange Book patent listings in 2023 and more than 300 additional listings in 2024 involving diabetes, weight-loss, asthma, and other drugs (Federal Trade Commission [FTC], 2023, 2024).

The FTC said improper listings can delay cheaper generic alternatives and keep brand-name prices high.

A patent dispute can also trigger a delay in generic approval lasting as long as 30 months (FTC, 2023).

The FTC challenged patent practices involving companies such as Teva and became involved in litigation involving Sanofi's Lantus insulin, where lower-cost competition was alleged to have been delayed through patent listings.

Companies can also build large groups of overlapping patents around a successful drug. These are often called patent thickets.

The influence path is clear:

Drug companies and trade groups lobby Congress and engage USPTO → companies seek layers of patents → patents become part of FDA's regulatory system → competitors can be delayed → exclusivity lasts longer → profitable markets stay protected.

Taxpayer-funded research can feed the same system.

Under the Bayh-Dole Act, universities and other recipients of federal research money can patent discoveries developed with public funding and license them to private companies.

That creates another chain:

Taxpayer-funded research → patent → private license → FDA approval → protected market → royalties and commercial revenue.

The federal government has legal march-in rights in some cases involving federally funded inventions. Yet federal agencies have never used those rights, even after petitions involving costly medicines (GAO, 2026).

Insurance Companies and PBMs: Control the Last Gate

FDA approval does not mean a patient can easily get a drug.

Insurance companies and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) control another major gate: coverage.

They decide which drugs get preferred placement, which require prior authorization, and what rebates manufacturers must offer.

The three largest PBMs are Caremark, Express Scripts, and OptumRx.

FTC investigators found that these PBMs and their affiliated pharmacies generated more than $7.3 billion in revenue above estimated drug acquisition costs on selected specialty generic medicines from 2017 through 2022 (FTC, 2025).

The system can work like this:

Manufacturer wants preferred coverage → manufacturer negotiates rebates → PBM controls formulary placement → preferred product gains patients → competitors can lose access → manufacturer keeps sales → PBM collects rebates, fees, or pharmacy revenue.

That affects patients directly.

A cheaper drug can exist and still be harder to get because another product has better formulary placement.

Patients can face higher prices, larger deductibles, higher coinsurance, prior-authorization delays, forced drug switching, and fewer lower-cost choices.

PBM and insurance decisions also affect development.

Drug and vaccine makers study whether insurers will cover a new product, how much they will pay, whether PBMs will prefer it, and whether government will purchase it.

That means insurance and reimbursement can help determine which products companies decide are worth developing in the first place.

The Revolving Door

Regulators, scientists, and consultants have left government positions and gone to work for industries affected by the systems they helped regulate.

Companies value former insiders because they know agency procedures, personnel, decision points, and pressure points.

This movement is often legal.

But it creates a clear conflict when a person can help shape or understand government decisions and later use that knowledge for a company that profits from those same rules.

The revolving door is not just theoretical. Former FDA officials and regulators have taken positions with pharmaceutical and vaccine companies after working on policies or products affecting those industries. A BMJ investigation, for example, identified two FDA vaccine regulators who later went to work for Moderna after holding oversight roles involving COVID-19 vaccines (Doshi, 2023, 2024).

Who Benefits?

Some of these policies produced real public-health benefits. That does not erase the financial interests around them.

The beneficiaries have included:

Sugar and processed-food companies, when health messaging shifted attention away from sugar.

Tobacco companies, when regulation was delayed or weakened.

Food, vitamin, and pharmaceutical companies, when nationwide fortification created larger markets.

Vaccine manufacturers, when federal approval, recommendations, insurance coverage, and government purchases created broad demand.

Drug companies, through patents, exclusivity, and favorable insurance placement.

Universities and inventors, through royalties from publicly funded discoveries.

PBMs and insurers, through rebates, fees, negotiating power, and pharmacy revenue.

Consultants and lobbying firms, which are paid to understand and influence government systems.

Professional and advocacy groups, which can gain funding, access, and policy influence when their positions become government policy.

Profit alone does not prove corruption.

But who made money belongs beside who funded the research, who had access, who applied pressure, and who made the decision.

What Is Still in Place?

Many of these systems are still active today:

Folic-acid fortification.

FDA advisory committees.

Federal vaccine recommendations and government purchasing.

Federal dietary guidance.

Tobacco regulation.

Drug patents and Orange Book protections.

Bayh-Dole licensing of taxpayer-funded discoveries.

Insurance formularies and PBM rebate systems.

Their continued use does not prove that every policy is good or bad.

It does mean that their history, conflicts, money flows, and effects on the public still matter.

What This Has Meant for the Public

The public has lived with the results of these systems. Health information has been shaped by financial interests. Warnings have been delayed. Regulation has been delayed or weakened. Profitable products have remained on the market while evidence of harm grew. Cheaper competitors have been delayed. Patients have paid more. Insurance rules have limited treatment choices.

People have waited for prior authorization while treatment was delayed. Patients have been forced to switch drugs because of insurance or formulary decisions rather than because their doctor believed another drug was better. Taxpayers have helped fund research and product development, while private companies later received patents, sales, and government contracts from those products. Government recommendations have created or expanded markets for medicines and vaccines. Industry lobbying has affected what lawmakers and agencies considered, funded, regulated, delayed, or approved.

The health effects have also been real. People were kept in the dark about smoking risks while tobacco companies fought regulation. Americans received decades of nutrition advice influenced by industry-funded research. Families were hit by addiction and overdose during the opioid epidemic. Patients have paid higher prices when patent strategies delayed cheaper drugs. People have faced restricted choices when PBMs and insurers favored one product over another.

The benefits also reached identifiable people. Families had fewer pregnancies affected by neural-tube defects after folic-acid fortification (CDC, 2015). Smokers who quit and nonsmokers protected by smoke-free laws had less exposure to tobacco-related disease. People protected from infectious diseases benefited from effective vaccines. Patients benefited when effective medicines reached the market and when generic competition lowered prices.

Those benefits do not erase conflicts, lobbying, financial pressure, delayed warnings, higher costs, or documented harm. Both belong in the record.

Over the last 30 years, Americans have become sicker in several major areas of chronic disease. The evidence in this article shows that industry influence, distorted research, delayed regulation, aggressive marketing, patent practices, and barriers to treatment contributed to some of that harm, even as other public-health policies produced real benefits.

At the same time, the system became more expensive and more complicated. More decisions now stand between the patient and the treatment: patents, insurance companies, PBMs, rebates, prior authorization, government purchasing, and large health-care institutions.

For the public, these systems have affected what people were told was healthy, what dangers they were warned about, what medicines were available, what doctors could easily prescribe, what insurance would pay for, how much patients paid, how quickly cheaper products reached the market, how taxpayer money was spent, and how long harmful practices continued before government acted.

The result has reached directly into people's doctor's offices, pharmacies, insurance plans, grocery stores, tax bills, family finances, and health. That is why the influence behind public-health policy matters. It is not only about government, industry, or institutions.

It is about what happened to the people who had to live with their decisions.

text:
Waxman, Oakley and Frieden: Public Health, Influence and Controversy

Henry Waxman, Godfrey Oakley Jr., and Thomas Frieden occupied different positions within the same expanding federal public-health system: Congress, CDC research and advocacy, and later CDC leadership.

Waxman helped strengthen federal preventive-health policy through legislation including the Preventive Health Amendments of 1992. He also became a major congressional figure in disputes involving tobacco, HIV/AIDS, pharmaceuticals and conflicts between government scientists and industry.

During the same period, CDC birth-defects director Godfrey Oakley Jr. was pushing another population-level intervention: folic-acid fortification.

FDA initially raised concerns about exposing the entire population, including vitamin-B12 masking, neurological injury, medication interactions and long-term exposure among people who were not the intended beneficiaries.

Oakley later wrote that FDA decided in May 1995 not to permit or require fortification.

According to Oakley, March of Dimes president Jennifer Howse and medical director Richard Johnston Jr. then applied the “political pressure” that changed the outcome. Howse and Johnston assembled support from pediatric, obstetric and genetics organizations. Johnston personally carried those letters into FDA Commissioner David Kessler’s office. During that meeting, Kessler consulted FDA nutrition officials and told Johnston that the rule would move forward.

FDA issued its mandatory fortification rule in March 1996.

At roughly the same time, researchers identified the common MTHFR C677T variant, showing meaningful genetic differences in folate metabolism. Oakley participated in later MTHFR research while continuing to advocate widespread folic-acid consumption.

The mainstream public-health interpretation was that MTHFR differences strengthened the case for adequate folate. Other researchers and critics raised concerns about unmetabolized folic acid, masking of B12 deficiency, neurological injury, medication interactions, possible cancer signals at higher exposures and whether genetically different populations respond identically to lifelong synthetic folic-acid exposure.

Those concerns do not establish that fortification broadly harms people with MTHFR variants, but they show that the safety debate continued after the original policy decision.

Oakley’s work also developed a pharmaceutical connection. While at CDC, he became co-inventor of technology combining folic acid with contraceptive/hormone products. Patent records later involved Ortho-McNeil Pharmaceutical and the U.S. government/HHS. Oakley subsequently disclosed that he was a paid consultant to Ortho-McNeil on folate.

The patent record dates the invention to 1998, but the records located so far do not establish when Oakley’s consulting relationship with Ortho-McNeil began.

Thomas Frieden worked at CDC during the early 1990s and later served as CDC director from 2009–2017. He promoted population-level interventions involving tobacco, HIV testing and nutrition and later publicly praised Oakley’s folic-acid work.

Frieden’s CDC tenure also included serious professional controversy. In 2014, CDC experienced laboratory-safety failures involving anthrax and highly pathogenic H5N1 influenza, including delayed reporting and inadequate oversight. Frieden acknowledged that CDC had failed to adequately address a broader laboratory-safety problem.

After leaving CDC, Frieden faced a separate personal controversy following an allegation of unwanted sexual touching. He ultimately pleaded guilty to the lesser violation of disorderly conduct; he did not admit the original allegation, and the more serious charges were dropped.

The documented connection is therefore not that Waxman, Oakley and Frieden jointly designed one program. It is that they occupied influential positions within the same evolving public-health structure: Waxman helped expand federal preventive-health authority, Oakley used CDC science and organized outside advocacy to push a population-wide intervention, and Frieden later led the same agency and continued the broader population-health model.

The folic-acid history also leaves several unresolved questions, particularly the timing of Oakley’s Ortho-McNeil relationship, the full list of organizations whose support was delivered directly to Kessler, and how much emerging genetic and safety evidence was formally reconsidered before nationwide implementation.

Public Officials and Private Power: CEO Connections, Corporate Funding, and Controversies

The first three articles in this series traced the overlapping careers of former Representative Henry Waxman, Dr. Anthony Fauci, and Dr. Thomas Frieden through HIV/AIDS policy, NIH and CDC, pharmaceutical development, the State Department, PEPFAR, and the financial beneficiaries of the expanding global-health system.

A fourth question follows naturally:

What relationships did these officials have with corporate executives, wealthy private funders, and industries affected by their work?

The record reveals several important connections, although their nature differs considerably. Fauci's relationships largely developed through pharmaceutical research and technology transfer. Frieden later became directly connected to billionaire-funded philanthropy, while CDC faced questions about corporate funding during his leadership. Waxman's relationship with corporate executives was predominantly adversarial through congressional oversight.

None of these relationships alone establishes corruption. Some, however, raise legitimate questions about conflicts of interest and the increasingly blurred boundary between government public health and private financial interests.

Fauci and Pharmaceutical Executives

As director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), Fauci interacted regularly with pharmaceutical companies developing vaccines and infectious-disease treatments.

One unusually direct example occurred during the COVID-19 vaccine trials.

In an NIH oral history, Fauci recalled that Pfizer Chief Executive Officer Albert Bourla personally called him before Pfizer publicly announced its vaccine efficacy results. Fauci described receiving a similar call from Moderna's CEO, Stéphane Bancel, regarding Moderna's vaccine results (National Institutes of Health [NIH], 2022).

The calls demonstrate the degree of direct communication between NIAID's longtime director and senior pharmaceutical executives.

They do not demonstrate a financial arrangement between Fauci and those companies.

NIH Royalties and Private Companies

A more consequential financial connection involves NIH's technology-transfer system.

When government scientists participate in inventions, NIH can patent the resulting technology and license it to private companies. Those companies pay royalties to NIH, and federal law permits government employee-inventors to receive portions of certain royalty income.

Records released through litigation showed that Fauci and former NIH Director Francis Collins received 58 royalty payments between 2010 and 2021. Most occurred before the COVID-19 pandemic (https://t.co/MAeMzzhRoN, 2023).

The existence of the payments is established. Their existence does not demonstrate pharmaceutical companies secretly paying Fauci.

The payments arose from the federal technology-transfer system.

Nevertheless, the controversy surrounding disclosure of individual royalty amounts and licensees raises legitimate transparency questions because NIH scientists can participate in research that subsequently becomes commercially valuable.

A federal court considering related disclosure litigation in 2025 recognized the public interest in information concerning inventor awards associated with NIH technology licensing (American Transparency v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, 2025).

The relevant financial chain is therefore:

Government research → NIH invention/patent → private company license → royalty payments to NIH → inventor awards to eligible government scientists.

Determining whether a specific payment created a conflict of interest requires identifying the invention, company, amount, and recipient rather than assuming misconduct from the existence of royalties alone.

Frieden and Billionaire Philanthropy

Thomas Frieden's private-sector connections became especially significant after he left CDC.

Frieden founded Resolve to Save Lives, an international public-health organization initially housed within Vital Strategies before becoming an independent nonprofit.

Its founding support came from several major philanthropic organizations associated with some of the world's wealthiest individuals, including:

Bloomberg Philanthropies — Michael Bloomberg

Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation — Bill Gates

Chan Zuckerberg-associated philanthropy — Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan

Resolve to Save Lives describes these organizations among its initial funders (Resolve to Save Lives, n.d.).

The original initiative involved approximately $225 million in funding.

Bloomberg Philanthropies subsequently announced an additional $115 million commitment supporting Resolve's cardiovascular-health work (Resolve to Save Lives, 2022).

This creates a direct post-government relationship between a former CDC director and billionaire-backed global-health philanthropy.

The relationship is publicly disclosed and is not evidence of misconduct.

It does, however, illustrate another recurring theme in this investigation: former government public-health leadership moving into organizations financed by enormous concentrations of private philanthropic capital.

Frieden's Personal Financial Benefit

Unlike the broader institutional funding examined earlier in this series, Frieden's nonprofit role also provides an identifiable personal financial component.

Public nonprofit filings report substantial compensation for Frieden in his role as president and CEO of Resolve to Save Lives, exceeding $500,000 annually in recent filings.

That compensation is publicly disclosed nonprofit executive compensation.

It should not be characterized as improper merely because the organization receives philanthropic funding.

It does, however, distinguish Frieden's post-government career from the government-era financial relationships examined elsewhere in this series.

CDC, Coca-Cola, and Corporate Funding

A potentially more significant controversy occurred during Frieden's tenure as CDC director.

Between 2010 and 2015, Coca-Cola contributed more than $1 million to the CDC Foundation, primarily supporting programs involving noncommunicable diseases.

The relationship became controversial because CDC simultaneously occupied an important role in public-health policy concerning obesity, nutrition, diabetes, and other conditions affected by consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages.

The scripting method that manifests in 72 hours.

A neuroscientist accidentally discovered the fastest manifestation method.

In 2,015, she wrote her ideal day in past tense, as if it already happened.
Seventy two hours later, everything she wrote came true.

Job offer, money.
Specific conversation. Word for word.
She tested it on 500 people.
73% reported exact manifestations within three days.
It's called future memory encoding.
Your brain can't distinguish between real memories and written ones.
When you script in past tense,
your subconscious believes it already happened and reality bends to match the memory.
Stanford Memory Lab, 2,015 false memory research.
They proved the brain stores imagined events the same way as real events.
Right. I received $5,000 today.
In Past Tense. Your brain files it as a memory,
not a wish, not a goal.
A memory of something that already occurred.
And the brain has one job.
Make reality match your memories.
72 hour scripting protocol.
Step 1 write in past tense.
This is critical. Wrong.
I will have money. Right.
Today I received unexpected money.
I felt so grateful. Past tense equals memory.
Future tense equals wish. Step 2 be insanely specific.
Don't write I got money. Write,
I received $3,000 from an unexpected source at two PM.
I felt shocked and grateful.
Specificity equals reality anchor.
Step 3 include emotions and sensations.
My heart raced when I saw the notification.
I smiled uncontrollably. Emotion encodes the memory deeper.
Step 4 write as if you're journaling yesterday.
Yesterday was incredible. This happened.
This tricks your brain into past timeline mode.
Step 5. Read it out loud once,
then forget it. Don't obsess.
Don't reread daily. Write it,
read it once, release.
Attachment blocks manifestation.
What happens in 72 hours? Your subconscious starts scanning for the memory.
It thinks this already happened.
Where's the evidence? So it creates synchronicities, opportunities,
coincidences to match the memory you encoded.
Because you didn't manifest the future,
you remembered it into existence.
Test this tonight. Write your ideal day.
Past tense, specific, emotional.
Read once, release.
Then watch the next 72 hours deliver exactly what you wrote.

A Small Price, If You Do Not Live in the City Being Priced

Valhalla VFT ran the rally clip under the cheerful heading of what a psychopath would do, and the tape does not require much help. The president tells the room the war is artificial, a bit exaggerated, a small price for the security of the world and the country, and then offers Los Angeles and San Diego as the kind of thing that can be destroyed and still count as a bargain, over very soon, almost over, unless it lasts a little longer because the other side has a great capacity for pain. The crowd cheers. Of course it cheers. Nothing flatters a rally like a hypothetical in which the blast radius is someone else’s zip code.

The strategic briefing that follows is doing a lot of work for a man who did not give one. San Diego is not a punchline with a pier. It is a Pacific Fleet hub, north of a hundred thousand active-duty personnel, tens of thousands of military children, and a couple hundred thousand veterans and retirees who made the mistake of settling near the water. Letting that city be destroyed is a small price only if the person naming the price has already decided the invoice goes to the Navy and not to the ballroom. Iran’s ballistic reach, as the host bothers to put on the screen, tops out well short of the California coast, and Tehran does not have the nuclear arsenal the sentence requires. So the scenario in which those two cities eat a warhead is either a novel, a threat pointed the wrong direction, or a sentence that got away from its owner. None of those is a comfort.

The scheduling is the part that deserves the slow clap. On the stump the war ends right after the midterms, a convenient month for a conflict to discover it was exaggerated. In the reporting the host stacks next to the clip, the Pentagon is moving a third carrier, the Theodore Roosevelt out of San Diego itself, plus the Makin Island group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, on a timeline that arrives in late November, which is to say after the voters have done their job and before anyone has to explain a ground option in daylight. Recruiting graphics say send me. The host’s friends still in uniform, he reports, have not formed a line. Netanyahu’s election trouble and a CIA note about Israeli internal fracture get folded in because this administration has never met a war it could not schedule around somebody else’s ballot.

Peak insanity is a high bar in this decade, and the channel may have spent it early. What the hour actually catches is smaller and funnier. A president pricing American cities as acceptable damage, a crowd applauding the discount, and a deployment calendar that treats Election Day as intermission. The war is artificial until the ships leave the harbor. Then it is merely someone else’s small price.

The absence of [purificatory] animal sacrifice has nothing whatsoever to do with animal welfare or vegetarianism.
Jesus' command "Rise Peter! Kill and eat!" should've made that clear.

The Christians fully acknowledge that the the blood of slain oxen or goats is purificatory to some degree, but they argue that God himself shed blood on this earth before rising and ascending and that this divine blood is much more purificatory.

Therefore, by partaking of the blood that Jesus shed via the eucharist we are cleansed of our sins and are "washed in the blood of the lamb." 

Paul discusses this:
"For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God." 

Christians do engage in animal sacrifice to saints, especially in countries like Greece, though it's not an purificatory practice like the Eucharist.

A gaslighting and a brainwashing by any other name are still the same. This quiz does not ask the student whether the claim is true. It asks her to sort the claim, and the claims have already been written.

The screen is a Minnesota college module, “What is Political Psychology?” The item is a Toulmin drill. A warrant, in that model, is the unstated assumption that ties a fact to a conclusion. The student is graded on naming the assumption. She is not graded on whether the assumption survives contact with the world. That is the trick. The falsehood is smuggled in as the practice material, and the only skill being tested is compliance with the frame.

One item offers “Mr. Trump’s hate speech is comparable to that of Adolf Hitler” as a live choice beside “crooked millionaire” and a line about his supporters being angry at politicians. The keyed answer on her screen is the immigration line, marked correct. The Hitler sentence did not have to be the key. It only had to sit there as a normal option, the way “the sky is blue” sits in a grammar test. Another item treats “Mrs. Clinton is a trustworthy politician” as the warrant. The reading under the module is a column on racial resentment that already knows who the villain is.

Call it rhetoric instruction and you have described the label on the jar. The jar is a loyalty test. Repeat the premise often enough, in the voice of a quiz worth points, and the student stops hearing it as a claim. She hears it as the rule the answer has to fit. That is not an education in argument. It is an education in which arguments she is allowed to have.

text:
♠️ ACR Poker Turns On Screen Capture Protection Selectively

The WPN network activated ScreenShield, but not for all players. On September 29, the operator contacted players that its detection flagged as running remote access or screen control software and turned on protection for them. The feature hides the table content along with hole cards from the screen capture and screen sharing methods it covers, while the player sees the tables as usual. According to WPN, a check of its own systems, software, and official downloads found no compromise.

The operator didn't turn protection on for everyone because of conflicts with legitimate use. Remote access programs are needed for work, presentations, and tech support. Players also stream, record sessions, and review their play with coaches, and ScreenShield affects those features. So other players can request protection through support, with activation taking up to 48 hours, and an in-client toggle is still in development.

Separately, WPN sent other operators a description of how to implement this kind of protection on their own. For the market, that matters more than the feature itself, because image output protection is being offered as a common approach, not as one room's special feature.

1. AB Kuai.Dong (@_forAB)【Open-Source Adobe Alternatives】

Core idea: AB Kuai.Dong highlights an open-source GitHub organization that released seven Rust-based creative tools, positioning them as free, local alternatives to parts of Adobe’s product suite. The Photoshop-like product drew the most attention, with some speculation that AI tools such as Claude may have accelerated development.

Why it matters: Even if these tools are still limited versus Adobe-grade software, the direction is important: AI-assisted engineering can lower the cost of building complex creative software. Open-source, local-first products may not kill incumbents overnight, but they can pressure expensive proprietary suites by attacking specific workflows from below.

Original: https://t.co/JKBYUK2rck

2. 憨厚的麦总 (@michael_liu93)【Crypto Moats Are Stronger Than They Look】

Core idea: 憨厚的麦总 argues that crypto businesses often have deeper moats than the market assumes. He points to Aave, Uniswap, USDT/USDC, Binance/Coinbase, and Hyperliquid as examples of products that continue to dominate despite repeated challengers.

Why it matters: His framework is: product strength shapes user habits, user habits concentrate liquidity, and liquidity then reinforces product competitiveness. In crypto, moats are not always patents or regulation—they are often liquidity, trust, integrations, and repeated user behavior.

Original: https://t.co/nKnLAVr3oD

3. AB Kuai.Dong (@_forAB)【Hyperliquid’s Regulatory Gray Zone】

Core idea: AB Kuai.Dong points to a Financial Times discussion of Hyperliquid’s unusual regulatory position: the protocol reportedly acknowledges a Singapore base, while arguing it falls outside MAS oversight because it is decentralized rather than a traditional company.

Why it matters: This captures one of the hardest questions in crypto regulation: how to supervise systems that have users, revenues, and economic impact, but do not fit cleanly into corporate categories. Hyperliquid’s case shows how decentralization can become both a product architecture and a regulatory boundary.

Original: https://t.co/8aHBWia42v

4. Cooker.hl (@cookerflips)【Trading Evolves Whether You Like It or Not】

Core idea: Cooker.hl argues that trading will keep evolving regardless of whether people approve of the newest methods—bundling, mobile apps, scripts, multi-wallet setups, or other edge-seeking tactics. He frames this as a continuation of crypto’s constant adaptation cycle.

Why it matters: His point is not that every new tactic is healthy or fair, but that markets reward adaptation before they reward moral judgment. In crypto, each cycle produces new tools, new distribution channels, and new microstructure games; traders who refuse to study them risk being structurally late.

Original: https://t.co/FD2GlWG2bX

5. 憨厚的麦总 (@michael_liu93)【Early Bull Markets Require Patience】

Core idea: 憨厚的麦总 says the early phase of a bull market often feels painful because bear-market psychology, profit-taking, and grinding corrections are still dominant. He argues that large new capital usually arrives only when Bitcoin approaches or breaks new highs.

Why it matters: His strategy is to stay patient and focus on assets with stronger fundamentals, alignment with crypto liquidity cycles, full circulation, and recent relative strength. The takeaway is that early bull markets are less about constant rotation and more about surviving shakeouts without losing exposure to the best assets.

Original: https://t.co/xoZKyOlYsa

6. hansolar (@hansolar21)【Wallet Security Still Comes First】

Core idea: hansolar shares a warning after a friend’s “Fomo wallet” was reportedly drained for $4 million. He advises users to avoid conference Wi-Fi, avoid scanning random QR codes, and never leave devices or belongings unattended.

Why it matters: Crypto security failures often come from ordinary habits, not exotic exploits. Events, conferences, and high-density networking environments are especially dangerous because users are distracted, connected to unfamiliar networks, and more likely to interact with strangers or unknown links.

Original: https://t.co/rOCjvgTQQm

7. Evanss6 (@evan_ss6)【Surviving Wealth Is Harder Than Making It】

Core idea: Evanss6 warns that many traders with $1–10 million in lifetime PnL may lose most of it over the next 3–5 years if they fail to derisk. His advice is to take profits and allocate some capital into “boring stuff.”

Why it matters: This is the other side of crypto wealth creation: making money in a volatile cycle is not the same as keeping it. Diversification, withdrawal discipline, tax planning, and lower-volatility assets may feel unexciting, but they are what keep traders alive after the market stops paying for risk.

Original: https://t.co/n3KbCXHOkI

8. Route 2 FI (@route2fi)【iAI Depends on Real Compute Demand】

Core idea: Route 2 FI analyzes iAI through the lens of compute-credit demand. He frames the broader 0G thesis as AI infrastructure that goes beyond inference, while noting iAI’s reported uptime advantage versus competitors.

Why it matters: His key metric is not narrative, but usage. For both 0G and iAI, the question is whether developers and users actually consume the infrastructure at scale. In AI x Crypto, adoption, uptime, and recurring demand matter more than abstract “AI infra” branding.

Original: https://t.co/A8KLvlvLt1

9. Ai 姨 (@ai_9684xtpa)【Binance Reserve Flows Show BTC Rotation】

Core idea: Ai 姨 summarizes Binance’s latest proof-of-reserves update: BNB, USDC, XRP, and USD1 reserve ratios dipped slightly, while BTC and USDT rose, with all still above 100%. She also notes that Binance users increased BTC holdings by about $536.7 million while reducing ETH by about $498 million.

Why it matters: She offers two possible interpretations: BTC may be absorbing liquidity from ETH, or ETH may have been accumulated and then withdrawn on-chain. Either way, the data gives a useful snapshot of capital rotation inside a major CEX, especially during periods when BTC dominance and ETH flows are actively debated.

Original: https://t.co/WDZTs8LLq8

10. qw (@qwqiao)【Crypto’s Unusual Wealth Creation Window】

Core idea: qw reflects on the 2010s to early 2020s as a uniquely powerful era for crypto wealth creation. In his view, anyone with an internet connection could access assets that later reached trillion-dollar scale while they were still valued at sub-billion levels.

Why it matters: His broader point is that crypto was unusually open compared with many other technology waves. AI and traditional tech often concentrate early upside among insiders, capital allocators, and Silicon Valley networks, while crypto gave global retail users a direct path into early ownership. That open access is a major reason the industry still commands cultural and financial attention.

text:
A thought for the small businesses, who may be struggling. Leverage your greatest asset, your people. 

The population has had it with logins, QR codes, digital coupons, authentication codes, endless texts and emails. Seize the opportunity to build your brand loyalty.

Simple basic good service is an asset you still own that big boxes have invested heavily against as they move further towards removing people. 

That’s a real competitive asset that doesn’t require software upgrades, more cloud storage, handheld devices, gimmicks...things that are not free. 

I cleaned out my inbox today deleting an annoying amount of electronic receipts, hello emails and “points” notifications I’d “earned.” 

Yes, I use filters, an email that goes to an inbox I never open and block senders but there is still enough to be a time waster, a pain in the a**. 

A good product, at a decent price that is part of my community, one that still accepts cash and has staff that make eye contact, acknowledge you and sometimes even smile is a Big Advantage. 

That is the personal experience that big box tech driven companies have abandoned. 

Trader Joe’s has no self-check out, no digital coupons, no video camera staring you down. Yes, they are a big, successful retailer. Their employees also still have conversations and they are highly visible in the store.

In many businesses there is a front of the house and back of the house. The front is your entrance to your
“living room” how inviting is yours? 

You can still do this better than big retail. Exploit it-especially as the holidays approach. Personalization in business is not best achieved via data. Data brought us creepy “surveillance” ads. 

Personalization isn’t about data, it’s about people. Hang on to your good people, train them well, treat them well and they will treat customers well. 

Make your brand about….

“We don’t offer points, just every day value for everyone. No phone needed, YES we accept cash 💵 our National currency” we are happy you are here.” 

If I had kids, I’d give them cash to go Holiday shopping at small businesses only this year. 

You don’t need the latest software. Look over you tech subscriptions and decide what you might be able to cut. 

Who really cares if your Optometrist sends you a “Birthday” Email. That’s disengaging and an unwanted crossover into my personal space. No Thank you “Constant Contact” 🙈

A genuine real person asking how is your day going, isn’t it nice out today will beat a BOT parroting “I understand how frustrating that must be” every time. 

And-Chick-fil-A CEO Andrew Cathy confirmed that, “the chain will not use artificial intelligence or voice AI to take drive-thru orders, choosing instead to keep human-to-human hospitality at the forefront of its service model.”

Stay Real-Be Genuine-Build your Hospitality-And Prosper 

USA-Shop Small this holiday season.

Last night Republican John James and Democrat Jocelyn Benson met in their first televised debate in their contest for Michigan governor.
Benson attacked James over supporting president Trump's tariffs, vowing to negotiate with Canada.: “These reckless tariffs have been supported by my opponent, and that's why we call them the John James tax because they are costing Michigan $5600 each household. ”
James denied voting to increase those tariffs:: “Specifically talking with the trade ambassador and saying that we must get back to the table, stop acting like children, and negotiate a reciprocal, fair, and mutually beneficial arrangement. ”
The two also clashed over the war in Iran and high fuel costs, tax breaks for data centers, and standing up to president Trump.

Federal authorities say Washington state resident James Cody Bryant conspired and encouraged an 18-year-old to carry out a February mass shooting at a school in Canada. Officials say that Bryant communicated with the shooter for 6 months before the attack, and did not report the plans to authorities.
The shooter killed two family members at home before attacking a nearby school, where he killed 6 people and wounded 25 others. Acting US Attorney Neil Floyd:: “After killing two of his own relatives, when the shooter had trouble starting his own car, Bryant provided advice and offered assistance on how to get the car started so that JVR could proceed proceed to the school and kill children. ”
He was later found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Attorneys for Christa Pike say the death row inmate is conscious and speaking in an undisclosed hospital. Turning to the investigation of an alleged gang rape on the Cornell campus - an attorney for one of the accused fraternity members is speaking out. Cornell University has hired former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an internal investigation of how the university handled Jane Doe's s allegations that she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 20-24.

Militants also took more than 250 hostages.
Gaza health authorities say Israel's subsequent bombardment and ground operations have killed more than 74-thousand people in Gaza.

Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan are facing multiple charges including conspiracy to commit child abuse and dissuading a witness.
Both have pleaded not guilty and are being held on a $20 million bond.

Russian health authorities are investigating the death of an employee at the anti-plague institute. Her death was attributed to pneumonia with an unknown cause.

With college enrollments dropping, more schools are slashing their tuition.: “A new Gallup poll finds only 3 in 10 Americans believe a college education is very important, so schools are trying to attract more students by lowering their prices. Some, like Emory and Henry University in Virginia, are cutting their tuition in half. Coe College in Iowa is dropping its tuition by 54%. UC Irvine cut its executive MBA fees by $48,000. However, experts warn that some of the schools cutting their sticker prices are making up for it by offering smaller scholarships. Michael Wallace, Worldwide News Network. ”

The Emmys rotated among the four major networks annually. The deal means the Emmys will have a long-term home. The awards will still be free to watch with no prime video subscription required.

text:
On this day in 2001, the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan began.

Operation Enduring Freedom opened with airstrikes on Taliban and al-Qaeda targets, less than a month after the September 11 attacks. 

The campaign followed the Taliban’s refusal to hand over Osama bin Laden and dismantle al-Qaeda’s camps. U.S. and British aircraft hit air defenses, command sites, and training facilities, while special forces linked up with the Northern Alliance on the ground.

Kabul fell in November. 

The Taliban regime collapsed by December. 

The war that started that night would last 20 years.

              ---------------------------

On the night of October 7, 2001, the United States and Britain opened a military campaign in Afghanistan that would become the longest war in American history. Less than four weeks after the September 11 attacks, cruise missiles, long-range bombers, and carrier aircraft struck Taliban military sites and al-Qaeda camps. President George W. Bush announced the operation from the White House Treaty Room as the first explosions were reported in Kabul.

The strikes were the start of Operation Enduring Freedom. 

Bush said the actions were meant to disrupt Afghanistan’s use as a terrorist base and to attack the military capability of the Taliban regime that had ruled most of the country since 1996. Britain joined the opening night. Other governments pledged forces, transit rights, or intelligence. NATO had already invoked its mutual-defense clause for the first time, treating the September 11 attacks as an attack on the alliance.

The path to that night ran through a short and unsuccessful diplomacy. Investigators quickly linked the hijackings to al-Qaeda and its leader, Osama bin Laden, who was sheltered in Afghanistan. Washington demanded that the Taliban close terrorist training camps, hand over al-Qaeda leaders, and release detained foreign nationals. Taliban officials refused to surrender bin Laden without what they called concrete evidence and floated alternatives, including trial in an Islamic court. 

Those offers were rejected. On October 7, Bush said none of the demands had been met and that the Taliban would pay a price.

US VP Vance said Iran must materially reduce its uranium-enrichment capability to secure a deal. In a newly published Reuters interview, he said Washington remains unsure whether Pezeshkian and Araghchi have the authority to deliver one. (RTRS)

Houthis attacked the international airport in the southern Yemeni town of Aden with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones early on Wednesday, Yemen's Transport Ministry said, as fighting intensified across several fronts between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces. (RTRS)

Fuel sellers are holding back from implementing Trump’s red-diesel policy while seeking clarity on whether the 24.4-cent-per-gallon federal tax is waived or merely deferred. The White House intends permanent savings, but industry groups say retailers could retain the liability. (Bloomberg)

The governing board of the International Energy Agency will hold an informal meeting at 1300 local time on Wednesday to discuss the proposed release of oil and diesel stocks, said two European Union diplomats. (RTRS)

Hormuz freight reached a record $1.3mn a day this week, versus $20,000–50,000 last year. Captains are being offered the equivalent of $100,000 a month plus $50,000 per trip, while war insurance can cost 6–10% of a vessel’s value. (FT)

MACRO:

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva urged governments to repair public finances as borrowing costs climb and global public debt approaches 100% of GDP, warning that energy and AI-related risks leave little room for delay. (FT)

Ray Dalio warned that artificial intelligence is a “classic bubble” that is nearing a bursting point thanks to rising interest rates and the need to turn wealth into cash. (BBG)

Florida declared an emergency in 25 counties as a Gulf storm developed; the NHC warned of increasing wind and storm-surge risks along the northern Gulf Coast. No production shutdown was verified in the reviewed material. (DeSantis, NHC)

Borrowers in the Asia Pacific are slowing deals in the dollar bond market, with the highest yields in more than two years sapping deal momentum. (BBG)

Japan’s real wages rose 1.5% Y/Y in August, matching expectations and extending gains to eight months. Nominal and base pay both rose 3.8%, with government relief helping purchasing power. (Bloomberg)

Business confidence at big Japanese manufacturers rose in October to its highest level in nearly five years, helped by robust chip demand, but sentiment among non-manufacturers deteriorated sharply amid rising costs, a Reuters monthly poll showed. (RTRS)

The Bank of Japan's new policymaker Ayano Sato said she supports the idea of raising interest rates in several stages, Kyodo news agency reported on Wednesday, highlighting awareness even among dovish board members of the need to combat inflation risks. (RTRS)

Japan Exchange Group Inc. is set to unveil the biggest-ever reshuffle of the Topix on Wednesday, a revamp that could shrink one of Asia’s broadest major equity benchmarks and intensify pressure on Japanese companies to boost their market appeal. (BBG)

Retail investors are estimated to have lost 2.3 trillion won ($1.7 billion) from leveraged exchange-traded products tracking South Korea’s two chipmaking giants in just months, according to a lawmaker’s office, in the first revelation of the magnitude of risks from such bets. (BBG)

Australian households are proving less vulnerable to interest-rate increases than their heavy debt loads might suggest, Deutsche Bank AG said, noting stronger household balance sheets are helping borrowers withstand tighter monetary policy. (BBG)

A hedge fund industry group has warned the Bank of England that proposed reforms to the market for short-term loans secured against UK government bonds, known as "repo", could backfire and reduce liquidity at times of market stress. (RTRS)

UK house prices were unchanged both M/M and Y/Y in September, versus forecasts of +0.1% and +0.2%, respectively. Prices fell 0.2% on a quarterly basis as higher mortgage rates weighed. (Reuters)

ECB’s Moulin said France’s bond-market situation is serious, but the conditions for central-bank intervention have not been met. He urged a 2027 budget deficit of no more than 5% of GDP, versus 5.4% forecast this year. (Bloomberg)

France no longer has any room for mistakes to get its fiscal house in order, and pressure from financial markets should help focus minds in Paris on reining in spending ahead of next year's presidential election, senior Citadel executive Angel Ubide told Reuters. (RTRS)

Brussels is considering a broader levy on large corporations that would capture US technology groups without explicitly targeting digital businesses. Changes to the existing proposal’s thresholds and contributions remain under discussion and would require unanimous EU agreement. (FT)

German industrial production rose 2.0% M/M in August versus 0.5% expected, reversing July’s 1.2% decline and marking the strongest monthly increase since March 2025. Output rose 2.3% Y/Y. (WSJ)

Swedish CPIF inflation excluding energy held at 0.5% Y/Y in September, below the 0.7% consensus and Riksbank forecast. Headline CPIF inflation was 1.5%, as expected. (Bloomberg)

Norway proposed withdrawing NOK608bn from its sovereign wealth fund in 2027, equivalent to 2.7% of its value and unchanged from this year’s share. The draft budget includes NOK6.4bn of tax cuts and still requires parliamentary negotiations. (Bloomberg)

India’s RBI raised its repo rate 25bp to 5.50%, its first increase since 2023. The rate decision was unanimous; members voted 4–2 to shift the stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. (WSJ)

FTSE Russell retained Indonesia’s emerging-market classification following transparency and market-structure reforms. It will update its treatment of Indonesian securities ahead of December’s review; MSCI’s separate decision is due in November. (BBG)

Vietnamese banks are planning nearly $7 billion in share sales as the country's fast-growing economy fuels demand for capital, opening a window for foreign investors to expand in the tightly controlled sector. (RTRS)

GEOPOLITICAL:

Washington formally pressed Moscow for details of the Siberian laboratory worker’s death, warning that limited disclosure conflicts with international health obligations. The pathogen remains unconfirmed; WHO assesses the risk outside Russia as very low. (WSJ)

Trump said he has a call scheduled soon with Putin to discuss the suspected plague case. He did not say the call had taken place. (Bloomberg)

Beijing made its first official comments on the suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia, saying it’s cooperating with Russia as health concerns intensify around the world. (BBG)

Russia launched a barrage of drones and missiles at Ukraine on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and damaging residential buildings, industrial facilities and infrastructure, Ukrainian officials said. (RTRS)

Airspace around Poland’s Lublin and Rzeszów airports closed for military activity during Russia’s overnight attack on Ukraine, according to NOTAMs flagged by Flightradar24. No reopening was verified before the cutoff. (Flightradar24)

North Korea threatened immediate, powerful retaliation for any border incursion following South Korean mine-clearance activity. Pyongyang denied responsibility for the earlier mine incident that injured three South Korean soldiers. (Bloomberg)

EQUITIES:

SpaceX is working on a $40bn financing package for Nvidia chips, led by Apollo and comprising roughly $10bn of bank loans and $30bn of investment-grade debt. Pimco is in talks; the package is expected to close in 2027 and is not yet secured. (FT)

Apple has co-developed LG-branded doorbells, thermostats, locks and cameras for its smart-home push, people familiar said. Apple’s hub and updated HomePod mini/TV hardware are planned for October 13, while the LG accessories remain months away. (Bloomberg)

Intel will continue working on Elon Musk’s Terafab chipmaking venture, CEO Lip-Bu Tan said, despite Musk’s separate discussions with TSMC earlier this week. (Bloomberg)

AMD’s Lisa Su is scheduled to meet Samsung chip chief Jun Young-hyun during her South Korean visit amid the memory shortage. No new supply agreement was announced in the report. (Bloomberg)

Constellation Brands reported comparable EPS of $3.74 versus $3.55 expected and revenue of $2.63bn versus $2.54bn. It raised GAAP full-year EPS guidance to $11.85–12.55 from $11.50–12.20; comparable EPS guidance was unchanged. (WSJ)

LG Electronics’ preliminary Q3 operating profit of KRW781.8bn missed the KRW1.028tn consensus despite rising 13.5% Y/Y. Revenue increased 8.9% to KRW23.827tn but also fell short of expectations. (WSJ)

Nanya reportedly notified customers of DRAM contract-price increases of up to 20% on some products. The company declined to comment on customer pricing; separately, TrendForce forecasts conventional DRAM contract prices rising 10–15% Q/Q in Q4. (CTEE)

Japan’s competition regulator began inspecting Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory over suspected coordination of beer-price increases. All four confirmed the investigation and said they were cooperating. (Bloomberg)

Shell’s Q3 refining margin jumped to a record $42 a barrel from $24 in Q2, far above its previous quarterly record of $28.04 in 2022. (WSJ)

HSBC plans to cut about half the management and specialist roles in its UK wealth business and close to 70% of financial advisers, people familiar said. Consultation is underway, with affected staff expected to leave at month-end. (FT)

Porsche plans to lift the average price of its top models roughly 20% to more than €330,000 by 2030 and cut development costs and model variants by 20%. It retained its 2030 operating-margin target of 10–15% and aims to lower breakeven volume below 200,000 vehicles. (FT)

The Dutch government plans to reduce its ABN Amro stake to 10.5% from 20.7% through a share-sale programme. (Bloomberg)

BHP agreed to sell its shuttered Kambalda nickel concentrator and associated land and mineral rights to Gold Fields for an undisclosed price. A decision on BHP’s remaining Nickel West assets is expected by February. (Bloomberg)

Aramco is preparing a potential carve-out of its domestic gas business under “Project Gamma”, which could lead to an IPO, people familiar said. The exploratory plan does not include its international LNG assets. (FT)

QatarEnergy secured a $3bn, five-year loan from four Chinese banks at SOFR plus 50bp for general working capital, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar. (Bloomberg)

PDVSA halted Venezuela’s 310,000-barrel-a-day Cardón refinery after a ruptured gas line serving boilers sparked a fire. It said the blaze was contained without injuries or major damage, while operations remained under evaluation. (Reuters)

Sequoia National Park (located in #California, United States) is an impressive national park renowned worldwide for its giant sequoia trees, which include the largest trees on Earth.

The Giant #SequoiaTrees: The park takes its name from the giant sequoia trees.
Its most famous resident is #GeneralSherman, the largest tree in the world by volume.
It stands nearly 84 meters tall and measures over 30 meters in circumference at the base.

Situated in the southern #SierraNevada, the park offers a spectacular landscape of deep canyons, wild rivers, vast mountain meadows, and granite monoliths. A major highlight is #MountWhitney —the highest mountain in the contiguous United States —located on the border with the adjacent #KingsCanyonNationalPark.
The park is popular among nature lovers and hikers.
Notable attractions include the #GiantForest (the grove containing the highest concentration of giant trees), #MoroRock (a climbable rock formation offering panoramic views), and #CrystalCave (an underground limestone cave).

Sequoia National Park is almost always mentioned in the same breath as Kings Canyon National Park, which lies directly to the north and merges seamlessly with it.
The two parks are often managed and visited as a single unit.

text:
長い距離を走っていると、あれほど頼りにしていた甘いジェルが、急に「もういらない」になることがあります。
舌が疲れて、味が分からなくなったから？　どうも、そう単純な話ではなさそうです🏃

■ 2時間、同じジェルを食べ続けた実験
2024年に、オーストラリアのモナシュ大学のチームが、こんな実験を発表しました(Martinezら)。
参加したのは、大会に出ている市民レベルの持久系アスリート20人です。
平均35歳で、女性は2割でした。
実験室で、息は上がるけれど無理のない強さで、2時間走ってもらいます。
その間、同じチョコレート味のジェルを20分ごとに1袋ずつ食べ続けました。
1袋に含まれる炭水化物(体を動かす燃料になる糖など)は30gです。

結果、20人中9人(45%)が、走っている途中で「味に飽きた」と答えました。
飽きは、走り始めて1時間ほどから増えていき、100〜120分ごろにいちばん強くなりました。
ただし、その多くは軽いもので、強い飽きを感じたのは20人中3人でした。
裏を返すと、半分以上の人は、2時間ではほとんど飽きなかったことになります。

面白いのは、このジェルはもともと「飽きにくさ」を意識して作られていたことです。
甘さが控えめな糖(マルトデキストリン)を主な材料に選んでいました。
それでも、2時間でおよそ半分の人に飽きが出たわけです。

この研究の注意点も書いておきます。
比べるためのグループはなく、試したジェルも1種類の味だけでした。
気温23℃の実験室で、トレッドミルを使った結果です。
もともと新しいジェルの「食べやすさ」を確かめる研究で、飽きはその中の1項目でした。

■ では、舌が鈍っているのか？
ここで、日本の研究を一つ。
京都女子大学などのチームが、2024年に発表した実験です(Narukawaら)。
参加したのは、運動選手ではない若い女性20人(平均21.6歳)。
自転車こぎ50分と、味のテスト10分を1セットにして、4回くり返しました。
テストは運動前にも1回やったので、全部で5回です。
運動中に口にしてよいのは水だけでした。

味見に使ったのは、市販のスポーツドリンクの粉を、溶かす量を変えて4つの濃さにしたものです。
すると、いちばん濃い液(ふつうの1.25倍)の味が、最後のセットでは運動前より強く感じられました。
濃い液を好む傾向も、セットを重ねるごとに強くなりました。
一方で、うすめの液では、はっきりした変化は出ませんでした。
香りの感じ方も変わりませんでした。

つまり、少なくともこの実験では「長く運動すると舌が鈍る」という結果にはなりませんでした。
むしろ、濃い味をより強く感じていたのです。

注意点は、運動をしない日と比べる条件が無かったことです。
変化のすべてが運動のせいだとは言い切れません。
また、若い女性だけの結果なので、年齢や性別、鍛え方が違えば結果も変わるかもしれません。
それに、この実験は「同じ物を食べ続けた」わけではありません。
測ったのは飽きではなく、味の感じ方です。

■ 飽きの正体は「うれしさ」の低下？
では、飽きは何が起きているのか。
ヒントになるのが、1981年の有名な実験です(Rollsら)。
食べ物の「飽き」の研究では、今も出発点として引用されます。

大学生32人に、8種類の食べ物を少しずつ味見して、「好ましさ」を採点してもらいました。
そのあと、8種類のうち1つだけを、満足するまで食べてもらいます。
2分後にもう一度採点すると、食べた物の点数だけが大きく下がりました。
−2〜+2の採点で、食べた物は平均で約1点の低下です。
食べていない物は、約0.3点しか下がりませんでした。

ここがポイントです。
もし舌そのものが疲れたのなら、食べていない物の点数も同じように下がるはずです。
でも実際に下がったのは、ほぼ「食べた物」だけでした。

別の実験(学生24人)では、満腹まで食べた直後に、予告なしで2皿目を出しました。
2皿目が別の食べ物だった人たちは、同じ物を出された人たちの約2倍の量(カロリー)を食べました。
「お腹いっぱい」でも「別の物なら入る」。いわゆる別腹に近い現象です。
研究者はこれを「感覚特異的満腹」と名づけました。
難しい名前ですが、要は「食べ続けた味だけ、うれしくなくなる」ということです。

ただしこれは、走っていない学生の昼食での実験です。
1皿目と2皿目で人を分けて比べた小さな実験でもあります。
「味を変えれば必ず2倍食べられる」という意味ではありません。

■ 3つをつなげると
3つの研究は、対象も測ったものも違います。
それをふまえて、無理のない範囲でまとめると、こうなります。
・同じジェルを2時間食べ続けると、半分近くの人に軽い飽きが出た(2024年)
・長い運動のあとでも、舌が鈍ったという結果にはならなかった(2024年)
・飽きは、食べ続けた「その味」だけに起きやすい(1981年)

ここから言えそうな、今日からの一手はこれです。
長い練習の日に、「味の方向」が違う補給食を2〜3種類、ポケットに入れて試してみる。
甘い、しょっぱい、ほろ苦い、のように方向を変えるのがコツです。

ただし、レース中に味を変えると飽きが減るのかを、直接確かめた実験はまだ見当たりません。
ここは研究者にとっても、これからの宿題です。
おなかとの相性は人それぞれなので、本番ではなく練習で試すのが基本です。

■ ここからは研究とは別の、道具の話
そこで面白いのが、米国のジェルブランドVFUEL(ブイフューエル)の「メープルベーコン味」です。
エナジージェルなのに、メープルの甘さにベーコンのスモーキーな塩気を重ねています。
思わず二度見しそうな味です。

VFUELは2011年、米国コロラド州エステスパークで、ウルトラランナーの仲間たちが始めたブランドです。
ブランドの説明では、創業者は2008年に標高の高い100マイルレース(リードビル100)を走りました。
29時間で58袋のジェルを食べて、ひどい胃の不調に苦しんだそうです。
「10時間後でも食べ続けられる味」を目標にしているのは、この経験からだといいます。

使っているのは、主にコロラドの山岳ウルトラ(リードビル、ハードロックなど)を走る人たちです。
日本では2026年4月、トレイルランニング用品の試走イベント「TOAD 2026」に登場しました。
ランニング専門店STRIDE LABのブースで、試食・販売が行われています。
日本上陸を記念した催しも開かれています。
国内のレビューはまだ少なく、トレイルランナーの間で名前が出始めた段階です。

先に、気になる点から書きます。
・1包あたりの値段は、国内の定番ジェルより高めです。
・炭水化物は1包27.5g。最近増えた40gクラスのジェルよりは少なめです。
・カフェインが入っています(量の表示はありません)。夜の練習や、カフェインに弱い人は注意。
・中鎖脂肪酸油(MCT)入りです。慣れない人はおなかがゆるくなることがあります。
・MCTで速く走れる、という確かな研究は見当たりません。
・ベーコン味は、正直、好みが分かれます。

それでも、このジェルには他にない良さがあります。

1つ目は、甘いジェルが続いたあとに「方向の違う味」を挟めることです。
食塩相当量は1包0.20g。同じシリーズの抹茶味(0.01g)のおよそ20倍です。
原材料に食塩を加えていて、甘さの後ろにはっきり塩気が来ます。
甘い味が3本続いたあとの4本目を、「またこれか」ではない1本にできます。

2つ目は、シリーズで味の方向がばらけていることです。
メープルベーコン(甘じょっぱい)、抹茶(ほろ苦い)、マウンテンベリー、クールシトラス。
甘い味の色違いだけでなく、しょっぱい方向や苦い方向まで、1つのシリーズにそろっています。
ポケットの中で、甘い・しょっぱい・苦いを並べておけます。

3つ目は、40gの小袋で、137kcalを持ち運べることです。
袋には「MADE IN JAPAN」とあり、米国ブランドですが日本で作られています。
原材料は、でんぷんを分解した糖やぶどう糖が中心で、果糖の表示はありません。
果糖入りのジェルが合わなかった人にとって、試してみる選択肢の一つになります。

使う場面を一つ描いてみます。
フルマラソンの30km付近。ポケットの残りが、どれも同じ甘い味だったとします。
取り出す手が、少し重くなるかもしれません。
そこに1本だけ、甘じょっぱい味が入っていたら。
次の補給が「またあれか」ではなく、「次はあの変な味だ」という小さな楽しみに変わります。
長い練習の日も、ポケットの中身を考える時間が少し楽しくなるはずです。

向いているのは、長い時間走る人、甘いジェルが続くと手が止まりがちな人です。
「補給食は味より値段」という人や、1本で炭水化物をたくさん摂りたい人には向きません。

甘いジェルが続く日の「次の1本」を、方向の違う味にしておける。
それだけで、長い練習のポケットの中身は結構変わります。

・Narukawa M, Nojiri K, Matsuda R, Murata M, Sakate S, Kuga S, Ue H. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 2024(DOI: 10.1080/15502783.2024.2441769)
・Rolls BJ, Rolls ET, Rowe EA, Sweeney K. Physiology & Behavior, 1981(DOI: 10.1016/0031-9384(81)90310-3)

―――

If you've ever run long, you may know the moment: the sweet gel you were relying on suddenly becomes "no thanks."
Is it because your tongue gets tired and stops tasting things? Research suggests it's not that simple 🏃

■ Two hours, the same gel every 20 minutes
In 2024, a team at Monash University in Australia published this experiment (Martinez et al.).
The participants were 20 recreational endurance athletes who compete in races.
Their average age was 35, and about one in five were women.
In the lab, they ran for two hours at a steady, moderate effort (60% of their maximal aerobic capacity).
Every 20 minutes, they ate one serving of the same chocolate-flavored gel.
Each serving carried 30 g of carbohydrate, the sugars and starches your muscles burn as fuel.

Nine of the 20 runners (45%) reported "taste fatigue" — getting tired of the flavor — during the run.
It started building about an hour in and peaked around 100 to 120 minutes.
But for most, it was mild. Only 3 of the 20 rated it as strong.
Put the other way round: more than half barely tired of the taste at all within two hours.

Here's the interesting part: this gel had been designed with taste fatigue in mind.
The researchers chose maltodextrin, a carbohydrate with a low sweetness, as the main ingredient.
Even so, close to half the runners started tiring of it within two hours.

A few caveats.
There was no comparison group, and only one flavor was tested.
It was a treadmill run in a 23°C lab.
The study's main goal was to check how well a new gel was tolerated; taste fatigue was one item among many.

■ So is the tongue going numb?
Here's a study from Japan.
A team including Kyoto Women's University published it in 2024 (Narukawa et al.).
The participants were 20 young women who were not athletes (average age 21.6).
They did four rounds of 50 minutes of stationary cycling followed by a 10-minute taste test.
They also took the test once before exercising, so five tests in total.
During exercise, they were allowed only water.

The samples were a commercial sports-drink powder mixed at four different strengths.
By the final round, the strongest version (1.25 times the normal strength) tasted more intense than it had before exercise.
The preference for stronger versions also grew as the rounds went on.
The weaker versions showed no clear change.
Smell perception did not change either.

So at least in this experiment, long exercise did not dull the sense of taste.
If anything, the strong drink tasted stronger.

The caveat: there was no comparison day without exercise.
We can't say every change was caused by the exercise itself.
And because all participants were young women, results could differ by age, sex, or training level.
Also, this study didn't have people eat the same thing over and over.
It measured how strongly things tasted, not whether people got tired of them.

■ Maybe fatigue is a drop in "enjoyment"
So what is taste fatigue?
A famous 1981 experiment offers a clue (Rolls et al.).
It is still a starting point for research on getting tired of foods.

Thirty-two university students tasted small bites of eight foods and rated how pleasant each one was.
Then they ate just one of the eight until they were satisfied.
Two minutes later, they rated all eight again. Only the food they had eaten dropped sharply.
On a scale from −2 to +2, the eaten food fell by about 1 point on average.
The foods they hadn't eaten fell by only about 0.3.

That's the key.
If the tongue itself were worn out, the uneaten foods should have dropped just as much.
Instead, the drop was mostly limited to the food they had eaten.

In a second experiment with 24 students, a surprise second course was served right after they'd eaten their fill.
Those given a different food ate about twice as much (in calories) as those given the same food again.
"I'm full" — yet "there's room for something else." Many of us call it a dessert stomach.
The researchers named this "sensory-specific satiety."
It sounds technical, but it simply means: you stop enjoying the flavor you've been eating, and only that one.

But this was students eating lunch, not running.
And the second experiment compared different groups of people in a small study.
It doesn't mean "switch flavors and you'll always eat twice as much."

■ Putting the three together
The three studies looked at different people and measured different things.
With that in mind, a careful summary goes like this:
・Eating the same gel for two hours led nearly half of runners to mild taste fatigue (2024).
・Even after long exercise, the sense of taste did not appear dulled (2024).
・Getting tired of food tends to be specific to the flavor you've been eating (1981).

One thing you could try today:
On your next long training day, carry two or three fuels that go in different flavor directions.
Think sweet, salty, and slightly bitter, rather than three kinds of sweet.

That said, I couldn't find any experiment that directly tested whether switching flavors during a race reduces taste fatigue.
That's still an open question for researchers.
Every stomach is different, so try new fuel in training, not on race day.

■ Separate from the research: a piece of gear
Which brings me to a fun one: the Maple Bacon flavor from US gel brand VFUEL.
It's an energy gel that layers smoky, salty bacon notes over maple sweetness.
It's the kind of flavor that makes you look twice.

VFUEL was started in 2011 in Estes Park, Colorado, by a group of ultrarunner friends.
According to the brand, the founder ran the high-altitude Leadville 100 in 2008.
The founder ate 58 gels in 29 hours and suffered serious stomach trouble.
The brand says that's why it aims for flavors you can still stomach ten hours in.

It's mainly been used by people running Colorado mountain ultras such as Leadville and Hardrock.
In Japan, it appeared in April 2026 at TOAD 2026, a trail-running gear demo event, with tastings and sales at the booth of running store STRIDE LAB.
There was also an event to mark the Japan launch.
Reviews in Japan are still few; it's just starting to get mentioned among trail runners.

First, the drawbacks:
・Per pouch, it costs more than the standard gels sold in Japan.
・Each pouch has 27.5 g of carbohydrate, less than the 40 g-class gels that have become common.
・It contains caffeine (the amount isn't listed). Be careful with evening runs or if you're caffeine-sensitive.
・It contains MCT oil. If you're not used to it, it can loosen your stomach.
・I couldn't find solid research showing that MCT makes you run faster.
・Honestly, bacon flavor won't be for everyone.

Even so, this gel does something few others do.

First, it lets you slot a "different direction" of flavor in after a run of sweet gels.
Each pouch contains 0.20 g of salt equivalent — about 20 times the matcha flavor in the same line (0.01 g).
Salt is added to the recipe, so a clear savory note follows the sweetness.
After three sweet gels in a row, your fourth doesn't have to be "this again."

Second, the lineup spreads across flavor directions.
Maple Bacon (sweet and salty), Matcha Green Tea (slightly bitter), Mountain Berry, and Cool Citrus.
Instead of just different shades of sweet, one line covers salty and bitter directions too.
You can carry sweet, salty, and bitter side by side in your pocket.

Third, each small 40 g pouch carries 137 kcal.
The pouch says "MADE IN JAPAN": it's an American brand, made in Japan.
The main ingredients are starch-derived sugars and glucose, and no fructose is listed.
If fructose-containing gels haven't worked for you, it's one option to try.

Picture this.
You're around 30 km into a marathon. Every gel left in your pocket is the same sweet flavor.
Reaching for the next one might feel a little heavy.
Now imagine one of them is sweet-and-salty.
Your next refuel changes from "that again" to "next up, the weird one" — a small thing to look forward to.
Even on long training days, deciding what goes in your pocket gets a bit more fun.

It suits people who run for hours and tend to stall on sweet gels.
It's not for you if fuel is all about price, or if you want as much carbohydrate as possible per pouch.

On days full of sweet gels, you can make "the next one" a different direction of flavor.
That alone changes what's in your long-run pocket more than you'd think.
Check it out 👇
