text:
Michigan's Little AI Secret: Is It Becoming the Midwest's AI Powerhouse?

When most people think about the centers of artificial intelligence, Michigan probably isn't the first place that comes to mind. California has Silicon Valley, Virginia has one of the world's largest concentrations of data centers, Texas is attracting enormous new campuses, and Seattle has its collection of technology giants. Michigan still brings to mind Detroit, automobiles, heavy manufacturing and the industrial economy of the last century.

That image may be badly out of date. Michigan has something the AI industry increasingly needs more than another office full of software engineers: enormous amounts of reliable electricity, existing industrial infrastructure and several nuclear sites capable of producing—or potentially producing—much more power. At the same time, the companies consuming extraordinary quantities of electricity are beginning to arrive.

That combination raises an interesting question. Michigan may never challenge Silicon Valley as the place where the newest AI models are invented, but could it become one of the places where the physical AI economy is actually built?

AI Is Quietly Becoming an Electricity Business

The first stage of the AI boom revolved around computer chips. Nvidia GPUs became the precious commodity, and technology companies competed to assemble enough computing power to train increasingly capable models. Chips still matter enormously, but another bottleneck has emerged: there isn't much value in owning hundreds of thousands of GPUs if you cannot find enough electricity to run them.

MISO, which manages much of the electrical grid across the central United States, expects data centers to become the primary driver of electricity-demand growth in its territory. Its forecasts have data-center demand climbing toward roughly 22 gigawatts by 2030. This isn't the gradual increase utilities have traditionally planned around. Individual hyperscale campuses can require a gigawatt or more, meaning a single customer can suddenly appear with electricity requirements comparable to a sizable city.

That changes the economics of old power plants. A nuclear reactor built during the industrial age can suddenly become a strategic asset for the AI age because it produces enormous quantities of electricity around the clock. Michigan happens to have several of those assets already sitting beside the Great Lakes.

Michigan Already Has a Nuclear Foundation

Michigan's existing nuclear foundation begins with DTE's Fermi 2 near Monroe and the two reactors at D.C. Cook near Bridgman. Cook's Unit 1 produces approximately 1,084 MW and Unit 2 approximately 1,194 MW, giving the site about 2,278 MW of generating capacity. Fermi 2 contributes roughly another gigawatt-scale reactor. Before Palisades returns to service, Michigan therefore already has several gigawatts of nuclear generating capacity.

D.C. Cook is especially important to northeast Indiana because it is owned by Indiana Michigan Power, which is headquartered in Fort Wayne. The two reactors may physically sit along Lake Michigan, but they are part of the utility system serving Indiana and Michigan. I&M says its Indiana peak electricity demand could rise from approximately 2,800 MW in 2024 to more than 7,000 MW around 2030. That is more than a doubling of peak demand in only a few years.

I&M is consequently preparing to seek another 20 years of operating authority for both Cook reactors. The NRC lists the company's subsequent-license-renewal application for early 2027. If ultimately approved, subsequent renewal can allow reactors to operate for as much as 80 years, which could keep these enormous Michigan generating assets contributing to the regional grid well into the middle of the century.

That matters because the cheapest new nuclear megawatt may increasingly be one that doesn't require building an entirely new reactor. Keeping a well-maintained existing plant operating longer, replacing equipment and uprating its output can potentially add dependable electricity far sooner than beginning with an empty field.

Fermi Has More Hiding Under the Hood

DTE Energy is taking exactly that approach with Fermi 2. Its new long-term resource plan includes a proposed 177-MW increase in the reactor's generating capability. An additional 177 MW doesn't sound spectacular beside announcements for multi-gigawatt data centers, but it is substantial electricity obtained without constructing another complete nuclear station. DTE's broader plan also calls for major additions of natural gas, renewable generation and storage as it prepares for much higher electricity demand.

Fermi has another asset that is considerably larger and much less discussed. In 2015, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued DTE a combined construction-and-operating license for Fermi 3, an ESBWR reactor proposed for the existing Fermi site. Michigan's nuclear feasibility study describes the project at approximately 1,530 MW.

DTE has not committed to building Fermi 3, so it would be wrong to count that electricity as future Michigan capacity. Nevertheless, an already licensed large-reactor project at an established nuclear site looks different today than it did before AI began consuming electricity by the gigawatt. The land, nuclear history, transmission connections and much of the regulatory groundwork already exist. Michigan's own nuclear study specifically identified Fermi as an unusual opportunity for additional nuclear development because substantial work has already been done there.

The value of that option becomes clearer when you look at what is happening on the demand side.

The Data Centers Are Already Arriving

DTE told investors in late September that it already has 2.4 GW of executed data-center agreements. About 1.4 GW is associated with the Oracle project already approved and under construction, while another 1 GW agreement involves Google. More strikingly, DTE says it has another 5 to 6 GW of prospective data-center opportunities, including about 2 GW in advanced discussions.

Those numbers are enormous. If the entire pipeline were eventually built—and there is no guarantee that it will be—the potential data-center demand facing one Michigan utility would be comparable to the output of several large nuclear reactors.

The first big example is already under construction. OpenAI, together with Oracle and its development partners, broke ground in June on the 1-GW Stargate campus in Saline Township. OpenAI says the infrastructure and energy required for the project are to be paid for by the project rather than passed along to local electricity customers.

Google is pursuing another roughly 1-GW development through DTE in Van Buren Township. Regardless of which particular AI company ultimately becomes the largest, the important number is the electricity demand. Michigan isn't talking about a few computer rooms being added to office buildings. It is confronting industrial facilities that consume power on a scale once associated with steel mills, automobile factories and entire communities.

That is why Michigan's old industrial infrastructure may be becoming an advantage again.

Then There Is Palisades

The most fascinating piece of Michigan's nuclear puzzle may be the plant that was supposed to be dead.

Palisades ceased operating in 2022 and entered the decommissioning process. Holtec International is now attempting something never before completed in the United States: returning a commercial nuclear plant to service after it had entered decommissioning. The federal government backed the project with a loan of up to $1.52 billion, and the Department of Energy says the restored plant would provide approximately 800 MW of firm generating capacity and could operate until at least 2051, subject to NRC approvals.

This isn't merely a proposal on a drawing board. Fuel loading began in August, and Holtec reported in September that Palisades had been reconnected to its 345-kV switchyard, which will eventually carry electricity from the reactor back onto the transmission grid. The plant still has restart work, testing and regulatory requirements to complete before it can be counted as operating generation, but this project is well beyond the discussion stage.

Holtec's ambitions at Palisades also extend beyond restarting the original reactor. On September 30, it submitted the Preliminary Safety Analysis Report for two planned SMR-300 reactors at the same site. Together, those two units are designed to provide another 680 MW. If the existing plant successfully returns and the two small modular reactors are eventually licensed and built, Palisades could evolve from a decommissioning project into a nuclear campus approaching 1.5 GW.

That may be the most important lesson in Michigan's position. Instead of asking where an entirely new nuclear facility could be placed, the state can ask what more can be done with nuclear sites that already exist.

Michigan's Advantage May Be Optionality

Put these pieces together and the picture becomes much more interesting. Michigan already has the Cook and Fermi reactors. Palisades could add roughly 800 MW if its restart succeeds. Fermi 2 has a proposed 177-MW uprate. Palisades has another 680 MW of proposed SMRs working through the regulatory process. Fermi 3 remains an already licensed option for roughly another 1.5 GW if DTE ever decides the economics justify building it.

Not all of those projects will necessarily happen, and they certainly won't happen simultaneously. The important point is that Michigan has choices. Much of the groundwork needed to produce substantially more firm electricity has already been laid, sometimes decades ago.

That optionality becomes valuable when data centers move much faster than power plants. A technology company can decide to build a giant computing campus in a few years. A completely new large nuclear station can take much longer. Existing reactors, uprates, restarts and additions at established nuclear sites offer ways of shortening at least part of that mismatch.

This Doesn't Stop at the Michigan Border

The effects could spread throughout the Midwest because the electrical and industrial systems don't stop at state lines. Cook sits in Michigan but belongs to a Fort Wayne-based utility. Indiana is experiencing its own surge in data-center construction. Ohio is attracting enormous technology investment, while Chicago remains one of America's major telecommunications, financial and transportation centers. All of them sit within interconnected regional power and supply networks.

That creates the possibility of something larger than isolated data-center developments. Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois could gradually form a Midwestern AI industrial corridor in which different states provide different pieces of the same enormous machine. Some locations will host the computers, others the power generation, and still others the factories producing electrical equipment, cooling systems, transformers and construction materials.

Fort Wayne is already close enough to see this happening. Google is developing its large data-center campus here, while I&M is simultaneously planning for Indiana peak demand to rise above 7,000 MW around 2030. The fact that I&M's largest generating assets happen to be two nuclear reactors just across the Michigan line suddenly becomes much more important than it appeared a decade ago.

The economic effects also extend far beyond programmers. Gigawatt-scale computing requires electricians, pipefitters, operating engineers, concrete crews, turbine technicians, nuclear workers, transmission crews, security personnel and enormous quantities of electrical equipment. Transformers, switchgear, substations, cooling systems and transmission lines have to be manufactured, transported, installed and maintained.

That is an economy the Midwest understands. AI may appear on the screen as software, but the infrastructure behind it increasingly resembles a massive industrial construction program.

There Is Still a Catch

None of this guarantees that Michigan becomes an AI powerhouse. Electricity demand projections can change, data-center projects can be canceled, nuclear projects can be delayed, and building enough transmission to connect all of this is itself a major undertaking. DTE is also planning to retire roughly 3 GW of coal capacity while simultaneously adding generation and serving enormous new customers, so some of Michigan's new investment will replace retiring generation rather than simply adding to what already exists.

There is also a financial question that every state chasing data centers eventually has to confront: who pays if the promised demand doesn't materialize? Utilities can build billions of dollars of generation and transmission infrastructure around projected loads. If an AI company later changes strategy, the physical infrastructure doesn't disappear with the computer order. Contracts that require large customers to shoulder the costs they create therefore may become every bit as important as the power plants themselves.

Those complications don't diminish Michigan's opportunity. They explain why the opportunity exists. AI has reached a scale where software companies increasingly have to think like industrial companies. They need dependable electricity, land, transmission, construction labor and long-lived infrastructure.

Michigan's Little AI Secret

So is Michigan becoming the next AI powerhouse? Perhaps the more useful question is what kind of powerhouse it could become.

Michigan probably isn't going to replace Silicon Valley as the center where America's leading AI models are invented. It doesn't have to. The next stage of the AI race increasingly depends upon who can provide the physical infrastructure necessary to operate those models at enormous scale, and that plays much more naturally to Michigan's existing strengths.

The state has large operating nuclear plants, a retired reactor being brought back from the dead, proposed small modular reactors, an existing reactor targeted for an uprate, an already licensed site for another large reactor and several gigawatts of data-center demand either contracted or under discussion. Meanwhile, neighboring Indiana is seeing its own data-center boom, including Google's enormous Fort Wayne investment, while the utility serving Fort Wayne owns Michigan's largest nuclear plant.

For decades, America's technology economy was largely discussed in terms of who could invent the next computer, write the next program or design the next semiconductor. Artificial intelligence is adding another question to that list: who can actually supply enough electricity and build enough physical infrastructure to run all of it?

Michigan may have spent the last century building exactly the kinds of things the digital economy suddenly needs again. If that continues, the real story won't simply be that Michigan attracted a few AI data centers. It will be that the industrial Midwest discovered a new customer for the infrastructure and skills it already knows how to build.

And if Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois begin feeding one another's power, construction, manufacturing and computing investments, the biggest surprise of the AI boom may be that one of its most important centers isn't Silicon Valley at all.

It may be the Midwest.

text:
An Iran-linked spy group used a fake job offer to go after a tech worker in Iraq's telecom and aviation sector.

The "recruiter" claimed to be hiring for Dubai Airports and sent over a coding test as a Visual Studio project. Opening it was enough. Visual Studio runs build steps in the background as soon as a project loads, and that's where the attackers planted their code. Nobody had to run anything.

From there the malware loaded itself through a legitimate, Microsoft-signed program and shut off logging that security tools use to catch this kind of thing.

Then it checked a private GitHub repo about once a minute for instructions, with a backup channel hidden in public GitHub Issues. To anyone watching the network, that looks like a developer doing normal work, and no company is going to block GitHub.

That's why blocking websites doesn't stop attacks like this. You catch them by watching what happens on the machine: a Microsoft program running from the wrong folder, or a code editor launching programs it has no reason to touch.

If a recruiter ever sends you a project to open, open it in a VM.

Unit 42's full report: https://t.co/h0TVoYKIuh

Gemini what is the responsibility of a president of the united states?

Simply put, the President of the United States has two main jobs: running the government and leading the American people.
Here is the simplest breakdown of what is expected:

💼 The Official Job (By Law)
•Enforce Laws: Make sure the country follows the laws passed by Congress.
•Lead the Military: Act as the top boss (Commander-in-Chief) of all U.S. troops.
•Handle Foreign Countries: Meet with world leaders and make deals (treaties) with other nations.
•Approve Bills: Sign new bills into laws, or veto (reject) them.

🤝 The Unofficial Job (By Custom)
•Comfort the Nation: Speak to the country and offer help during disasters or national tragedies. 
•Fix the Economy: Keep jobs up and prices (like gas and groceries) down.
•Represent America: Act as the face and symbol of the United States to the rest of the world.

is President Trump doing all this

Yes, President Trump is using his official powers to do these things, but because of how the government works, there is a big difference between what he can do completely on his own and what he is promising to do later.
Here is the simple breakdown of what he is actually doing right now versus what is still just a plan:

🛠️ What he is doing right now (On His Own)
Because Congress is away, Trump is using executive orders and federal agencies to bypass them. These are real, active actions:
•The Healthcare Checks: He successfully ordered the Treasury Department to start mailing out the $500 Obamacare refunds and the $90 Medicare credits to seniors this month.
•The Diesel Tax Break: He signed the emergency order allowing truck drivers to use cheaper, untaxed "red-dyed" diesel on public highways to cut shipping costs.
•The Tech Name Change: He officially ordered the Department of Justice to switch the legal phrase "artificial intelligence" to "super intelligence."

📋 What he cannot do yet (Needs Congress)
Some of his biggest announcements are campaign promises or proposals that he legally cannot finish without a vote from Congress:
•The $5,000 "Trump Dividend": He cannot hand out this money on his own. He needs Congress to write a bill and approve the billions of dollars to pay for it, which is why he is asking voters to elect Republicans in November to help him pass it.

•The National Gas Tax Holiday: He asked for the federal gas tax to be paused, but only Congress has the power to suspend that tax. For now, only a few states have paused their own state-level taxes.

text:
In 2000 Jim Chanos shorted Enron, the most admired company on Wall Street. He was not betting on fraud. He was betting on one number nobody else would look at.

Every analyst rated Enron a strong buy. It always beat earnings. It was called the future of energy.

Chanos read one filing. Even if you believed every number Enron reported, the company earned about 6% on its capital. Six cents for every dollar it put to work.

So he asked the question no one else asked. Why is the whole market paying a tech multiple for an energy fund that earns 6%?

He invited the bullish analysts to lunch and walked them through it. They shrugged. The company always makes good, they said. It always beats.

He shorted it in November 2000 and added all the way down, because every piece of bad news was worse than the last.

Near the end, a rival named Dynegy offered to buy Enron. On the call an analyst asked its CEO about Enron's accounting. He said he had looked closely, and it was the same as his own.

Chanos shorted Dynegy the next morning. It fell 90%, from $28 to $3.

He never needed to prove fraud. He just read the number everyone was too excited to read.

text:
Indiana's Nuclear Ambition: Mike Braun Wants Indiana Ready Before the Reactors Arrive

Indiana doesn't have a commercial nuclear power plant of its own. That makes Governor Mike Braun's nuclear strategy a little unusual, because Indiana is behaving increasingly like a state that expects nuclear power to become a significant part of its economy.

The latest step came this week when Braun opened applications for Indiana's Advanced Nuclear Ready Communities Program. Instead of waiting for a nuclear developer to pick a location and then beginning years of local debate, the state wants communities to decide beforehand whether they are interested, educate residents, examine potential sites, develop a workforce plan and work their way toward being able to tell a developer: we're ready to talk.

New Haven is already holding a public meeting about the program, while Fort Wayne's mayor's office told 21Alive that the city is reviewing it and wants to remain involved in discussions that could bring investment and jobs to the region. That makes this more than an Indianapolis policy exercise. Northeast Indiana is already being drawn into the conversation.

Braun Is Building the Pieces Before the Plant

The Nuclear Ready program has three stages: Nuclear Aware, Nuclear Prepared and Nuclear Ready. Communities progress by organizing local stakeholders, examining potential sites and infrastructure, preparing workers and eventually establishing more formal relationships with developers. Indiana says the program is the first state designation system of its kind.

That tells us quite a bit about Braun's approach. He isn't announcing that Indiana will build five reactors by some arbitrary date. He is trying to remove the obstacles that normally consume the first several years of a nuclear project before a developer ever pours concrete.

Braun started putting that structure together shortly after taking office. In April 2025 he created the Nuclear Indiana Coalition, bringing together state agencies, utilities, nuclear companies and universities to develop recommendations for nuclear deployment. He also created a broader energy task force that has made nuclear deployment part of Indiana's long-term strategy for meeting rapidly increasing electricity demand.

The state has also changed its laws. Indiana enacted legislation allowing utilities to recover approved development costs associated with small modular reactor projects, including engineering, federal licensing, environmental studies and early site work. Utilities can recover 80% of approved development expenses through a rate mechanism, with the remaining 20% deferred to a future rate case. One version of the law specifically encourages utilities to bring in outside partners—including large electricity customers—to share the financial burden.

That's important because nuclear's biggest problem isn't producing electricity once a plant exists. It is getting somebody to accept the enormous financial risk involved in being first to build one.

Indiana has also created a tax credit for companies manufacturing small modular reactors in the state. In other words, Braun isn't looking only at generating electricity. Indiana wants part of the nuclear manufacturing supply chain as well.

Indiana Has Something Nuclear Developers Need: Old Coal Plants

Perhaps Indiana's biggest advantage is sitting in places most people would consider part of the state's energy past.

Coal plants.

Purdue University and the Indiana Office of Energy Development identified eight retired or retiring coal sites that deserve further investigation for small modular reactors. The state's energy plan estimates that reusing these locations could reduce SMR project costs by roughly 7% to 26% because much of the expensive infrastructure already exists.

A coal plant already has high-capacity transmission lines, access roads, industrial land, water infrastructure and a community accustomed to hosting a large generating station. It may also have a workforce familiar with power generation.

Instead of abandoning that investment when the coal units retire, Indiana could replace one form of around-the-clock generation with another.

We are already seeing this at Rockport in southern Indiana. Indiana Michigan Power is evaluating its existing Rockport power-plant property as a potential small modular reactor site and has pursued federal funding for early site-permit work involving GE Hitachi's BWRX-300 reactor technology.

AES has also examined advanced nuclear deployment at its Petersburg site. Indiana therefore isn't merely drawing hypothetical reactor locations on a state map. Utilities are already looking at actual power-plant properties.

Then AI Changed the Electricity Equation

This is where Braun's nuclear ambitions connect directly to what we were discussing about Michigan.

Indiana's electricity demand is beginning to change dramatically because of data centers, advanced manufacturing and other large industrial projects. The state's own Nuclear Indiana presentation explicitly describes its nuclear effort as part of “Indiana's Action in the AI Race.”

That wording is revealing.

The state understands that attracting AI investment isn't simply about offering tax incentives and inexpensive land. A gigawatt-scale data center needs something close to a gigawatt-scale power strategy behind it.

Fort Wayne is already watching Google build a massive data-center campus. Meta is developing its enormous project at the LEAP district near Lebanon. Eli Lilly has committed billions to manufacturing and research facilities in the same region. Indiana University and the state are pursuing additional high-performance computing infrastructure.

Those projects eventually collide with the same question:

Where does the electricity come from?

Natural gas will almost certainly be part of Indiana's answer, and renewables and storage will remain part of the mix as well. Braun describes his policy as “all of the above.” But nuclear offers something particularly attractive to industrial and data-center customers: enormous quantities of electricity available around the clock without depending upon sunshine or wind.

That is why Indiana is doing the preparation now, even though most advanced reactors aren't commercially ready for mass deployment.

Indiana May Get Its First Reactor Sooner Than Expected

There is another interesting development that makes all of this less theoretical.

The federal government announced in September that Naval Weapons Station Crane will receive an advanced nuclear microreactor by September 2028. The project is intended to provide independent, continuous electricity for critical military operations and would become Indiana's first power-producing nuclear reactor.

Crane isn't going to power Indianapolis or Fort Wayne. This is a military microreactor rather than a commercial utility plant.

But it could give Indiana something valuable before the larger SMR industry gets moving: people with actual experience constructing, regulating, operating and supporting advanced nuclear technology inside the state.

That workforce doesn't disappear at Crane's fence.

Neither does the supply chain.

If Indiana eventually begins building commercial SMRs at Rockport, Petersburg or another site, having an existing advanced nuclear project in the state could become useful experience.

There Are Real Risks

None of this means Indiana will have a fleet of small modular reactors five years from now.

SMRs still face serious economic questions. America's first wave of advanced-reactor projects must prove that the technology can actually be built at the prices and schedules being advertised. First-of-a-kind nuclear projects have historically carried substantial construction and financing risks.

Indiana's own energy plan acknowledges that first-of-a-kind reactor construction costs remain high and that workforce development and community acceptance are significant obstacles. A Purdue survey cited by the state found that 61% of Indiana respondents had never heard of advanced nuclear plants or SMRs, while concerns about accidents and radioactive waste remain significant.

There is also a legitimate debate about who assumes the financial risk. Indiana's laws allow utilities to recover certain approved SMR development costs from customers, including under circumstances where a project is ultimately canceled. Supporters argue that utilities won't spend hundreds of millions developing nuclear projects if every early dollar is placed entirely at risk. Critics argue that ratepayers shouldn't become the financial backstop for experimental projects that might never generate electricity.

That argument will become considerably louder if an Indiana utility proposes an actual multibillion-dollar reactor.

Braun's Real Nuclear Ambition

What makes Braun's strategy interesting is that Indiana isn't waiting for that argument to begin preparing.

The state is identifying old coal sites. It is creating a Nuclear Indiana Coalition. It has changed utility financing laws. It has created nuclear manufacturing incentives. It is working with Purdue on the workforce and engineering side. It is getting communities to decide whether they want nuclear development before developers arrive. Rockport is already being evaluated for SMRs, and Crane is scheduled to receive an advanced microreactor.

Indiana even became an NRC Agreement State on October 1, assuming responsibility for regulating certain radioactive materials previously overseen directly by the federal government. The NRC still regulates commercial nuclear reactors, but Indiana is clearly building more nuclear regulatory experience within state government.

Taken together, this doesn't look like a governor merely saying that he likes nuclear power. It looks like an attempt to build an ecosystem around it.

And the timing may be the most important part.

Michigan already has nuclear reactors and is looking for ways to extend, restart and expand them. Indiana doesn't have that inheritance, so Braun is taking a different route: prepare the sites, communities, laws, workforce and manufacturers now so that when advanced reactors are ready for serious deployment, Indiana isn't starting from zero.

If AI electricity demand continues growing anywhere near current projections, that head start could become extremely valuable.

The Midwest could then develop an interesting division of labor. Michigan has large existing reactors and potential expansions. Indiana has enormous industrial electricity growth, retired coal sites with valuable grid connections, a manufacturing base and a state government actively trying to attract the next generation of reactors.

For a technology that may take a decade to deploy at scale, the states that wait until they desperately need the electricity may already be too late.

Braun appears to have decided that Indiana shouldn't take that chance.

PH, Discord hold talks on tracing online predators, other threats
By Raymond Carl Dela Cruz

MANILA – The Philippine government held talks with social media platform Discord on tracing online predators and other threats, as it moves to strengthen safeguards for young people online.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) said the two sides discussed how Discord can support Philippine authorities in identifying and tracking malicious actors operating on the platform, as well as measures to monitor and address Nihilistic Violent Extremists (NVEs).

Philippine officials led by Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Secretary Henry Aguda and CICC Assistant Secretary Alvin Navarro met virtually with Discord Senior Public Policy Advisor Vasundhara Singh and Discord Head of U.S. Public Policy Allison Peters on Tuesday evening, Manila time.

Aguda expressed his appreciation to Discord officials for their continued cooperation and commitment to working with the Philippine government in addressing online violence.

The discussion, arranged by the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Philippine Embassy in Washington, D.C., was attended by representatives from the CICC, National Bureau of Investigation and Philippine National Police-Anti-Cybercrime Group.

The meeting follows the lifting of the DICT's temporary ban on Discord in September, after the platform committed to cooperating with Philippine authorities on online child safety measures.

Discord had earlier reached out to the CICC after the agency gave it 24 hours to designate a resident agent or local representative who could facilitate Philippine jurisdiction and improve coordination with authorities.

"We decided to grant them an extension since they responded within the 24 hours and we want to give them the opportunity to work with us because what we want is accountability and a clear mechanism for government to coordinate with the platforms," CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Aboy Paraiso said on Sept. 24, 2026.

Discord had also offered to brief the CICC on its Global Teen Experience, which includes age-assurance measures, its Family Center tools and its Kodex system, which allows law enforcement agencies to submit lawful takedown and data requests and receive fast-tracked responses. (PNA)

Workplace Relations Commission awarded maximum amount available citing ‘particularly egregious’ treatment.
By Emmet Malone 
Awards of more than €30,000 each to two Zimbabwean healthcare workers who travelled to Ireland believing they would have jobs, only to find the work did not materialise, have been upheld by the Labour Court.
Tatenda Ncube and Brenda Mubaiwa had both been offered work by Unity Healthcare, which had a contract with Tusla to provide emergency care to vulnerable children, and were told they would be working at a centre in Virginia, Co Cavan.
The pair were among nine Zimbabwean workers to take cases to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), saying they were left without work or money to pay basic bills by the company. They said it only told them almost a year after they arrived that its contract had been cancelled and there would be no work.
The workers said they had been unable to take up alternative employment because of delays by Unity in issuing them with the letters they required under permit regulations to allow them to work for another employer.

text:
I just watched this video, and it reminded me of a dream I had a few days ago that I haven't really been able to get out of my head.

What makes it even stranger for me is that I have died twice during my life here on Earth, and there were parts of this dream that felt remarkably similar to what I experienced during those 2 times.

I don't say that as some attempt to convince anybody that I know what happens after we die, because I don't. I can tell you what I experienced, but I cannot tell you with certainty what those experiences were, and I certainly cannot tell anybody else what they should believe because of them.

I just know that when I was inside of this dream, there was a feeling I recognized.

It was as if I had suddenly been pulled out of this entire experience here on Earth and found myself somewhere else, and somehow I understood that my life here had been something I had gone through in order to learn, experience and become whatever I had intended to become before coming here.

I remember being in this place that seemed incredibly futuristic, and there were 2 individuals there trying to explain to me that I was already done.

They were basically telling me that I had already gone through the entire experience of Earth, that I had accumulated the knowledge and wisdom I was supposed to gain from it, and that there was no reason for me to go back.

I remember absolutely losing it.

I didn't feel relieved.

I didn't feel accomplished.

I didn't care that they were telling me I had supposedly done everything I came here to do.

I just kept thinking about everything and everyone I had left behind.

I remember asking about my mother.

That was one of the first things that came out of me.

What about my mother?

What about my family?

What about all of the people I Love?

What about all of the people I had intended to help with however much time I still had left here?

What about the children I still wanted to feed?

I remember crying uncontrollably and trying to explain to them that I wasn't finished, while they kept trying to explain to me that I was.

And the strangest part was that whatever this place was, however advanced it seemed, I didn't want anything from it.

I didn't care what I could learn there.

I didn't care what I could see there.

I didn't care if somebody was about to explain every mystery I had spent my entire life trying to understand.

I wanted to come back here.

I wanted my mother.

I wanted another chance to sit beside her, to hear her voice, to tell her things I have probably assumed she already knows simply because I have carried them inside of me for so long.

More than anything, I wanted her to know how profoundly grateful I was that, out of every possible life I could have experienced, somehow I got one in which I was her son.

Because standing there believing that my entire experience on Earth had already ended, I wasn't thinking about everything life hadn't given me.

I was thinking about what it had.

And somehow, among everything I had experienced here, one of the things that hurt the most to imagine leaving behind was the woman whose Love had been there from the beginning of it.

I wanted her to know that.

Not after I was gone.

Not through something I had written that she might someday find.

Not through somebody else telling her what I had said about her.

I wanted to come back and tell her myself.

And that was when something about the whole experience became almost unbearable, because I started thinking about how many things we carry in our hearts for people while assuming there will eventually be some perfect moment to say them.

Sometimes there isn't.

Sometimes the greatest thing you could ever tell another human being is something they deserve to hear while they are still standing in front of you.

And if I had really reached the end of my time here, I didn't want one of my final realizations to be that my mother had spent her life Loving me while I had somehow left this world without adequately telling her what having that Love had meant to mine.

I wanted my family.

I wanted the people I Love.

I wanted the life that, only moments before, I probably would have been able to give you a fairly long list of complaints about.

I wanted another day of it.

That feeling became so intense that I remember this horrible weight in my chest while I was pleading with them to send me back.

I kept trying to explain that there were still people I wanted to help. There were still things I wanted to make right. There were still people I hadn't met yet. There were still things I needed to tell people.

There were still children I wanted to feed.

There were still people suffering whom I wanted to help. There were still people I hadn't met yet who might someday need something I could give, even if all I could give them was a meal, a little hope, or the reassurance that somebody somewhere cared about what happened to them.

There was still so much of myself that I wanted to give away before I could ever accept that my time here was finished.

And I think that was what hurt the most.

I wasn't begging to come back because there was something else I wanted to acquire.

I was begging because there was still so much I wanted to give.

There is something about that realization that has stayed with me ever since I woke up.

I have spent an almost ridiculous amount of my life trying to understand existence. I have wanted to know why we're here, what consciousness actually is, what God is, why suffering exists, what death really means, and whether there is something beyond what we currently understand as life.

Yet in that dream, when I suddenly found myself somewhere that seemed to be beyond this life, I didn't give a damn about any of those answers.

All of those enormous questions that have occupied so much of my mind became completely insignificant compared with the thought of never hearing my mother's voice again.

I think that is probably the part that affected me the most.

You can spend your entire life trying to understand the universe, only to discover that if everything were suddenly taken away from you, the thing you would miss most might be someone you have sat beside a thousand times without thinking twice about it.

Maybe it would be your mother calling your name from another room.

Maybe it would be your child asking you to come look at something while you're trying to work.

Maybe it would be somebody you Love laughing at something that isn't even funny.

Maybe it would be the person sleeping next to you, or a friend who sends you ridiculous messages, or an animal that waits for you to come home every day as though your return is the most important event happening anywhere in the world.

And for some people, they already know exactly what I mean because the person or animal that came into their mind while reading this isn't here anymore.

Those people know how strange Grief can be.

Sometimes you don't want some enormous moment back.

You want 5 completely uneventful minutes.

You want to hear the door open again.

You want them sitting in their chair.

You want to hear the same story you've heard 50 times.

You want them to call and interrupt whatever you're doing.

You want to hear their laugh coming from somewhere else in the house.

You just want them there.

And I think there is something heartbreaking about realizing that somebody, somewhere, is living those 5 minutes right now and has absolutely no idea what they are worth yet.

I didn't understand that in some intellectual way during the dream...

I felt it.

Everything I thought I still had years to do had suddenly become something I would never get to do.

Every conversation I thought I could have later had already happened for the last time.

Every person I assumed I would see again had already seen me for the last time.

That was what I couldn't accept.

And because I have died twice before, there was something especially unsettling about how familiar certain parts of this felt.

Again, I don't know what that means.

Maybe my mind carried something from those experiences and recreated pieces of that feeling while I slept. Maybe consciousness is considerably stranger than we understand. Maybe there is something happening here that none of us currently have the words to adequately express.

I really don't know.

I just know that it felt familiar enough that I woke up shaken.

I was sweating even though I sleep in a cooled environment, and I realized that I was still kind of pleading under my breath when I woke up.

I sat there for a minute trying to collect myself, and once I realized where I was, I felt this overwhelming appreciation for the fact that I was here.

Nothing had changed.

My problems were still my problems. The things I was worried about before I went to sleep were still waiting for me. There was no great transformation of my circumstances.

But I was here.

My mother was here.

My family was here.

There were still people I could help.

There were still children in this world who would wake up hungry, and I was still here with another opportunity to put food into some of their hands.

There were still people I could tell that I Love them.

There were still things I could fix instead of wishing I had fixed them.

There were still people I hadn't met yet who might become important to me, and people somewhere in the world whom I might someday be able to help through something they don't even know is coming yet.

And for some reason, all of that felt incredibly beautiful.

I think we become so accustomed to having people in our lives that we forget how unbelievable it is that we have them at all.

We get annoyed. We get distracted. We get busy. We assume we'll call later, visit another time, have another Christmas, another birthday, another dinner, another morning, another chance to say whatever we didn't say today.

Most of the time there probably will be.

Until eventually there isn't.

And nobody tells you which time is going to be the last one.

I think about that differently now.

Not in some depressing way where I want to spend every moment thinking about death, but almost the opposite.

I don't want to become so obsessed with what comes after this life that I fail to appreciate the fact that I am currently inside of it.

Whatever waits beyond this place can wait for me.

I'll find out eventually.

Right now, I have people here that I Love.

I have a mother I am unbelievably grateful for.

There are children who still need to be fed.

There are people suffering whom I may still be able to help.

There are things I still want to create.

There are people I haven't met yet.

There are conversations that haven't happened yet.

There are probably people who will eventually become incredibly important to me whose names I don't even know today.

I like knowing that.

I like knowing there is still more of my life that hasn't happened.

And after this dream, I am strangely grateful even for the fact that there are things I haven't finished yet.

Because unfinished means there is still something here for me to do.

Maybe that's why I was fighting so hard to come back.

Those 2 individuals were trying to tell me that I had already gained all of the knowledge and wisdom I needed from this experience, and I was trying to explain something they didn't seem to understand.

Knowledge wasn't enough of a reason for me to be here anymore.

The people were.

Love was.

Being able to take whatever I had learned and use it to make somebody else's time here a little easier was.

I don't know what this dream was...

I don't know why parts of it felt so remarkably similar to what I experienced when I died...

And I'm not going to pretend to have an answer simply because an answer would make the story more interesting.

Maybe someday I'll understand it.

Maybe I never will.

But when I woke up, I realized something that I don't want to forget again.

I had spent that entire experience begging for another chance to come back to the very life I had been inside of the entire time.

That really messed with me.

Because how many things in our lives are like that?

How many people are we currently taking for granted who would become absolutely priceless to us the moment they were gone?

How many things do we complain about today that we would give anything to have back if they disappeared tomorrow?

How many moments are happening around us right now that we won't understand the value of until they become memories?

I don't know.

I just know that when I thought everything was over, I didn't want more money, more recognition, more possessions, more answers, or some better existence waiting somewhere else.

I wanted to come back here.

I wanted another chance to Love the people who are here with me.

I wanted another chance to feed a child who might otherwise go to sleep hungry.

I wanted another chance to help somebody who had started believing nobody cared whether they were alright.

I wanted another chance to sit beside my mother and tell her, while I still could, how profoundly grateful I am that out of every life I might have experienced, somehow I got to experience the one as her son.

I wanted more time.

Then I opened my eyes.

And somehow, I had it.

So whatever that dream was, whatever my experiences with death were, and whatever ultimately waits for any of us beyond this life, I think I'm a little less concerned with figuring all of it out today or any time soon for that matter...

I'm here now.

The people I Love are here now.

There are still children I can feed.

There are still people I can help.

There is still something I can do with whatever time I have left.

And after believing, even for a little while, that all of it had been taken away from me, I can't explain how grateful I am that I wasn't actually finished.

Because the truth is, I don't feel finished at all.

There is still far too much Love in me that I haven't had the chance to give away yet.

And before I end this, there is something I want every single person who follows me, reads my work, listens to what I create, or has simply crossed paths with me here to know while I am still here to actually say it.

I genuinely Love each and every single one of you, unconditionally.

I don't need to know everything about you first. I don't need you to agree with everything I believe, support everything I do, think the way I think, or give me anything in return for me to care about what happens to you.

You don't have to earn that from me.

And if there ever comes a day when life becomes too heavy and you simply need another human being to talk to, whether you're hurting, confused, grieving, frightened, lonely, angry, completely overwhelmed, or you simply need somebody to listen without making you feel like a burden for needing to be heard, please know that as long as I am here and capable of being that person, I will do my very best to be.

I may not always have the answer, or always know exactly what to say...

I certainly cannot promise that I can fix whatever you are going through.

But I can listen.

I can care.

I can try to understand.

I can offer whatever perspective or advice I am capable of giving, and if there is nothing I can say that will make what you're carrying any lighter, then I can at least remind you that you don't have to carry every difficult moment believing that absolutely nobody gives a damn about what happens to you...

Because somebody does.

I do.

And I don't need a reason.

That is something I wish more people understood about Love. I don't believe another human being should have to prove that they are worthy of being cared about before somebody cares about them.

You already matter because you're here.

So for however long I am fortunate enough to remain here with all of you, I will continue doing the best I can to brighten your day whenever I have the opportunity, make you laugh when you need one, sit with you through the things that aren't funny, listen when you need to get something off your chest, share whatever I have learned when you ask for advice, and remind you whenever life manages to convince you otherwise that you are not walking through all of this completely alone.

And although I don't need a single reason to care about you, so many of you somehow continue giving me reasons every single day.

Through the messages you send me.

Through the pieces of your lives you trust me enough to share.

Through your kindness.

Through your encouragement.

Through the stories you tell me about what you have survived.

Through the times you have made me laugh when I needed it too.

Through every person who has ever told me that something I wrote, created, said, or did happened to reach them at precisely the moment they needed it.

You may think I am the one trying to brighten your lives, but more of you have brightened mine than you will probably ever know.

Maybe that is another reason I was fighting so hard to come back.

Because when I said there was still too much Love inside of me that I hadn't had the chance to give away yet, I wasn't only talking about my family, the children I still want to feed, or the people standing physically beside me.

I was talking about you, too.

So if there is ever a moment when you find yourself wondering whether anybody out there genuinely cares about you without needing something from you in return, I hope you remember this.

As long as I am here, there is at least one person somewhere in this strange world who wants you to make it through whatever you're facing, who hopes tomorrow is gentler with you than today was, who wants to see you become everything you still have the opportunity to become, and who genuinely cares that you are here to experience another day.

You don't owe me anything for that.

You never did.

I am simply grateful that, somehow, during this brief experience of being alive at the same time on this planet, our paths crossed at all.

I Love you.

Unconditionally.

Agape.

And for however long I am fortunate enough to still be here, I will continue doing my best to make sure you never have to wonder whether somebody cares.

Because I do.

And though I have never needed a reason to...

so many of you give me so many reasons every single day.

What I Saw on Oct. 7: Leadership and Israel’s Greatest Generation - by Ophir Falk 

We are going to change the map of the Middle East,’ Netanyahu said two days after the massacre.

Every Jew and Israeli remembers where he was on Oct. 7, 2023.

My day started shortly after 6:30 a.m., when Tzachi Braverman,  the prime minister’s chief of staff, called me and said, “Get up! Come  to the Kirya immediately,” referring to our military headquarters. I got  dressed within minutes and rushed downstairs to wake my 19- and  21-year-old sons. I told them, “We’re at war. Get to your units.” My  eldest asked, “Hezbollah or Hamas?” “Hamas,” I said. “OK,” he replied in  what sounded like a sigh of relief.

As  I walked out the door, I passed my younger son, who was sitting in the  living room waiting to be called up. “Don’t worry, it’s going to be a  long war. You’ll get your chance,” I told him. He did get his chance and  much more.

I  got in my car at about 7 a.m. I drove past my neighbor, an Air Force  squadron commander, who was getting into his car. “Avner, are all your  pilots coming?” I asked.

“They will all come,” he said.

“This isn’t another round. This time we need to go all the way,” I warned.

“Absolutely,” Avner shouted in agreement.

I arrived at the Kirya shortly after 8 a.m. when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was receiving updates on the unfolding attack. Horrific photos and  videos of wounded and dead Israelis overwhelmed WhatsApp. Some showed  Israeli civilians being slaughtered in their kibbutz homes and on the  streets of Sderot.

Shortly  after 9:30 a.m., Mr. Netanyahu entered the situation room to receive a  briefing from the military chiefs. “It’s going to be a long war,” the  prime minister told me on the way to the meeting. Mr. Netanyahu, the Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, several other officials and I huddled around a small table. You could have heard a pin drop.

In  the room, the prime minister was briefed that “we were somewhat  surprised” that “there are still a number of skirmishes and a large  number of casualties.” He was told that “the situation should be under  control before nightfall,” but that “we need to call up 100,000  reservists.” Mr. Netanyahu interjected: “Call up 300,000 troops  immediately.” After intense questioning, he summarized, “Verify that, as  I instructed this morning, a division was sent to the North and is  holding a strong defense. Prevent the crossing of anyone back to Gaza. This is not another round of fighting. This is war.”

At  about 11:30 a.m., the prime minister addressed the public. “We are at  war. Not an operation, not another round—at war.” He soon formalized the  declaration of war and the war’s objectives in a meeting with the  security cabinet.

France’s President Emmanuel Macron  was the first foreign leader to call. He urged diplomacy and offered to  mediate. “Hamas is ISIS,” Mr. Netanyahu replied. “If it is not  dismantled in Gaza, you will meet it in Paris.” The prime minister also  emphasized that he didn’t want Mr. Macron to convey any message from him  to anyone. “Hamas will soon get the message,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

The next call came from then-President Joe Biden.  “How can I help, Bibi?” he asked. Mr. Netanyahu said, “Hamas is worse  than ISIS. They need to be dismantled.” He asked Mr. Biden to send two  U.S. aircraft carriers toward Lebanon’s shores and to warn Iran and its  Hezbollah proxy not to join the war. Mr. Biden promised he would. He gave the “Don’t” speech several days later, warning Iran and its proxies against escalation.

As  that fateful day ended, Israel’s enemies thought the Jewish state would  collapse. Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals believed he was finished. Both were  mistaken.

On  Oct. 9, the prime minister met with community leaders in southern  Israel. “I ask that you stand steadfast because we are going to change  the map of the Middle East,” he told the group.

Three  years later, Mr. Netanyahu has been proved right. Hamas has been  decimated in Gaza, Palestinian terror infrastructure has been uprooted  in Judea and Samaria, Hezbollah is on its knees, and Yemen’s Houthis  have been hit like never before. Bashar al-Assad’s army in Syria is gone  and, most important, the weakened Iranian regime will never assert the  same power.

After  1,096 days of fighting a war of redemption across seven fronts, Israel  and its American ally are stronger than ever. Mr. Netanyahu has emerged  as our greatest wartime leader, and the young soldiers of Oct. 7 are  proving to be Israel’s Greatest Generation.

Mr. Falk is foreign-policy adviser to Prime Minister Netanyahu.

text:
AN HUMBLE ATTEMPT TO PROMOTE EXPLICIT AGREEMENT AND VISIBLE UNION OF GOD’S PEOPLE - IN EXTRAORDINARY PRAYER - FOR THE REVIVAL OF RELIGION AND THE ADVANCEMENT OF CHRIST’S KINGDOM ON EARTH
By Jonathan Edwards (1703 – 1758)

Continuing...

SECT. II
Observations on the text

In the text we have an account how this future glorious advancement of the church of God should be introduced; viz. By great multitudes in different towns and countries taking up a joint resolution, and coming into an express and visible agreement, that they will, by united and extraordinary prayer, seek to God, that he would come and manifest himself, and grant the tokens and fruits of his gracious presence.

Particularly we may observe,

1. The duty, with the attendance on which the glorious event foretold shall be brought on; viz. The duty of prayer.—Prayer, some suppose, is here to be taken synechdochically for the whole of divine worship; prayer being a principal part of worship in the days of the gospel, when sacrifices are abolished. If so, this is to be understood only as a prophecy of a great revival of religion, and of the true worship of God among his visible people, the accession of others to the church, and turning of multitudes from idolatry to the worship of the true God. But it appears to me reasonable to suppose, that something more special is intended, with regard to the duty of prayer; considering that prayer is here expressly and repeatedly mentioned; and also considering how parallel this place is with many other prophecies, that speak of an extraordinary spirit of prayer, as preceding and introducing that glorious day of religious revival, and advancement of the church’s peace and prosperity, so often foretold. Add to this, the agreeableness of what is here said, with what is said afterwards by the same prophet, of the pouring out of a spirit of grace and supplication, as that with which this great revival of religion shall begin. (Chap. xii. 10.)

2. The good, that shall be sought by prayer; which is God himself. It is said once and again, “They shall go to pray before the Lord, and to seek the Lord of hosts.” 315 This is the good they ask for, and seek by prayer, The Lord of hosts himself. To seek God, as the expression may perhaps be sometimes used in Scripture, may signify no more than seeking the favour or mercy of God. And if it be taken so here, praying before the Lord, and seeking the Lord of hosts, must be synonymous expressions. And it must be confessed to be a common thing in Scripture, to signify the same thing repeatedly, by various expressions of the same import, for the greater emphasis.

But certainly that expression of seeking the Lord, is very commonly used to signify something more; it implies that God himself is the great good desired and sought after; that the blessings pursued are God’s gracious presence, the blessed manifestations of him, union and intercourse with him; or, in short, God’s manifestations and communications of himself by his Holy Spirit. Thus the psalmist desired God, thirsted after him, and sought him. (Psal. lxiii. 1, 2, 8.) “O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee. My flesh longeth for thee, in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is; to see thy power and thy glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary. My soul followeth hard after thee. ” (Psal. lxxiii. 25.) “Whom have I in heaven but thee? And there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee.” The psalmist earnestly pursued after GOD, his soul thirsted after him, he stretched forth his hands unto him, &c. (Psal. cxliii. 6.) And therefore it is in Scripture the peculiar character of the saints, that they are those who seek God. (Psal. xxiv. 6.) “This is the generation of them that seek him.” (Psal. lxix. 32.) “Your heart shall live that seek God.“ If the expression in the text be understood agreeably to this sense, then by seeking the Lord of hosts, we must understand a seeking, that God who had withdrawn, or as it were hid himself for a long time, would return to his church, and grant the tokens and fruits of his gracious presence, and those blessed communications of his Spirit to his people, and to mankind on earth, which he had often promised, and which his church had long waited for.

And it seems reasonable to understand the phrase, seeking the Lord of hosts, in this sense here; and not as merely signifying the same thing with praying to God: not only because the expression is repeatedly added to praying before the Lord, in the text; but also because the phrase, taken in this sense, is exactly agreeable to other parallel prophetic representations. Thus God’s people seeking, by earnest prayer, the promised restoration of the church of God, after the Babylonish captivity, and the great apostacy that occasioned it, is’ called their seeking God, and searching for him; and God’s granting this promised revival and restoration is called his being found of them.Jer. xxix. 10, 14. “For thus saith the Lord, that after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon, I will visit you, and perform my good word towards you, in causing you to return to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think towards you, saith the Lord, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end. Then shall ye go and call upon me, and I wilt hearken unto you; and ye shall seek me and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart; and I will be found of you, saith the Lord, and I will turn away your captivity.” And the prophets, from time to time, represent God, in a low and afflicted state of his church, as being withdrawn, and hiding himself. Isa. xlv. 15. “Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour.” (Chap. lvii. 17.) “I hid me, and was wroth.” And they represent God’s people, while his church is in such a state, before God delivers and restores the same, as seeking him, looking for him, searching and waiting for him, and calling after him. (Hos. v. 15.) “I will go and return unto my place, till they acknowledge their offence, and seek my face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him. ”

And when God, in answer to their prayers and succeeding their endeavours, delivers, restores, and advances his church, according to his promise, then he is said to answer, and come, and say, Here am I, and to show himself; and they are said to find him, and see him plainly. (Isa. lviii. 9.) “Then shall thou cry, and he shall say, Here I am“ (Isa. xlv. 19.) “I said not unto the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain.” Chap. xxv. 8, 9.) “The Lord will wipe away the tears from off all faces, and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off the earth. And it shall be said in that day, Lo, this is our God, we have waited for him, and he will save us: This is the Lord, we have waited for him; we will be glad, and rejoice in his salvation.” Together with the next chap.” ver. 8, 9. we have waited for thee; “the desire of our soul is to thy name, and to the remembrance of thee. With my soul have I desired thee in the night; yea, with my spirit within me will I seek thee early. For when thy judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness.” Isa. lii. 6-8. “Therefore my people shall know my name; therefore they shall know in that day, that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace, that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation, that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth! Thy watchmen shall lift up the voice, together shall they sing; for they shall see eye to eye, when the Lord shall bring again Zion.”

3. We may observe who they are, that shall be united in thus seeking the Lord of hosts: the inhabitants of many cities, and of many countries, yea, many people, and strong nations, great multitudes in different parts of the world shall conspire in this business. From the representation made in the prophecy, it appears rational to suppose, that it will be fulfilled something after this manner: There shall be given much of a spirit of prayer to God’s people, in many places, disposing them to come into an express agreement, unitedly to pray to God in an extraordinary manner, that he would appear for the help of his church, and in mercy to mankind, and pour out his Spirit, revive his work, and advance his spiritual kingdom in the world, as he has promised. This disposition to prayer, and union in it, will gradually spread more and more, and increase to greater degrees; with which at length will gradually be introduced a revival of religion, and a disposition to greater engagedness in the worship and service of God, amongst his professing people. This being observed, will be the means of awakening others, making them sensible of the wants of their souls, and exciting in them a great concern for their spiritual and everlasting good, and putting them upon earnestly crying to God for spiritual mercies, and
282
disposing them to join in that extraordinary seeking and serving of God.

In this manner religion shall be propagated, till the awakening reaches those that are in the highest stations, and till whole nations be awakened, and there be at length an accession of many of the chief nations of the world to the church of God. Thus after the inhabitants of many cities of Israel, or of God’s professing people, have taken up and pursued a joint resolution, to go and pray before the Lord, and seek the Lord of hosts, others shall be drawn to worship and serve him with them; till at length many people and strong nations shall join themselves to them; and there shall, in process of time, be a vast accession to the church, so that it shall be ten times as large as it was before; yea, at length, all nations shall be converted unto God. Thus (Zech. viii. 23.) “ten men shall take hold, out of all languages of the nations, of the skirt of him that is a Jew,” (in the sense of the apostle, Rom. ii. 28, 29.) “saying, We will go with you; for we have heard, that God is with you. ” And thus shall be fulfilled, Psal. lxv. 2. “O thou that hearest prayer, unto thee shall all flesh come.”

4. We may observe, the mode of their union in this duty. It is a visible union, an union by explicit agreement, a joint resolution declared by one to another, being first proposed by some, and readily and expressly followed by others. The inhabitants of one city shall apply themselves to the inhabitants of another, saying, Let us go, &c. Those to whom the motion is made, shall comply with it, the proposal shall take with many, it shall be a prevailing, spreading thing; one shall follow another’s example, one and another shall say, I will go also. Some suppose, that those words, I will go also, are to be taken as the words of him that makes the proposal; as much as to say, I do not propose that to you, which I am not willing to do myself. I desire you to go, and am ready to go with you. But this is to suppose no more to be expressed in these latter words, than was expressed before in the proposal itself; for these words, let us go, signify as much. It seems to me much more natural, to understand these latter words as importing the consent of those to whom the proposal is made, or the reply of one and another that falls in with it. This is much more agreeable to the plain design of the text, which is to represent the concurrence of great numbers in this affair; and more agreeable to the representation made in the next verse, of one following another, many taking hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew.

And though, if the words be thus understood, we must suppose an ellipsis in the text, something understood that is not expressed, as if it had been said, those of other cities shall say, I will go also; yet, this is not difficult to be supposed, for such ellipses are very common in Scripture. We have one exactly parallel with it in Jer. iii. 22. “Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backsliding. Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the Lord our God,” i. e. the backsliding children shall say, “Behold, we come unto thee,” &c. And in Cant. iv. 16. and v. 1. “Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits. I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse,” i. e. her beloved shall say, “I am come into my garden.” We have the like throughout that song. So Psal. l. 6, 7. “The heavens shall declare his righteousness; for God is judge himself. Hear, O my people, and I will speak,” i. e. the Judge shall say, “Hear, O my people,” &c. So Psal. lxxxii. 1, 2. The psalms and prophets abound with such figures of speech.

5. We may observe the manner of prayer agreed on, or the manner in which they agree, to engage in and perform the duty. Let us go SPEEDILY to pray; or as it is in the margin, Let us go continually. The words literally translated are, Let us go in going. Such an ingemination, or doubling of words, is very common in the Hebrew language, when it is intended that a thing shall be very strongly expressed. It generally implies the superlative degree of a thing; as the holy of holies signifies the most holy. But it commonly denotes, not only the utmost degree of a thing, but also the utmost certainty; as when God said to Abraham, “In multiplying, I will multiply thy seed,” (Gen. xxii. 17.) it implies both that God would certainly multiply his seed, and also multiply it exceedingly. So when God said to Adam, “In the day that thou eatest thereof, in dying thou shall die,” (as the words are in the original,) it implies, both that he should surely die, and also that he should die most terribly, should utterly perish, and be destroyed to the utmost degree.

In short, as the ingemination of words in the Hebrew, generally denotes the strength of expression, so it is used to signify almost all those things that are wont to be signified by the various forms of strong speech in other languages. It signifies not only the utmost degree of a thing, and its great certainty; but also the peremptoriness and terribleness of a threatening, the greatness and positiveness of a promise, the strictness of a command, and the earnestness of a request. When God says to Adam, ” Dying thou shall die,” it is equivalent to such strong expressions in English, as, Thou shalt die surely, or indeed; or, Thou shalt die with a witness. So when it is said in the text, “Let us go in going, and pray before the Lord,” the strength of the expression represents the earnestness of those that make the proposal, their great engagedness in the affair. And with respect to the duly proposed, it may be understood to signify that they should be speedy, fervent, and constant in it; or, in one word, that it should be thoroughly performed.

6. We may learn from the tenor of this prophecy, together with the context, that this union in such prayer is foretold as a becoming and happy thing, what would be acceptable to God, and attended with glorious success.

From the whole we may infer, that it is a very suitable thing, and well-pleasing to God, for many people, in different parts of the world, by express agreement, to come into a visible union in extraordinary, speedy, fervent, and constant prayer, for those great effusions of the Holy Spirit, which shall bring on that advancement of Christ’s church and kingdom, that God has so often promised shall be in the latter ages of the world. And so from hence I would infer the duty of God’s people, with regard to the Memorial lately sent over into America from Scotland, by a number of ministers there, proposing a method for such an union as has been spoken of, in extraordinary prayer, for this great mercy.

And it being the special design of this discourse, to persuade such as are friends to the interests of Christ’s kingdom, to a compliance with the proposal and request made in that Memorial, I shall, First, give a short historical account of the affair to which it relates, from letters, papers, and pamphlets, that have come over from Scotland. Secondly, I shall annex the Memorial itself. And then, I shall offer some arguments and motives, tending to induce the friends of religion to fall in with what is proposed; and lastly, make answer to some objections that may possibly be made against it.

To be continued next Wednesday, DV

text:
The first thing I remember about my first night exercise in the army was how damn dark it was.

Not “I can’t see very well” dark.

I mean I can barely see my own hand dark.

We were out in the jungle, moving quietly through the trees.

No streetlights.

No buildings.

No glowing phone screen to tell you where you were.

Just darkness.

And every few steps, I had this little voice in my head asking:

“Are we even going the right way?”

The problem was, you couldn't see very far ahead.

You could only see the next few metres.

So you stopped trying to see the whole journey.

You focused on the next step.

Check the ground.

Move.

Look around.

Move again.

Listen for instructions.

Move.

At one point, I remember hearing something in the bushes.

Crunch.

Everyone froze.

Nobody said a word.

We waited.

Another crunch.

My heart started beating a little faster.

Turns out it was nothing.

Probably just some animal.

But that moment taught me something I've never forgotten.

When you can't see what's ahead, you don't need to know the entire path.

You just need to know what to do next.

Funny enough, I've found business can feel exactly the same.

Especially when you're starting something new.

You don't know exactly where the next client will come from.

You don't know if your offer is perfect.

You don't know whether the next email will get a reply.

You don't know how everything will turn out six months from now.

And that's where people get stuck.

They try to figure out the entire journey before taking the next step.

But you don't need the whole map.

You need the next move.

Write the email.

Send the pitch.

Talk to the prospect.

Improve the offer.

Then do it again.

One step at a time.

That's also why I like story-based sales emails.

You don't need to scream at people with another generic sales pitch.

You can take them somewhere.

Give them a moment.

Let them feel something.

Then naturally connect that story to the problem your product solves.

If you need help turning ordinary moments into emails that people actually want to read, that's exactly what I’m working on.

I write story-based sales emails designed to grab attention, keep people reading, and lead naturally into your offer.

You don't need to see the whole path.

Just take the next step.

Etymology and Meaning Evolution

Red giants are evolved from main-sequence stars with masses in the range from about 0.3 M☉ to around 8 M☉.[13] When a star initially forms from a collapsing molecular cloud in the interstellar medium, it contains primarily hydrogen and helium, with trace amounts of "metals" (in astrophysics, this refers to all elements other than hydrogen and helium). These elements are all uniformly mixed throughout the star. The star "enters" the main sequence when its core reaches a temperature (several million kelvins) high enough to begin fusing hydrogen-1 (the predominant isotope), and establishes hydrostatic equilibrium. (In astrophysics, stellar fusion is often referred to as "burning", with hydrogen fusion sometimes termed "hydrogen burning".) Over its main sequence life, the star slowly fuses the hydrogen in the core into helium; its main-sequence life ends when nearly all the hydrogen in the core has been fused. For the Sun, the main-sequence lifetime is approximately 10 billion years. More massive stars burn their fuel disproportionately faster and so have a shorter lifetime than less massive stars.[14]

When the star has mostly exhausted the hydrogen fuel in its core, the core's rate of nuclear reactions declines, and thus so do the radiation and thermal pressure the core generates, which are what support the star against gravitational contraction. The star further contracts, increasing the pressures and thus temperatures inside the star (as described by the ideal gas law). Eventually a "shell" layer around the core reaches temperatures sufficient to fuse hydrogen and thus generate its own radiation and thermal pressure, which "re-inflates" the star's outer layers and causes them to expand.[15] The hydrogen-burning shell results in a situation that has been described as the mirror principle: when the core within the shell contracts, the layers of the star outside the shell must expand. The detailed physical processes that cause this are complex. Still, the behavior is necessary to satisfy simultaneous conservation of gravitational and thermal energy in a star with the shell structure. The core contracts and heats up due to the lack of fusion, and so the outer layers of the star expand greatly, absorbing most of the extra energy from shell fusion. This process of cooling and expanding is the subgiant stage. When the envelope of the star cools sufficiently it becomes convective, the star stops expanding, its luminosity starts to increase, and the star is ascending the red-giant branch of the Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram.[14][16]

CNN’s analysis called the sentence construction “unfortunate” and “incoherent,” not a deliberate offer to let Tehran hit those cities. He has used the same “small price to pay” line before about gas prices versus a nuclear Iran, including earlier the same day in a Nebraska TV interview and in Iowa on September 28, when he said something like “if you want to see turmoil and a travesty, let them take out a city with a nuclear weapon.”

So, the viral claim compresses a real, badly phrased rally line into a statement he did not make.
