How yesterday's Nvidia engineer technical blog By Mark Chmarny and Nathan Taber is monumental to IREN valuation yet not currently priced in to any analysts, $IREN financial models, in regards to the genius of the Mirantis acquisition;

🚀 Executive Summary: IREN's Software Catalyst via AICR v1.0 & Mirantis

Strategic Value & Technical Validation
•The Software Catalyst: AICR v1.0 is an open reproducibility contract published by NVIDIA on 6 October 2026 for GPU Kubernetes clusters. Combined with Mirantis, it allows IREN to rapidly turn raw power and GPUs into a fully managed cloud, directly addressing the software gap analysts cited against CoreWeave and Nebius.

•System Stability: GPU clusters often fail when kernels, drivers, runtimes, networking, storage, operators, and frameworks drift out of lockstep. AICR pins a tested combination as a stable recipe, rendering it for Helm, Argo CD, Flux, or Helmfile, and validates the live cluster with signed evidence.

•Hardware & Workload Breadth: Coverage spans Hopper through Blackwell and Rubin-class GPUs, supporting both training (Kubeflow, Slurm) and inference (Dynamo, NIM).

•Integration Status: Mirantis k0rdent is a key consumer of this contract for multi-cluster management. Mirantis is an early integrator of the stable v1 interfaces, not the author.

The Mirantis Acquisition
•Deal Terms: IREN agreed to buy Mirantis in May 2026 for ~$625 million in stock, closing on 4 August 2026. Mirantis operates as the foundational software layer under IREN’s physical footprint.

•Corporate Pedigree: Mirantis serves over 1,500 enterprise customers, is a founding independent software vendor in NVIDIA’s AI Cloud Ready program, integrates k0rdent AI with NVIDIA DSX OS, and was named an inaugural NVIDIA Certified Hypervisor.

Architecture & Site Standardization
•Inference Control Plane: k0rdent uses declarative templates to stand up clusters instantly upon hardware arrival. This includes the NVIDIA GPU and Network Operators, Run:ai, GPU partitioning, multi-tenancy, a model registry, high-performance runtimes, and a localized inference mesh for routing and metering.

•Geographic Uniformity: AICR sits beneath k0rdent, allowing data centers in Texas, British Columbia, Spain, and South Australia to deploy identical, signed recipes instead of inventing localized driver matrices.

Competitive Positioning & Financials
•The Catch-Up: VanEck’s Matthew Sigel noted the deal targets a full-stack neocloud offering to rival CoreWeave (known for Kubernetes-native orchestration and turnkey working clusters) and Nebius (known for a deeply productized orchestration layer) at 4x to 5x Mirantis revenue.

•Physical & Commercial Lead: IREN commands ~2.9 GW secured capacity (Childress: 750 MW, Sweetwater: ~2 GW, Canada, Spain/Nostrum: ~490 MW, Bundey/South Australia: 800 MW). Anchors include a ~$9.7B Microsoft contract, a ~$3.4B NVIDIA AI Cloud contract, and a 5 GW DSX partnership. Fleet plans target 150,000 GPUs and >$3.7B run-rate revenue.

Commercial Outcomes & Market Narrative
•Value-Add Monetization: Instead of selling just bare metal and power, k0rdent and AICR allow IREN to sell managed inference, slice GPUs, quicken time-to-revenue, and offer sovereignty/audit trails for EU and APAC hyperscalers.

•Equities Impact: The acquisition is public, so a re-rating on the purchase alone is late. However, external proof that the stack utilizes NVIDIA's open contract—rather than an uninspectable proprietary stack—presents a narrative shift. If analysts treat this as closing the software gap, IREN's multiple could pivot from a power/GPU lessor toward a managed-cloud operator. This shift depends on actual contract conversions, GPU deliveries, and CoreWeave-like utilization. Models do not yet reflect this day-old AICR post.

text:
What's going on with the James Talarico campaign?

I've been wondering that lately, and this certainly isn't going to quiet those questions.

Sheena Flanary isn't a Republican operative attacking Talarico. She's vice chair for voter engagement for the Texas Democratic Party.

And now she's been caught on an undercover recording describing her own experience trying to help his campaign.

Flanary says she reached out several times, asking for absolutely nothing for herself, and felt rebuffed.

Then came the part I find really strange.

She and her husband even offered to hold a fundraiser for Talarico.

According to Flanary, the campaign wasn't interested.

She finally asked:

“Do you want Black people to help you or you don't want Black people to help you?”

That's quite a statement coming from the Democratic Party's own vice chair for voter engagement.

Talarico has publicly acknowledged concerns about Democrats taking Black voters for granted and has been making a major effort to increase his outreach to Black voters.

So how does a high-ranking Black official in his own party end up saying she repeatedly tried to help his campaign and was brushed off?

Something doesn't add up here.

See the link to the article in the comments.

text:
A young woman alleges that seven young men sexually assaulted her after she had become severely intoxicated and incapacitated. There are powerful drugs like Ketamine, apparently, and lots of alcohol.  Some will say that the young woman was drinking and went to the party voluntarily to have group sex. I'm not particularly interested in adjudicating the case here. I’m interested in a simpler question. Where was the one good man? The Good Samaritan who looked at this young woman and saw her as a human being in need of help? Where was the guy who told everyone else to knock it off? Where was the guy who should have stood up for her, gathered her clothes and taken her home? Where was the guy who didn't particularly care whether his friends thought he was being uptight or ruining everybody's evening? Where was he? That's what bothers me.
 
When we hear about these kinds of situations we often generalize the type of people we think might engage in this kind of behavior. Surely they were thugs or rich, privileged white boys from Connecticut boarding schools, right? Some kind of clue that makes us feel better about how it happened.
 
But the young men in this story don't fit neatly into one of those boxes. They are racially diverse. They came from different families with different circumstances. What they had in common was that they had somehow clawed their way to the top. Into an incredibly competitive Ivy-League school. Cornell isn't exactly taking everyone who wanders through the admissions office. In 2026, Cornell received 75,523 applications. They only accepted around 8% of applicants. They only accept the very best our country has to offer.
 
These are—or were—the future leaders of America, the future titans of industry. They were, ostensibly, the finest our country had to offer. Young people who were smart, worked hard, and earned their way into the Ivy Leagues. That’s what bothers me.
Somebody raised these kids. They got them into the right pre-school, took them to soccer practice, piano lessons and travel baseball games. Somebody made sure they had lunch money, did their homework and made good grades. Somebody kept them out of trouble and somebody helped them navigate the choppy waters of middle and high school. They accumulated AP credits, academic awards and accolades that their parents bragged about at work. They were the kids every parent dreams about.
 
So help me understand how seven boys can reach the pinnacle of academic performance without developing an ounce of character? Did we confuse accomplishment with character? They aren't the same thing. Intelligence isn't character. Achievement isn't character. Education isn't character. Getting into Cornell certainly isn't character. Character is what happens when you're standing in a room and everybody else is doing something you know is wrong. And you stop it.
 
These boys grew up with video games, on-line gambling and high-definition pornography, on-demand. Stuff that previous generations couldn't fathom. What does all that pornography teach a thirteen-year-old boy about women and intimacy? What does it teach young men and women about the normality of group sex? Pretending it has no effect is insane.
 
And snorting ketamine, a Schedule III narcotic? A drug so powerful it’s used for anesthesia during surgery? When did college kids start recreationally snorting prescription narcotics at parties? 
Setting porn and group sex aside, there’s something every boy should be taught. Something simple. When someone is vulnerable, you protect them. If a young woman is too intoxicated to take care of herself, you take care of her. Basic decency is basic because, well, it‘s part of being human. Maybe we should spend less time preparing our children for the Ivy Leagues and more time preparing them to be good human beings. For the final exam: the opportunity to be the one good man who steps up when nobody is watching…or maybe when everybody is watching.

text:
Some of you are charging a $400/month tech fee + pay per call because someone told you it was easy to sell.

Now you're stuck at ~$5K/month and hate the business you've built.

Here's what you need to change 👇

I consult and speak to hundreds of agency owners every week.

The same problem keeps coming up.

You sign small clients because they're easier to close.

They can only afford a few calls. You don't make much from each account.

So you sign more.

More campaigns. More client calls. More questions. More people to replace when they leave.

We has someone join Closing Clients System last week in this exact position:

12 leadgen clients.
Only $4K/month net.

It does NOT have to be this way.

But telling him to “just charge more” wouldn't fix it.

Here's what would:

1. Change WHO you're selling to

If your client makes very little from each customer you bring them, there's a limit to what they can pay you.

Before you sign them, ask:

→ What does a customer pay you over the time they stay?
→ How much do you keep after delivering the work?
→ How many qualified sales calls turn into customers?
→ How many new customers can your team handle?

You want clients with a proven offer, money to spend and the ability to close and fulfil the business you bring them.

A client who can handle 50 calls and profit from them is a very different account from one who can barely handle 5.

You don't necessarily need a new industry.

You might just need bigger, better businesses in the industry where you already have results.

2. Stop pitching “we'll book you calls”

Tell them WHO you'll connect them with and WHAT those people would buy.

If an agency sells paid ads to e-commerce brands, “we get agencies more leads” tells them very little.

Your approach should explain:

→ Which e-commerce brands you'll target
→ Why those brands would need their service
→ How you'll reach the person who buys it
→ What you've done for a similar client

Now you're having a conversation about getting them customers for the thing they sell.

They can see you've thought about THEIR business.

3. Put a number on the opportunity during the sales call

Ask:

“How many new customers do you want over the next 3 months?”

“What would those customers be worth to you?”

“What's stopping you getting them now?”

Then work through the calls required using their real close rate.

If they want 5 customers and close 20% of qualified, attended calls, you need 25 of those calls.

Check they can handle the customers. Check you can deliver the calls.

Now explain your fee against that specific result.

You've given them a reason to pay you more than the guy offering a cheap tech fee and some calls.

4. Charge for the work you do BEFORE the calls arrive

If you're researching their market, building their prospect list, writing the campaign and setting everything up, show them that work.

Explain exactly what gets built and what the engagement fee pays for.

Don't bury all of that inside a $400/month tech fee and hope you make it back later.

Then agree the ongoing fee, what makes a call qualified and the delivery target.

Before you sign another account, work out:

→ What they'll pay you
→ What delivery will cost
→ What it costs you to sign them
→ How long they're likely to stay

More clients won't fix a business where you barely make anything from each one.

Stop signing whoever says yes.

Find clients who can make enough from your work to pay you properly.

The Carbyne trail reaches Utah Valley before Charlie’s death. UVU’s own after-action review identifies Metro Dispatch as the center handling incoming 911 calls for UVU police, Orem, Provo and Lindon.

In October 2023, Carbyne published an account of Metro’s deployment. Manager Heather Perkins said its Universe platform had gone live on August 28. Her example was practical: a caller’s video helped dispatchers assess a brush fire.

Provo’s payment record lists $15,000 to Carbyne on September 12, 2023. A week later, council minutes describe a text sent to callers that allows them to share pictures or video with dispatch. The minutes also say that material could be shared with first responders. Perkins said the grant covered a year and that she would seek continued funding.

That is why this matters to Charlie. A call for help can create more than an audio recording. Depending on the product and configuration actually used, it can also create messages, location information and caller-supplied media.

The missing link is the September 10, 2025 operating record. I have the announced deployment and the university’s identification of Metro’s role. I do not yet have the renewal, enabled-feature record or incident logs showing which calls used Universe that day.

I want those questions answered at the level of individual records: which incident-related calls reached Metro; whether a multimedia session opened; what was received; where the original was stored; and who viewed, exported or shared it.

UVU’s campus dispatch also had its own service-request role. The report lists documenting calls, assigning officers and bookmarking security video among its duties. That gives us a second set of records to follow. Treating every dispatch function as one system would obscure where evidence might have originated.

A vendor announcement cannot establish an incident’s full chain of custody. But an identified deployment at the identified 911 center gives a concrete reason to ask for that chain.

text:
Since 1987, small US companies have trailed big ones this badly only twice: in the dot-com bubble and in 2025. They're back there now.

The S&P 500 is 0.3% from its record. Small companies are 7% below their record and down four weeks in a row.

Earnings are carrying the market, and a few big names are carrying the earnings. So the question is, where are 5% bond yields already doing damage? Small companies.

The Russell 2000, an index of about 2,000 smaller US companies, closed at 2,847 on Oct 5.

That's 7.2% below its Aug 14 record. Over the last three months, it fell 5% while the S&P 500 rose 3.9%. Q3 was small caps' worst quarter against the S&P 500 since early 2020.

The reason is debt.

Goldman Sachs estimates that about 30% of Russell 2000 companies' debt is floating-rate, meaning the interest bill rises as soon as rates do. For the S&P 500, it's 7%.

And more than 40% of Russell 2000 companies don't make a profit. With the 10-year at 5.28% and the Fed hiking again, a company that borrows to stay alive gets hit first.

Plus, the money is leaving the index too. IWM, the biggest Russell 2000 fund, lost $3.3 billion in one week in September, its third-largest weekly outflow in nine years, the Kobeissi Letter reported.

This is what I flagged yesterday.

The broad US market is less than 1% below its peak, yet more than half of its stocks have fallen 20% or more from a high since June 1. The giants hide it.

Here's what seems interesting.

Profitable small companies are still growing. The S&P 600 is a small-cap index that admits only profitable businesses. Since early July, analysts have raised its profit forecast by 3%. Over the same time, the index fell about 8%. Investors used to pay 16.1 times expected earnings for these companies. Now they pay 14.4.

That's the same pattern I showed for the big index earlier today: profits up, price per dollar of profit down. Small caps just offer it at a lower price.

The bulls have a case emphasized by the fact that Russell 2000 trades about 34% below its 20-year average valuation.

Even so, buying the whole index feels like the wrong bet. The Russell may be an early warning sign that the economy is tilting fast: tech is driving more and more of overall growth, and the rest of the market can’t keep pace.

Perhaps never will?

text:
The S&P 500 is up 14% in a year. Expected earnings are up 37%. The market got cheaper while going up.

I want businesses that grow profits fast and don't cost too much. Right now the whole index is offering exactly that.

A year ago, analysts expected the S&P 500 to earn about $294 per share over the next 12 months. Today they expect $403. That's 37% more profit in one year.

The good part is that you are paying less for more.

The forward P/E, what investors pay for each dollar of next year's profit, fell from 22.8 to 19.0. The whole 14% gain came from earnings. Prices just didn't keep up.

I mean if you liked the S&P at 22.8 times earnings a year ago, today you get a much faster-growing business for 17% less.

That's the setup I hunt for in single stocks. Seeing it across the whole index is rare.

So why am I not all in? Bonds.

Flip the P/E upside down and you get the earnings yield: how much profit $100 of stock buys you. At 19 times earnings, every $100 in the S&P buys about $5.26 of next year's profit.

A 10-year Treasury paid $5.28 on Oct 2, guaranteed, the highest since 2002.

A year ago it was $4.39 for stocks against $4.13 for the bond. Stocks paid you a little extra for taking the risk. Investors call that extra the equity risk premium. Today it's about zero and the risk-free coupon is 28% higher.

So owning stocks pays you nothing extra today. You are betting entirely on growth. That's a bet I'm comfortable with, because growth is what I look at first. The bond's $5.28 never grows.

If S&P profits grow just 10% next year, the $5.26 becomes about $5.79 on today's price. As long as that gap keeps opening, I'll take the stocks.

Central banks aren't making it easier. The Fed, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan all hiked in September, the first time all three raised in the same month. That pushes the yields even higher.

The risk is simple.

If earnings growth slows while the 10-year stays above 5%, stocks pay the same as a risk-free bond with all the risk still attached. Our MRMI still says play defense, and I'm partly listening to it.

Q3 earnings season starts in mid-October, with the big banks first. If profits keep beating, 19 times looks cheap. If companies cut their outlooks with yields this high, that's when I get defensive for real.

The next question is who is actually producing those earnings. Spoiler: not everyone.

"Although a number of legal tech companies use LLM consensus and multiple model strategies already, Pilot5 and its new adversarial Legal AI product specifically taps five frontier models with ‘one assigned to attack the emerging consensus and the lawyer receives a single recommendation’ to their query.

text:
The S&P and Nasdaq had just touched new highs when overnight futures started giving the gains back. The market has not suddenly stopped believing in AI; it is repricing “money” and “electricity.”

Over the past twelve hours, what has actually been reposted again and again is not any single star stock rising a few points, but three things stacking together: the 30-year Treasury yield back near highs not seen since 2002, Brent back above $100, and the September FOMC minutes still not out. At the same time, the AI capex story is still being dialed up. SpaceX is reportedly raising about $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips, and Microsoft and Jensen Huang are set to unveil a laptop today that can run agents locally. The money to buy the chips, the electricity to run them, and the rate used to discount long-term projects are all getting more expensive at the same time.

This round of discussion shows the market is trading “demand is still there, but financing conditions and energy are no longer free.” The noise is individual product launches and emotional short slogans on memory stocks. What actually matters over the next twelve hours is this afternoon’s 10-year Treasury auction and the minutes—whether they turn “another hike in December” from verbal pricing into market pricing.

Memory is sharper. Micron’s Taoyuan union in Taiwan won strike authorization by an overwhelming vote. Timing is undecided and the company says talks continue, but discussion boards are already using it to cool the HBM premium. Seagate and Western Digital’s sharp drop in the prior session shows capital is dismantling the assumption that “memory will be short forever,” not trading a production halt that has already happened. On the other side, Marvell raising its growth guidance, AMD talking about demand remaining strong over the next few years, and Constellation Energy surging on a Google nuclear deal all show money is still moving downstream along the compute chain: chips, networking, and power.

Record highs are a result, not a reason. If the minutes lean hawkish, the auction sees weak demand, and oil gets another push from Hormuz headlines, the tech pullback is not a “healthy consolidation”—it is the discount rate reclaiming valuation. If the auction is orderly and the minutes offer no new path, today’s futures decline is mostly overnight noise. The laptop event is worth watching; do not treat it as a fundamental inflection.

Not investment advice—just a summary of market chatter.

text:
标普和纳指刚摸到新高，隔夜期货就开始往回吐。市场不是突然不信 AI 了，它是在重新给“钱”和“电”标价。

过去十二小时，真正被反复转发的不是某一只明星股涨了几个点，而是三件事叠在一起：三十年期美债收益率回到 2002 年以来高位附近，布伦特重新站上 100 美元，9 月 FOMC 纪要还没出。与此同时，AI 资本开支故事还在加码。SpaceX 据报要筹约 400 亿美元买英伟达芯片，微软和黄仁勋今天要发布能在本地跑智能体的笔记本。买芯片的钱、跑芯片的电、给长期项目贴现的利率，却在同时变贵。

这轮热议说明，市场交易的是“需求还在，融资条件和能源不再免费”。噪音是单条产品发布，以及存储股上的情绪化空头口号。下一个十二小时真正重要的，是今天下午的十年期国债拍卖和会议纪要，会不会把“12 月还要再加息”从口头定价变成盘面定价。

存储这边更尖锐。美光台湾桃园工会以压倒性票数拿到罢工授权，时点未定，公司说继续谈；但讨论区已经用它给高带宽内存溢价降温。希捷、西部数据前一交易日的大跌，说明资金在拆“记忆体永远缺”这个假设，不是在交易一份已经落地的停产。另一边，Marvell 上调增长指引、AMD 谈未来几年需求仍强、星座能源因为谷歌核电协议大涨，又说明钱还在往算力链条下游走：芯片、网络、电力。

纪录高点是结果，不是理由。纪要偏鹰、拍卖需求差、油价再被霍尔木兹标题推一把，科技股回吐就不是“健康整理”，而是贴现率在收回估值。拍卖平稳、纪要没有新路径，今天的期货下跌多半是隔夜噪音。笔记本发布会可以看，别把它当成基本面拐点。

非投资建议，仅为舆情整理。

text:
Washington wants Latin America under its security umbrella. Cocaine is the sales pitch. Yet bigger deployments and louder victory speeches have not answered the obvious question: why does the drug trade keep expanding?

Cartels do not wait for a committee meeting. They reroute shipments, replace crews and move cash while agencies argue over jurisdiction. The DEA, US Navy and local forces can all announce a successful operation without producing a successful strategy. A seized cargo makes good television. The replacement cargo rarely gets a camera crew.

The political bargain is easier to follow. Regional leaders offer access, cooperation and a friendly line toward Washington; Washington offers backing and fewer awkward questions. Allegations of criminal ties should not disappear because an ally signs the right security agreement. Loyalty is not a background check.

China is the other target in this campaign for influence. Military access and economic leverage last longer than a drug bust. That does not prove every raid is a sham. It does mean voters should ask what success looks like: fewer drugs and safer streets, or more US control? Those are not the same thing.

text:
Canada is turning toward Europe—again.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is pursuing a deeper economic and security partnership with the European Union as Canada tries to reduce its dependence on the United States.

It sounds new. But Canada confronted a remarkably similar problem more than 50 years ago.

In 1969, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau famously described the Canada/US relationship this way:

“Living next to you is in some ways like sleeping with an elephant.”

Two years later, President Richard Nixon imposed a 10% surcharge on American imports. Canada expected an exemption because the two economies were so closely connected.

It didn’t get one.

The “Nixon Shock” exposed an uncomfortable reality: Canadian jobs and exports depended heavily on the United States, but Canada had little control over decisions made in Washington.

At the same time, American companies owned large portions of Canadian industry, while Britain’s entry into the European Economic Community weakened Canada’s traditional economic relationship across the Atlantic.

In 1972, Trudeau’s government responded with the “Third Option.”

Canada could maintain the existing relationship, integrate more closely with the United States—or strengthen its domestic economy while developing new markets in Europe, Japan and elsewhere.

Trudeau chose the third.

Canada eventually signed an economic cooperation agreement with Europe in 1976. But the policy never substantially reduced its dependence on the United States.

Historian and former diplomat Paul Meyer attributes that failure to “the powerful pull of geography and the inertia of established trading patterns.”

Today, Canada is looking toward Europe once again—through trade, defence, critical minerals, energy and technology.

The Third Option offers both inspiration and a warning:

Canada can diversify its partnerships.

But overcoming the economic pull of the elephant next door has never been easy.

text:
Wednesday's window is a China hardware day wearing an application-layer costume. Huawei is pushing its homegrown chip line deeper into shipping phones, a Washington think tank has put a hard number on China's lithography stockpile, and a Chinese lab landed a memory-endurance result in Science. Meanwhile most of the model news is a promise with a date attached to it.

Start with Huawei, because it is the one story here with real units moving. The company is accelerating its self-developed Tau chip architecture across the new Mate 90 series while the Mate XT 2 trifold closes on a million sales and expands overseas, all of it under US export curbs, per the South China Morning Post. Separately, rotating chairman Xu Zhijun says Ascend AI chips now hold 50 percent of the Chinese market against Nvidia's 8 percent — a reversal he dates to 2022 — with Huawei leaning on its Peerium architecture and UnifiedBus interconnect to route around advanced-node limits. Take that split with the salt it deserves: it is a company defining a market it partly fills with its own silicon, and no independent shipment data backs the 50-versus-8 framing. The volume story is the credible one. A trifold phone approaching a million units at that price point is demand the sanctions never touched.

The number that should worry policymakers is 343. A Washington think tank estimates Chinese-owned fabs had acquired roughly that many immersion DUV lithography systems by early 2026, prompting former US officials to press for a total Western blockade on tool exports, the South China Morning Post reports. Export controls govern flow, not inventory. Whatever gets announced next is a debate about what China can still buy, not what it already owns — and the stockpile is the part of this story that no new rule can unwind.

Then the actual engineering, which is where this window earns its keep. Chinese researchers demonstrated a 100-fold endurance improvement in wurtzite ferroelectric memory, passing 10 billion write cycles by restricting nitrogen-vacancy movement, published in Science. Endurance was the barrier keeping ferroelectric memory out of high-performance computing and AI workloads, and a lab result clearing 10 billion cycles is a real step toward candidacy. Not a product, not a fab process, not something to price into a roadmap — but this is the category of news that ages well.

SenseTime, by contrast, is selling a category name. It unveiled SenseMart OS, a "physical operating system" for retail tying together robots, store equipment and commercial operations, with its SenseMart Go robotic stores already running in more than 20 locations across China. "Physical operating system" is a phrase from a press release, not a spec sheet, and 20 stores is a pilot, not a platform. Watch the deployment count, not the vocabulary — embodied retail is one of the few places where autonomy claims get audited at a cash register.

The day's biggest number is also its least corroborated. AMD has reportedly agreed to an all-stock deal worth about $8.2 billion for World Labs, the spatial-intelligence lab co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, who would join the chipmaker as executive vice president and chief scientist once the transaction closes. One report, one all-stock price, no independent confirmation in this batch. Chipmakers buying model labs is the fashion of the year; an all-stock figure is a currency swap wearing a valuation's clothes until filings show up.

Humanoid robots produced the window's best argument for never trusting a single number. People's Daily reports Chinese humanoid shipments hit 40,000 units in the first half of 2026 — 97 percent of the global total — and frames the industry's yardstick as shifting from running and jumping to whether a robot can grasp, assemble and handle tools. IDC, via TechNode, puts the same half-year at just over 19,000 units, 77.9 percent of a worldwide total that grew 432.1 percent year on year, with a 2030 forecast above 750,000. Both counts cannot be describing the same denominator, and neither write-up reconciles its definitions. The directional claim — China dominates humanoid manufacturing and dexterous hands are the real frontier — survives. The percentages do not.

ByteDance's personal-agent push arrived twice in one morning and contradicted itself. One report describes Doubao working on an agent internally codenamed Spell, tested since April, moving from chatbot answers toward autonomous task completion. A second says the company is trialling a personal assistant tentatively named Xiaodou, meant to ship as a standalone app, with the name and features still in flux. Two names, two framings, one product that has not shipped — the shape of nearly every agent announcement this year.

Ant Group's InclusionAI pushed out Ling-3.1-flash: 560 billion parameters with roughly 25 billion active per token, aimed at agent tasks, search and office software. The trial runs two weeks at a 256,000-token context, with open-source release and a one-million-token window promised afterward. Note the structure — the verifiable artifacts today are a parameter count and a capped trial, while every headline capability sits on the far side of the trial. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 turned up somewhere more interesting: reachable through OpenAI's enterprise Codex channel via US inference provider Baseten, letting enterprise customers bill usage against existing OpenAI spending commitments. Sina Finance calls it the first time a Chinese open model has entered OpenAI's enterprise billing system — that framing is Sina's, not OpenAI's, and the contractual details are worth waiting for before anyone calls it a distribution breakthrough. Meituan moved LongCat-2.5-Preview to its API platform with image understanding and improved coding, a release note with no benchmark and no artifact. And Tencent is recruiting closed-beta testers for Goose Dimension, an AI game companion that reportedly handles voice chat and recognises on-screen gameplay, while confirming almost nothing about what it does. That is the entire announcement.

Two regulatory items from Beijing deserve more than they got elsewhere in this batch. The Payment and Clearing Association issued a self-regulatory convention for agentic payments, requiring members to build "know your agent" mechanisms, define authorisation boundaries and cap transaction amounts — the first serious attempt to fit autonomous spenders inside payments rules, and a template other jurisdictions will copy or fight. And an Economic Daily commentary took direct aim at local AI industrial policy, naming a subsidy race of near-identical schemes, low disbursement rates and duplicated projects and asking for tiered, locally tailored programs instead. Self-criticism of this kind from a state-affiliated outlet is the closest thing to a policy signal you get without a document number.

The rest of the policy layer was thin. A commentary on AI plus transportation claimed concrete gains in ports, railways and postal logistics while listing chip, sensor and data-barrier bottlenecks as unresolved. A national Corpus Innovation Ecosystem Alliance launched in Beijing with 50 founding institutions, 42 scientific corpus standards and a new journal — infrastructure that matters in aggregate and cannot be judged on day one. The Chinese Academy of Sciences' Panshi research intelligence platform shipped version 1.0 alongside an initiative close to 100 research institutes have joined. The science association put two models on stage at its New Tiangong Kaiwu showcase: the Lizhi Uni-MoE multimodal model and the Caihua MatVerse materials foundation model. And a brain-computer interface forum delivered the usual root-technology rhetoric alongside a genuinely necessary warning about neural data privacy and human agency.

Elsewhere: MIPS says it is working unusually closely with Chinese firms on RISC-V standardisation as the open architecture pushes past automotive, industrial and IoT uses into physical AI and data centres — the one corner of US-China technical collaboration the chip rivalry has not closed. A column argues Alibaba's Xianyu can defend its second-hand e-commerce lead under new CEO Wang Chengyuan with an AI-plus-community strategy; it is an argument published during a content-moderation controversy, and the evidence offered is the strategy itself. One item has nothing to do with AI, which is exactly why it is here: Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers proposed driving direct seawater electrolysis with alternating current so hydroxide ions are consumed before they can form magnesium and calcium precipitates, the bottleneck that has long crippled the approach, with proof-of-concept work across three reaction systems in Angewandte Chemie.

The tail was three LoRA drops for FLUX and SDXL, a robot photo gallery from the China-ASEAN Expo, and a headline redefining AI as superintelligence that arrived bundled with a domain-registration statistic. Nothing there needs your attention.

The through-line is simple. Hardware and policy are compounding; applications are still mostly promises with launch dates attached. And if two respectable sources can count the same six months of humanoid shipments 40,000 and 19,000 units apart, treat every deployment statistic in this sector as a draft.

☀️ PREMARKET FLOW: WED 10/7 🌊

Futures were red overnight and are bouncing: SPX -11.25 (-0.14%), NASDAQ -129.25 (-0.41%), DOW -178 (-0.34%),

The macro engine this morning is yields, oil, and two geopolitical escalations. Yields: the 10y is ~5.307% (+3.6bp), back near Monday's 24-year high of 5.349%, and the 30y is ~5.68-5.70%, the highest since 2002. The October skip is now the base case: Polymarket has the hold at 82.5% (+2pp overnight, $625K 24h volume) with the 25bp hike down to 16.5%, and December is the live meeting at 74.5% for a 25bp hike. The 2:00pmSeptember FOMC minutes today are the test of how close the last hike was and whether anyone wanted 50bp, with the caveat that they predate the payrolls miss and the "no urgency" pivot. The $39B 10y auction at 1:00pm is the another test after yesterday's $58B 3y barely cleared: 4.932%, the highest yield since May 2006, on a 2.62x cover with the weakest foreign demand since February. The uncomfortable read nobody reconciles: the bond market prices a fiscal/supply risk the rate-odds story doesn't, which is why the 10y barely budged off its 24-year high after the hike story was pushed to December.

Oil: Brent is back over the big $100 mark and WTI sits near $90. The tug-of-war is intact: Kpler shows Hormuz crude flows down to 74% of prewar after a week of tanker attacks (WSJ), while the bypass routes keep headline exports near prewar, Saudi's East-West line pumping ~5.8M bpd per the energy minister's claim, and Vitol's CEO saying ~12M bpd of crude left the Middle East in the last 7-10 days. The market doesn't expect normalization anytime soon: Polymarket has Hormuz traffic normal by year-end at just 17.5% (-1pp). Underneath, the EIA's October outlook raised Brent's 2026 average to $96.32 and the Q4 average to $105, flagging extreme distillate tightness with East Coast inventories 20-30% below the 5-year average, and refined-product exports still sit at only 50-58% of 2025 levels. A Gulf storm that may become 2026's first Atlantic hurricane is a second supply tailwind. 10:30am brings the EIA petroleum report, with API's -2.1M draw overnight diverging from the +1.7M build consensus.

On Iran, VP Vance set the public bar for ending the war: a "meaningful" reduction in enrichment capacity, "not words for actions," while admitting Washington doesn't know who makes decisions in Tehran. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer and warned operations could intensify after the midterms. The Fairford plot details got sharper: a multi-stage IRGC operation with UK-recruited operatives and weaponized drones launched near the base, five British men arrested plus a dual UK-Iranian national, the UK prime minister citing "strong indications" of Iranian involvement. That's an attack vector inside a NATO ally, qualitatively different from the strait, and the market isn't pricing it.

Single names: yesterday's prints were strong across the board. $LW beat by $0.16 (adj EPS $0.75 vs $0.59), raised FY27 guidance to $3.05-3.35, +7.5%. $RPM beat ($1.98 vs $1.95) on record $2.22B sales, +2.5%. $APOG nearly doubled the street ($1.17 vs $0.59), raised guidance, +13-20%. $STZ reported before the open (not after, as we listed yesterday): comp EPS $3.74 vs $3.55, beer +5%, acquired SpikedAde for $75M, +2.6%. text:
BOTH COASTS HIT: THE AMERICAN UMBRELLA OVER SAUDI OIL IS GONE

Tuesday, October 6, brought a set of satellite frames almost nobody in the Western press is leading with. They show damage at the Jeddah refinery, hit two days earlier, on the same Red Sea coast as Yanbu. Yemen is striking both ends of Saudi oil. The shield Riyadh paid for is not there.

THE FRAMES
➡️ New satellite images show the extent of the damage at the Jeddah refinery.
➡️ This is the first time those frames are coming out.
➡️ They appear to be released from the Iranian side, not from Riyadh or Washington.
➡️ Reports two days earlier had already said Jeddah was attacked.
➡️ The strike lands on the oil facility itself, close to Yanbu.

BOTH ENDS OF THE BARREL
➡️ What Yemen is doing inside Saudi Arabia is simple.
➡️ Both sides are being hit, the eastern coast and the western coast, and the pipeline between them.
➡️ Jeddah on the Red Sea. Yanbu beside it. The export workaround and the plant in the same picture.
➡️ A drone strike the same night is reported to have killed a Pakistani commander inside Saudi Arabia, with casualties called high.
➡️ That is a war on the infrastructure, not a headline about a border skirmish.

THE UMBRELLA THAT WAS NOT THERE
➡️ Asked what defensive help the United States is actually providing inside the Kingdom, the answer is: apparently not much.
➡️ PAC-3 and Patriot batteries might work against drones.
➡️ They do not work against the ballistic missiles the Houthis are firing.
➡️ America is not sitting on warehouses of unused weapons it can happily hand over.
➡️ The United States is under a lot of pressure, so it cannot do a lot for Saudi Arabia.
➡️ That is one of the shocking discoveries for the Saudis.
➡️ They thought the Americans had their back. Then they realized the Americans were nowhere to be seen.

NOBODY ELSE IS COMING
➡️ Pakistan and Turkey are the other names on the card. They bring nothing.
➡️ A Pakistani defense minister denied the troop report, in an interview carried by Al Mayadeen.
➡️ “We’re not going to commit troops to the fight with the Houthis.”
➡️ Put Pakistani or Turkish batteries on Saudi soil and it is still not clear they do any good.
➡️ They do not have much to offer.

THE PROXY STORY
➡️ Riyadh is fighting through a proxy army in Yemen and losing badly.
➡️ They lost yesterday. They are losing again today.
➡️ Claims of advances and of heavy airstrikes read as gaslighting.
➡️ Air power only matters if controllers on the ground can pass exact coordinates to the pilot.
➡️ The Saudi-backed PLC forces do not appear to have that capability.
➡️ The map marks newly captured ground in blue, moving in Ansar Allah’s favor.

THE FORCE MATH
➡️ The Saudi land force is about 75,000.
➡️ Add the National Guard, about 125,000.
➡️ All services together, maybe 225,000 active.
➡️ Across the border sits a Yemeni force of 350,000 that can ramp to 800,000.
➡️ The Saudis do not even have the force necessary to take on and effectively fight the Houthis.
➡️ Inside the GCC there is nobody of consequence. No large standing armies. Hired guns, not citizens fighting for a flag.

THE BOTTOM LINE
The pictures of the Jeddah refinery are out. The pipeline is being hit from both coasts. The Patriot screen is not stopping the missiles, Pakistan has denied the troops, and the proxy army is losing ground. The point the coverage keeps stepping around is this: Saudi oil infrastructure is being destroyed, and the umbrella Riyadh trusted is nowhere to be seen.

text:
If you’re an e-commerce brand, here’s what I’d actually do with your email marketing in October before BFCM:

1. Start growing the list now

Don’t wait until BFCM week to suddenly care about email capture.

Look at your current popup conversion rate first.

Then test ONE meaningful change every week in October (if you haven't already):

• Offer: 10% off vs. $10 off vs. giveaway
• Timing: 5 seconds vs. 15 seconds
• Trigger: time-based vs. exit intent
• Creative: product-led vs. offer-led

The goal is simple: get more of October’s traffic onto your list so you have several weeks to nurture them before BFCM.

2. Wake up people who have stopped engaging

Build a segment of subscribers who used to engage but haven’t opened or clicked recently.

Send them 2–3 emails specifically designed to get a signal from them:

• “Which one would you pick?” with 2 products
• Your best-selling product + why people buy it
• A genuinely useful piece of content related to what you sell

Now you’re learning who is still paying attention BEFORE your biggest sale of the year.

3. Start collecting product-interest signals

If someone clicks your moisturizer 3 times in October, that matters.

If someone keeps browsing your running shorts collection, that matters too.

Create segments around your biggest BFCM product categories based on clicks, browsing behavior, and past purchases.

When November comes, you don’t have to send the exact same message to everyone.

4. Check the flows that all these new subscribers are entering

Go through your Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Checkout Abandonment and Post-Purchase flows.

Actually read them like a customer.

Are there outdated offers?
Broken links?
Old products?
Emails that haven’t been touched in a year?

Fix those immediately.

5. Start watching your engaged audience grow

Create a 30-day engaged segment now and note how many people are in it.

Check it again every week through October.

That number is a much better BFCM asset!!!

PS. Overall, keep things simple. Don't complicate everything.

text:
CDE MAHOMVA CHALLENGES CITIZENS: DEVELOPMENT IS A TWO-WAY STREET, NOT A GOVERNMENT SOLO ACT 

A fresh wake-up call on national development has come from Cde Richard Mahomva, who argues that citizens cannot keep demanding a better country while shirking their own share of the bargain.

At the heart of his message is a principle the social contract debate often ignores: reciprocity. Yes, the State owes citizens service delivery, accountability and a functioning economy. But citizens, too, owe something back to the society they expect the State to build.

Nowhere is this clearer than in the fight against corruption. Bribes are not only taken, they are offered. Shortcuts are not only created, they are sought. Every envelope passed at a roadblock and every backdoor deal for public resources chips away at the very institutions citizens later expect to work for them.

The same hard truth applies to productivity. The worker who takes pride in output, the entrepreneur who hunts for new markets and the citizen who guards public property are not just minding their own business, they are nation-builders in their own right.

His conclusion is blunt: a country cannot out-develop the habits of its people.

The social contract, then, is not a one-sided petition. It is a two-question deal, what must the State deliver, and what must citizens contribute?

text:
If you still think $XRP will stop here, read every word. 

This is a long one, but I think it will wake you up to how big the next phase really is.

I want you to forget the price for a minute.

Forget the candles.
Forget what happened this week.

Look at the system being built underneath $XRP.

Because Ayo Akinyele just gave one of the clearest explanations I have seen of where XRPL is heading.

At XRP Seoul, Ripple’s Senior Director of Engineering laid out four priorities:

Trust.
Confidentiality.
Scale.
AI agents.

Those four words completely changed how I connect the next stage of XRP’s utility.

My biggest takeaway is simple:

XRP may be moving toward an economy where software becomes one of its users.

And software does not sleep.

It does not take weekends.
It does not get tired of rebalancing a treasury.
It does not care about crypto tribalism.
It searches for rules, permissions, liquidity, cost and settlement certainty.

Then it acts.

Ayo described AI agents as software “driving economic activity.”

That distinction matters.

A chatbot can answer a question.
An economic agent can move money.

It can own a wallet.
Pay for a service.
Buy compute.
Pay for AI inference.
Trade.
Manage liquidity.
Interact with markets.

And XRPL already has tooling built for this.

Ripple launched the XRPL AI Starter Kit on June 9, 2026.

It supports agent interaction with the ledger and x402 payments using XRP and RLUSD.

The x402 process is almost painfully simple.

The software requests something.
The service asks for payment.

The agent pays.

XRPL settles.

The service receives proof.
The software keeps going.

Nobody types card information.
Nobody creates a billing account manually.
Nobody has to wake up at 3 AM to approve a tiny machine payment.

That changes the meaning of a financial user.

And the numbers show something is already happening.

Earlier in the year, Ayo said XRPL agentic activity had passed 1 million transactions.

At XRP Seoul, reporting cited him saying the figure had exceeded 11 million.

Tracking around October 3 placed x402-related XRPL payments around 11.97 million with more than 500,000 per day over the preceding seven days.

Roughly one million became roughly twelve million within months.

Now ask yourself what happens when the software evolves beyond buying APIs.

XRPL already has a Trading Skill.

An agent can read the XRPL DEX order book.

Create limit orders.
Cancel orders.

Interact with AMM and trading infrastructure.

Payments can become trading.

Trading can become liquidity management.

Liquidity management can become treasury management.

And Ripple Treasury is already using AI agents across liquidity, forecasting, risk, reconciliation and reporting through GSmart.

Its September 10 expansion added policy-governed treasury agents with customer-defined rules and audit trails.

Ripple Treasury says its network connects to 13,000 banks and provides visibility across $12.5 trillion in payment volume.

I find that convergence fascinating.

RippleX is developing a ledger capable of serving autonomous software.

Ripple Treasury is putting agents into real treasury workflows.

The financial industry is moving assets onchain.

The pieces are moving toward each other.

A machine economy needs a very different kind of blockchain infrastructure.

It needs certainty.

XRPL gives 3 to 5 second deterministic finality.

If an agent pays for an API, it needs to know the exact result because its next action depends on the answer.

Success means continue.

Expiration means stop or retry.

Software cannot run serious financial workflows around vague settlement.

That is why Ayo begins with trust.

XRPL has operated since 2012.

Ripple has reported more than 4 billion processed transactions, more than 7 million active wallets and around 120 independent validators.

Then the ledger is gaining infrastructure for operations far more complex than ordinary payments.

Batch Transactions can group up to eight transactions.

Atomic mode allows the entire group to succeed together.

Picture an autonomous financial agent doing this:

Acquire asset.

Post collateral.

Settle payment.

Pay fee.

Transfer ownership.

Five actions.

One economic decision.

If the workflow requires every component to complete, the machine needs a system capable of treating them as one coordinated event.

Batch helps move XRPL in that direction.

XRPL 3.3.0 introduced BatchV1_1, ConfidentialTransfer, DynamicMPT, PermissionDelegationV1_1 and Sponsor.

XRPL 3.4.1 brought further Batch hardening.

fixBatchV1_2 was expected to activate on October 9, 2026 if validator support stayed above the threshold.

Now bring institutions into the same picture.

Ayo said financial activity is moving onchain.

We can already see it.

Ondo’s OUSG is live on XRPL.

It supports 24/7 minting and redemption using RLUSD.

Its structure includes exposure to BlackRock’s BUIDL.

Guggenheim Treasury Services-administered digital commercial paper is issued natively on XRPL through Zeconomy.

It is secured by U.S. Treasuries and carries a Prime-1 Moody’s rating.

Aviva Investors has plans with Ripple to tokenize traditional fund structures on XRPL through 2026 and beyond.

CSD BR began using XRPL on September 29 as an additional recording and audit layer for financial assets, starting with BTG Pactual investment-fund shares.

Now think about what autonomous software eventually has available to manage.

A ledger containing Treasury products.

Commercial paper.
Fund shares.
Stablecoins.
Credit instruments.
RLUSD.
XRP.
Future tokenized assets.

That is a much richer economy than a payment chain.

And the number of possible financial routes rises with every new asset.

Imagine five assets.

The routing problem is manageable.

Imagine hundreds.

Then thousands.

Bank deposit tokens.

Dollar stablecoins.

Euro stablecoins.

Money-market funds.

Tokenized bonds.

Private credit.

Commercial paper.

Funds.

Securities.

The number of potential asset pairs grows rapidly.

Deep direct liquidity between every possible pair is inefficient.

A common bridge becomes more useful.

XRP was designed for bridge liquidity from the beginning.

Now place an AI agent on top of that liquidity.

The machine does not care about XRP Twitter.

It does not care whether someone called one token better than another.

It runs the numbers.

If Asset A to XRP to Asset B gives the best route, it can choose XRP.

Automatically.

Over and over.

That could completely change the emotional side of the XRP bridge debate.

Humans argue.

Algorithms route.

Software can choose the cheapest path thousands of times without forming an opinion about the token.

For me, that may become one of the purest utility cases imaginable.

And the native role does not end at liquidity.

x402 supports direct XRP payments.

An agent can earn XRP.

Hold XRP.

Spend XRP.

Every ordinary XRPL transaction also consumes XRP through the network fee.

The current standard minimum is 10 drops before load scaling.

The fee for one transaction is tiny.

Machine scale changes the conversation.

One human might make five transactions.

One agent could make thousands.

One company could deploy thousands of agents.

Ripple Treasury cites Gartner projections suggesting an average Fortune 500 company could eventually operate more than 150,000 agents by 2028.

Imagine only a small percentage receiving authority to perform financial actions.

That still produces an enormous new category of economic actor.

Account reserves create another connection.

Institutional accounts.

Agent wallets.

Applications.

They all interact with XRPL’s reserve system.

Sponsored Fees and Reserves could allow enterprises to centralize those costs and hide the blockchain friction from the end user.

Imagine a bank creating one million wallets.

The customers never need to learn how to buy XRP on an exchange just to activate the experience.

The bank sponsors the infrastructure.

Underneath that interface, XRP still carries the network resource requirement.

That feels much closer to mass financial adoption.

People do not need to understand TCP/IP before opening a website.

Future users may not need to understand every XRPL mechanic before using a tokenized financial product.

The infrastructure can disappear behind the application.

Institutions also need privacy.

A public financial network cannot expose every commercially sensitive position forever.

Imagine J.P. Morgan moving a large block.

BlackRock managing a position.

A hedge fund rebalancing.

A corporate treasury moving hundreds of millions.

A market maker shifting liquidity.

A securities depository processing sensitive activity.

They cannot broadcast every detail to every competitor.

XLS-96 Confidential Transfers changes what becomes possible.

It uses EC-ElGamal encryption and zero-knowledge proofs to conceal individual balances and transfer amounts while allowing overall supply to remain verifiable.

Balances can be encrypted for the holder.

The issuer.

An optional auditor.

The public sees what needs to remain public.

Authorized parties can access what needs oversight.

That is serious financial architecture.

Think about an institution moving $250 million of tokenized Treasuries.

The counterparties know.

The issuer can know.

An authorized auditor can know.

The whole world does not need to know the position.

Now combine that privacy layer with Multi-Purpose Tokens.

MPTs support issuer controls, metadata, supply limits, freeze, clawback and authorization.

Suddenly XRPL has a much richer framework for tokenized funds, bonds, credit instruments and other financial claims.

Then add Permissioned Domains.

Enabled in February 2026.

Access can depend on accepted credentials.

A Permissioned DEX can exist.

A Lending Protocol can operate in a controlled market.

Institutions can use shared XRPL infrastructure with regulated access around a specific financial application.

Then add native lending.

Single-asset vaults.

Fixed-term lending.

Offchain underwriting.

Permissioned access.

First-loss protection structures.

A tokenized asset can move beyond simply sitting in an account.

It can become collateral.

It can enter credit.

It can generate liquidity.

It can support borrowing.

Financial markets begin forming around the assets.

Now add Permission Delegation.

One account can grant another limited authority over certain transaction types.

This could become extremely important for autonomous agents.

The agent does not need the master key.

It does not need unlimited treasury access.

The institution gives it a specific job.

Specific permissions.

Specific transaction types.

Authority can be revoked.

Then the Agent Wallet Skill separates transaction construction from key management and signing.

KMS/HSM external signers can protect the keys.

Open Wallet Standard can enforce policies and isolate keys across multiple agents.

SourceTag and Memos can identify which agent performed which action.

WebSocket monitoring can track activity.

Now picture a Fortune 500 treasury five years from now.

Agent #17 monitors dollar liquidity.

Agent #28 watches FX.

Agent #62 manages stablecoin balances.

Agent #91 monitors a Treasury portfolio.

Agent #133 routes payments.

Agent #204 watches credit conditions.

Each one operates inside defined policies.

Every action leaves a trail.

XRPL gives deterministic settlement.

And when liquidity routing touches multiple tokenized assets, XRP can sit in the middle whenever it produces the best execution.

That idea gets much larger once you see what is arriving around the ledger.

RLUSD had already reached $2.409 billion circulating as of September 24, backed by about $2.5315 billion in reserves.

Ondo is bringing tokenized Treasury exposure.

Guggenheim is bringing commercial paper.

Aviva Investors is preparing tokenized fund structures.

CSD BR and BTG Pactual are bringing regulated asset-recording use cases.

Ripple is expanding deeper into institutional finance beyond the ledger too.

On October 6, Ripple announced an expanded relationship with Brevan Howard.

Brevan Howard manages around $35 billion.

Ripple Prime will provide multi-asset prime brokerage, clearing and financing to its funds.

Brevan Howard affiliates also participated in Ripple’s earlier $500 million strategic investment.

Meanwhile Ripple is a Premier member of the Linux Foundation x402 Foundation.

Look at the names around that table.

Google.

AWS.

Visa.

Mastercard.

Stripe.

American Express.

Coinbase.

Cloudflare.

Shopify.

Circle.

Stellar.

More than 50 organizations are working around open internet-native payments for agents, APIs and applications.

Think about the direction of travel.

Traditional assets are becoming tokens.

Institutional finance is becoming more programmable.

AI agents are becoming economic participants.

Internet-native payment standards are emerging.

Treasury software is becoming autonomous.

Private financial activity needs compliant confidentiality.

Complex actions need atomic execution.

Machines need deterministic settlement.

Digital markets need liquidity.

XRPL is being engineered around those exact problems.

And XRP is already native to the network.

That is why my long-term thought around XRP keeps expanding.

The original vision focused heavily on bridging currencies.

I think the next version can become far larger.

A bridge among tokenized financial assets.

A machine sees:

tokenized deposit

to XRP

to tokenized Treasury.

Another sees:

fund token

to XRP

to RLUSD.

Another sees:

stablecoin

to XRP

to commercial paper.

Another sees a direct route without XRP and takes it.

Fine.

The point is that every additional asset creates more possible routing.

XRP does not need to win every route.

It needs deep enough liquidity to become the most efficient route often enough for software to select it automatically.

Now multiply those decisions by autonomous systems operating 24/7.

That is the part of the thesis I think people are seriously underestimating.

Machines can create economic activity at a frequency humans never could.

A human trader sleeps.

A treasury agent does not.

A human gets tired.

Software keeps checking.

A human manually handles one workflow.

An autonomous system can monitor thousands.

The entire network can move from human-speed finance toward machine-speed finance.

Ayo’s four pillars make perfect sense under that future.

Trust, because machines and institutions need definite execution.

Confidentiality, because financial positions cannot all be public.

Scale, because the number and complexity of operations can multiply.

AI agents, because software itself becomes a financial participant.

Then every other XRPL feature connects.

Credentials decide who can enter.

Permissioned Domains create controlled markets.

MPTs represent the assets.

Confidential Transfers protect balances and amounts.

Batch coordinates multi-step workflows.

Lending creates credit.

Permission Delegation controls agent authority.

Sponsored Fees remove onboarding friction.

Secure agent wallets protect keys.

x402 lets machines pay.

The DEX lets machines trade.

XRP handles fees.

XRP can handle direct machine payments.

XRP can provide bridge liquidity when the route is best.

It is one system.

Ayo asked what XRPL needs to become for the next wave of adoption.

I think the question underneath his entire keynote is even bigger:

What happens when trillions of dollars of financial assets and millions of software agents eventually meet on the same network?

You need privacy.

You need permissions.

You need credit.

You need deterministic settlement.

You need atomic transactions.

You need secure signing.

You need auditable activity.

You need machine-native payments.

You need liquidity.

XRPL is being built toward all of it.

And I keep coming back to the same thought.

XRP’s future user may not always be a person.

It may be an algorithm moving value between two financial assets because XRP offered the best route.

No emotion.
No hype.
No hesitation.

Just liquidity.
Execution.
Settlement.

Again.
Again.
Again.

24 hours a day.

If tokenization keeps expanding and AI agents really do become major economic actors, XRP could end up serving a financial environment much larger than the cross-border-payment market people originally associated with it.

-Thousands of assets.
-Millions of agents.
-Constant liquidity routing.
-Institutional transactions.
-Machine payments.
-Credit.
-Treasury management.
-DEX activity.

And XRP sitting directly inside the ledger all of it runs on.

That is the $XRP future I think Ayo Akinyele was quietly laying out in Seoul.

And I do not think most people have fully understood how big it can become yet.

text:
What if Hong Kong and China become the next major catalyst for $XRP?

I’ve been thinking about this a lot after going through everything developing across China, Hong Kong, stablecoins, trade finance, Ripple Payments, RLUSD and XRPL.

The obvious version of this thesis would be simple:
China opens crypto again.

More people can buy XRP.
Price goes up.

I think that barely scratches the surface.

The much more interesting possibility is that Hong Kong becomes the regulated bridge between mainland China and the global digital-asset economy, and $XRP is already positioned inside that bridge before any broader opening fully happens.

Look at what has already happened.

Hong Kong has built a regulated crypto market instead of opening the floodgates without controls.

Its measured crypto economy reached around $192.2 billion during the latest period.

Institutional-platform activity grew 87% year over year.

Institutional platforms represented around 16% of service inflows, almost three times the share seen elsewhere in East Asia.

Hong Kong also received almost $24 billion in inbound B2B crypto flows.

That matters because I’m not looking only at retail speculation.

I’m looking at companies.
Trade.
Treasury movements.
Cross-border capital.
Institutional settlement.

And that is where Hong Kong starts looking very important to XRP.

Now look at mainland China.

Despite years of restrictions, Chainalysis estimated the mainland Chinese crypto economy at roughly $176.3 billion.

Self-custodied stablecoins alone moved around $104.1 billion across 18.1 million transfers.

Unique wallets sending stablecoin P2P transactions increased 43× between Q1 2024 and Q2 2026.

That tells me something very simple.

Chinese demand for digital value transfer did not disappear.
It adapted.

So if China eventually gives companies, institutions or even individuals more regulated ways to use blockchain and digital assets, the market is not starting from zero.

There is already a huge base of activity underneath the restrictions.

Now bring Hong Kong into that picture.

Hong Kong increasingly describes itself as the “super connector” between mainland China and global markets.

And that role is becoming real.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is already working with mainland Chinese infrastructure.

CargoX connected Hong Kong’s Commercial Data Interchange with a digital trade platform operated by the Shanghai Data Bureau.

Five major banks participated:
Bank of China (Hong Kong)
Hang Seng Bank
HSBC
ICBC (Asia)
Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong)
And this was not a presentation deck.

The connection had already enabled 10 trade-finance loans worth HK$180 million.

The HKMA plans to expand the model into additional mainland provinces and cities.

That is exactly the kind of development I care about.

Because if China’s first major blockchain opening happens through companies and cross-border trade rather than unrestricted retail speculation, that could fit Ripple’s core business extremely well.

Ripple has spent years building around:

cross-border payments
B2B settlement
treasury movements
stablecoins
fiat payments
liquidity
XRPL settlement

And Ripple Payments already reaches both China and Hong Kong.

In June 2026, Ripple added CN_CFXPS for USD payouts into China through the China Foreign Exchange Payment System.

It also added HK_BANK_PAYOUT for HKD bank payouts through CHATS.

Ripple’s APAC payment documentation now explicitly lists China CNY payouts, China USD payouts and Hong Kong HKD payouts.

I do not need to claim every one of those payments uses XRP.

That would be wrong.

The importance to me is that Ripple already has payment connectivity into the exact region people are now discussing as a possible future blockchain and crypto catalyst.

Then look at XRP itself.

On July 29, 2026, OSL HK became the first Hong Kong exchange to make XRP available to retail investors through its regulated platform.

XRP/USD is supported.
XRP/HKD is supported through OTC.

And OSL supports XRP deposits and withdrawals through XRPL.

Professional investors already had access before that.

So if Hong Kong keeps becoming a controlled gateway into digital assets, XRP is not waiting outside hoping to get listed someday.

It is already inside.
Then add RLUSD.

OSL HK listed RLUSD in February 2026.

RLUSD/HKD.
RLUSD/USDT.
Institutional OTC support.

OSL and Ripple also said they would explore synergies between their compliant global payment networks.

Now think about the structure developing in one jurisdiction.

You have:
XRP
regulated retail and professional access.
Then:
RLUSD
stable-dollar liquidity and institutional access.
Then:
Ripple Payments
bank payout infrastructure reaching Hong Kong and China.
Then:
XRPL

the settlement and liquidity layer underneath the ecosystem.

That is a much stronger setup than simply saying China might like crypto again.

And Hong Kong itself is moving deeper into regulated digital money.

The Stablecoins Ordinance came into force in August 2025.

Then in April 2026, the HKMA issued its first two stablecoin issuer licences to HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial.

Anchorpoint involves:

Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong)
HKT
Animoca Brands.
Those are not Ripple licences.
I’m not pretending they are.
But think about what happens when multiple regulated forms of digital money begin existing in the same market.
HKD stablecoins.
USD stablecoins.
RLUSD.
Tokenized deposits.
e-CNY.
Other digital assets.
Tokenized funds.
Trade-finance assets.

Now you have a new problem.

How do all of these assets move between one another efficiently?

That is where I keep coming back to XRP.

XRPL was built around moving value between different currencies and assets.

If a payer owns one asset and the recipient wants another, XRPL can search the available liquidity and complete the conversion inside the payment.

When XRP provides the better route, it can automatically become the bridge.

The classic example is:
USD → XRP → MXN.

But the same architecture can become far more interesting when the number of digital assets explodes.

Imagine a future Asian market containing:
HKD stablecoins
USD stablecoins
CNY-linked digital assets
JPY stablecoins
SGD stablecoins
tokenized deposits
Treasury products
trade-finance assets
institutional RWAs.

The number of possible direct trading pairs becomes huge.

Maintaining deep liquidity between every single combination is inefficient.

A common intermediary can reduce that complexity.
That is the XRP bridge-liquidity thesis.

And I think the tokenization era may make that thesis more important than the old remittance era ever did.
Because the world is creating more forms of money, not fewer.

Hong Kong itself is proving that.
It is building around:

crypto
stablecoins
tokenized securities
tokenized deposits
custody
funds
asset management
secondary markets.

The SFC launched a framework in April 2026 allowing secondary trading of tokenized SFC-authorized investment products through licensed virtual-asset platforms under defined conditions.

That means Hong Kong is developing into a regulated digital capital market.

Now consider Ripple’s earlier connection to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.

Ripple and Fubon Bank were selected for the HKMA’s inaugural e-HKD Pilot Programme.

Their project explored:
e-HKD
tokenized real estate
programmable lending.

The project used a private ledger based on the same underlying technology as XRPL.

So Ripple already has history working inside Hong Kong’s central-bank-led digital-money experimentation.

Again, I’m not trying to stretch that into something it is not.

I care about the direction.

Hong Kong is becoming a regulated digital-money and digital-asset hub.

Ripple has already worked with the HKMA.
Ripple Payments already reaches Hong Kong and China.

RLUSD already has Hong Kong market infrastructure.
XRP already has regulated retail and professional access in Hong Kong.

XRPL was built around moving and converting different forms of value.

Then there is the mainland connection.

Around 80,000 e-CNY wallets had been registered using Hong Kong mobile numbers by January 2026.

The number of Hong Kong merchants accepting China’s digital yuan had risen to around 5,200 from roughly 300 initially.

So Hong Kong and mainland China are already becoming more connected through digital money.

The emerging model does not look like one digital currency replacing everything.

It looks more like:
e-CNY
HKD digital money
stablecoins
tokenized deposits
other digital assets
interoperability.
I keep coming back to that final word.
Interoperability.

The more different digital forms of value exist, the more important liquidity and conversion become.

Then take the cross-border trade angle even further.

In March, the HKMA, Shanghai Data Bureau and the National Technology Innovation Center for Blockchain signed an MOU to develop digital cargo-trade and financial infrastructure connecting Shanghai and Hong Kong.

They agreed to explore a cross-border platform under Project Ensemble involving:

electronic bills of lading
trade finance
cargo data
cross-border financial cooperation.

This is already getting very close to the future Joseph Chee was describing.

His scenario was not simply Chinese retail investors buying coins again.

He specifically talked about blockchain technology being used by Chinese companies and cross-border trade.

And here we are watching Hong Kong and Shanghai build infrastructure around exactly that kind of activity.

Now imagine what happens if this keeps developing.
A Shanghai manufacturer exports equipment.

The trade documents are digital.
Cargo data is verified.
Financing is approved.
The buyer pays with a regulated stablecoin or tokenized deposit.

The exporter wants another currency.

A payment platform handles the transaction.

XRPL could be one possible liquidity and settlement environment.

If XRP gives the best route, the transaction can move:
buyer asset → XRP → seller asset.

The company does not need to become an XRP investor.

It does not need to hold XRP for years.

XRP simply provides temporary liquidity while value moves.

That distinction matters a lot to me.

Enterprise utility is very different from retail speculation.

The company cares about:
speed
cost
liquidity
settlement certainty
FX conversion
capital efficiency.
If XRP can improve any of those functions, that is utility.

Now zoom out to APAC.

Research commissioned by Ripple and produced independently by CoinDesk Research estimated Asia-Pacific represented 51.2% of global identified stablecoin-payment volume, with around $30.9 billion across 28 countries.

B2B transfers represented 37.1%.

So we are already talking about the world’s largest identified stablecoin-payment region.

Now imagine China gradually becoming more integrated into regulated digital-asset infrastructure.

That could add activity to a region already leading the world in stablecoin payments.

And XRP has a unique position because it can potentially benefit on two fronts.

First:
investment access.
If broader Chinese access develops, XRP already has regulated Hong Kong distribution.

Second:
utility.
If companies and trade become more blockchain-enabled, XRP was designed around cross-border liquidity and currency conversion.

Many crypto assets would mainly benefit from additional buyers.

XRP could potentially benefit from:

more buyers
more Asian liquidity
more market makers
more corporate payments
more digital currencies
more tokenized assets
more FX relationships
more bridge opportunities.

That is a much wider thesis.

I see three possible stages.

The first is already developing:

Hong Kong becomes a major institutional digital-asset gateway connected to mainland China.
XRP is already inside that market.

The second would be Chinese companies receiving greater permission to use digital assets and blockchain infrastructure for trade.

That overlaps directly with Ripple’s enterprise payment focus.

The third would be broader regulated mainland retail access.

With a measured Chinese crypto economy already around $176.3 billion, that could represent an enormous liquidity catalyst.

But I actually think stage two may matter more for XRP over the long run.

Corporate trade creates real demand for currency conversion.

And currencies are becoming digital.
Deposits are becoming digital.
Trade assets are becoming digital.
Financial products are becoming tokenized.

The more of that happens, the larger the network of value that eventually needs to be connected.

So when I ask whether Hong Kong and China could become a major XRP catalyst, I am not thinking about one headline saying “China unbans crypto.”

I’m thinking about a sequence.

Hong Kong expands regulated access.
Institutional activity grows.
China-Hong Kong infrastructure deepens.
More corporate blockchain use becomes permitted.
Digital money multiplies.
Cross-border trade becomes increasingly programmable.
More assets need liquidity.

XRP’s bridge architecture becomes more useful.
Then broader access could eventually add another layer of capital on top.

And XRP is already positioned at the Hong Kong gateway before any of that reaches its full scale.

That is the scenario I’m watching.
