text:
One of the things that Donald Trump tried to negotiate in this trade deal, was better access to Canadian markets for US airlines.

Right now when an American carrier flies from Miami to Toronto, it can't go back to the U.S.A. via Winnipeg-Calgary-Seattle (as an example) and offer cheap short-haul flights to Canadians.

The US airline market is clearly better for everyday travelers on price and choice. The gap is large on short domestic trips and smaller on long-haul comfort.

Costs are the sharpest difference. Canada’s taxes, airport improvement fees, security charges, and navigation fees are far higher.  Air Canada’s own figures put average domestic base fares in a similar range on both sides of the border, so the extra fees is what makes Canadian tickets expensive.  Recent data also showed Canadian domestic averages rising into the high C$500s to about C$700, while US domestic averages  sit around the mid-US$200s for a typical ticket that often covers longer distances.

Competition drives that gap. The US has four large network or high-frequency carriers (American, Delta, United, Southwest) plus real low-cost and ultra-low-cost options (Frontier, Allegiant, JetBlue, Breeze, and others). No carrier holds a dominant national share. Here, Air Canada and WestJet still account for most domestic capacity; Porter, Flair, and smaller regionals add pressure mainly on a limited set of city pairs. Many Canadian routes have one or two nonstops; many US city pairs have three or more.

Cabin classes are closer. Both markets offer basic economy, standard economy, premium economy, and lie-flat business on long-haul.   But US carriers field more ultra-cheap bare-bones seats and, because of scale, more routes with premium cabins, lounges, and frequent-flyer redemption options. Air Canada might be competitive on major international routes, but the everyday Canadian flyer sees fewer fare brands and fewer luxury seats on domestic trips.

Carney is not protecting Canadians by refusing to allow US airlines onto domestic flights, he's promoting a monopoly.

text:
Not asking for $5,000 more at your first job can cost you $1.4 million by retirement.

Most people never ask. It feels rude, so they take the first number.

The math is quiet. A $5,000 higher starting salary, with ordinary 3% raises, adds up to $377,000 more pay over a 40-year career. Every raise is a percentage of what you already make, so the gap never closes. Invest that difference at 7% and it grows to about $1.46 million.

Carnegie Mellon economist Linda Babcock put the lifetime cost of not negotiating at $1 million to $1.5 million. In her study, 57% of men negotiated their first offer. Only 7% of women did.

Stanford professor Margaret Neale has spent her career studying how deals get made. Her talk on getting what you want is free, and her method has four steps:

1. Assess. Is this something you can actually move? A first offer usually is.
2. Prepare. Know what you want, what they need, and what you'll do if they say no. "He or she with a better alternative does better."
3. Ask. The other side can't give you what you never request.
4. Package. Don't haggle one item at a time. Trade: if I give you this, then I get that.

She used it on her own dean. He told her she'd go from five courses a year to six. Everyone got the same email. She came back with a package, and was the only faculty member who got an exception.

Every raise you'll ever get is a percentage of the number you accept on day one.

Send this to someone about to accept an offer.

text:
Law Catches Up With ‘Sharp Boy’ Francis Kamau Who Locked Himself in a Metal Cage and Threatened a Magistrate

Francis Kamau Karanja’s story has begun to look like one of those Nairobi crime dramas that starts with a small amount of money, gathers police officers, lawyers, court orders and angry messages along the way, then suddenly becomes much bigger than anyone expected.

For months, Francis had fought investigators over a disputed KSh 78,250 payment tied to a technology job, and at one point he even secured High Court protection restraining specified officers from arresting, tracking, or raiding him while his petition remained pending.

That victory could easily have looked like Francis had beaten the system, pushed detectives back, and bought himself enough breathing room to keep fighting, but October brought a completely different problem that put him back in the criminal justice system.

He is now facing a fresh cyber harassment charge over a message sent to Magistrate Margaret Murage, who is named as the complainant, and he is expected to be remanded before appearing at Milimani Court as the new case begins.

The allegation has given Francis’s story a new edge, because the man who had previously gone to court seeking protection from police interference is now returning to court as an accused person facing a separate complaint involving a judicial officer.

The route that brought him here is exactly what makes his story fit into Kenya’s growing conversation about the so-called “Sharp Boys.”

The trouble started after Anthony Karanja reported at Dandora Police Station that he had paid Francis KSh 78,250 for technology services that were  never delivered, prompting investigators to begin examining what had happened after the payment was made.

Police later obtained court authority to access the M-Pesa account linked to Francis, and the resulting statement showed the KSh 78,250 entering the account through a Standard Chartered Bank business payment shortly after 2am on March 1, 2026.

From there, the money began moving through a series of transactions involving household expenses, electricity, supermarkets, the Nairobi Expressway, food, entertainment and transfers to different women, creating the kind of financial trail that can later become extremely uncomfortable when investigators start reading it backwards.

Among the names appearing repeatedly in the records was Linda Muthoni Maina, including one transfer of KSh 47,000; the lady is said to be one of his many girlfriends.

That detail still feeds the popular Nairobi joke about the Sharp Boy who receives money today and begins spending it around women tomorrow.

Police later told the High Court that Francis reported the payment as suspicious only after the money had already been used, an allegation he disputes, but one investigators relied upon when explaining why they believed the matter required further criminal investigation.

What might have remained a small argument between two men over a technology job had now become a police file supported by M Pesa records, statements, court applications and allegations that Francis had received money without delivering the agreed service.

Then detectives came to his door

Police say detectives travelled to Francis’s residence in June using an official DCI vehicle, first reporting to Highridge Police Post before proceeding to the apartment together with uniformed officers who had been requested to assist them.

According to the investigating officer’s affidavit, Francis allegedly locked himself inside a metal caged verandah, refused to open after officers identified themselves, and insisted that the people outside were connected to interests he believed were behind his problems.

The officers say they eventually decided against forcing entry and instead gave Francis an opportunity to present himself at Dandora Police Station, but by then the case had already become a confrontation between one man and the investigators pursuing him.

Francis responded by moving to the High Court, where he secured temporary protection restraining specified officers from raiding his home, arresting him, tracking him, or otherwise interfering with his liberty pending determination of his application.

For anybody watching from outside, that was the sort of move that strengthens the Sharp Boy legend, because police had come knocking, Francis resisted, lawyers entered the matter, and the High Court temporarily restricted what the officers could do next.

The danger with winning one battle is that confidence can quickly become something else, and the Francis story became even more dramatic after prosecutors later accused him of sending a message to a magistrate that crossed into criminal territory.

The case involving Magistrate Margaret Murage

A charge sheet dated October 6 accuses Francis of cyber harassment over a communication allegedly sent on September 28 to Magistrate Margaret Murage, with prosecutors claiming that the wording accused her of bias and caused apprehension or fear.

The text read 

“Greetings Hon: I have noted the great bias in the case of Gabriel Saka. It seems you have taken sides and we will not allow it. I will not stop at anything to ensure justice is done, be warned. Chunga kazi yako. Na ujichunge sana. Tunajua kwako.”

The magistrate is listed as the complainant, meaning Francis had moved from fighting a private complainant and detectives into a completely different case where the alleged recipient of the disputed communication was an officer of the Judiciary.

That development gives the story its strongest twist, because there is a significant difference between arguing with police officers over an investigation and becoming accused of sending language that prosecutors say amounted to harassment of a magistrate.

The Kenyan “Sharp Boy” has become a familiar character

Francis’s case is much smaller than the major cybercrime and wash-wash cases Kenya has seen, but his story sits comfortably inside a culture Nairobi residents now recognise almost immediately when the signs begin appearing.

The Sharp Boy is usually confident, understands technology, talks about business constantly, dislikes the idea of ordinary employment and seems determined to reach the expensive car, apartment, nightlife and social status long before the slow route can realistically provide them.

Sometimes the money is completely legitimate, because Kenya has produced plenty of young entrepreneurs who built technology businesses, trading companies and digital ventures that genuinely made them wealthy much earlier than previous generations would have considered normal.

The suspicion begins when the lifestyle becomes much larger than the visible business, and the explanation for the money keeps changing between forex trading, consulting, crypto, gold, tenders, international deals, technology contracts, and investments nobody can clearly identify.

Around Nairobi, the expensive car can become part of the business card, because somebody claiming to control millions looks considerably more convincing arriving in a Range Rover than arriving in an old Toyota with cracked seats.

The apartment can serve the same purpose, since an address in Kilimani, Kileleshwa, Lavington or Westlands can help create the appearance that whatever mysterious business the person claims to run must be doing extremely well.

Women, restaurants, designer clothes, bottles and frequent travel then complete the picture, creating an expensive public image that tells friends, victims and social media followers that the man has already escaped the ordinary life everyone else is still struggling through.

When the FBI becomes part of the story

Kenya has already watched several cybercrime suspects discover that an operation carried out from Nairobi can eventually attract investigators from the United States, especially when money, American institutions or victims are involved.

Kenyan suspects have faced extradition proceedings over allegations involving business email compromise, computer intrusions, wire fraud and identity theft, with American investigators sometimes building cases for years before the accused even realise how much information has been collected.

That reality destroys one of the biggest Sharp Boy fantasies, because distance does not necessarily protect somebody whose money moves internationally, and a laptop in Nairobi can create a criminal file sitting inside an American federal office.

The person may change phones, move houses, replace cars and disappear from social media, yet financial records, email accounts, devices, immigration movements and former associates can remain available to investigators long after the lifestyle has changed.

INTERPOL notices and extradition proceedings are rarely part of the Instagram fantasy when the money first arrives, but they become very real when somebody discovers that a foreign investigation never actually disappeared.

Ramon Abbas, better known as Hushpuppi, remains the international example that should have frightened every aspiring Sharp Boy, because his social media pages displayed exactly the life so many young men dream about achieving instantly.

His photographs showed luxury hotels, private jets, designer clothes, expensive watches, and high-end cars, creating the image of a man who had somehow found the shortcut to wealth that millions of ordinary workers spend decades chasing.

Then American investigators produced a completely different account involving money laundering and proceeds from online fraud, before Hushpuppi eventually pleaded guilty and received a federal prison sentence of more than eleven years.

His story became famous because the contrast was almost ridiculous, with millions of followers still able to scroll through photographs of luxury vehicles and designer outfits after the man who posted them had already exchanged Dubai comfort for American federal custody.

Kenya has seen an ending worse than prison

Samuel Mugoh Muvota offered Kenya a darker example after police linked him to an alleged network involving ATM fraud, SIM swapping and women accused of drugging victims before money was taken from their accounts.

Police accounts released after his death painted the picture of a man surrounded by money, expensive vehicles, women and repeated allegations of fraud, creating another version of the Sharp Boy life that appeared untouchable for years.

Then in May 2022, a gunman approached his vehicle on Mirema Drive and shot him repeatedly in broad daylight, turning the same kind of expensive car that usually represents success into the place where the story ended.

Francis and the problem with believing you are always smarter

What makes Francis story remarkable is how that amount allegedly opened one door after another, producing a police complaint, M Pesa investigation, attempted arrest, High Court case, temporary protection and eventually a completely separate criminal matter involving a magistrate.

That progression captures the weakness behind the Sharp Boy mentality, where surviving one problem can create the belief that intelligence will always produce another escape, even when the number of institutions, witnesses and records around the person keeps growing.

The modern Sharp Boy may believe technology protects him because money moves instantly and messages can be deleted, yet the same technology creates detailed records showing transfers, dates, accounts, communications and movements that can later be placed before a court.

For Kenya’s Sharp Boys watching from expensive apartments and powerful cars, Francis Kamau’s story carries a simple warning that should be easier to understand than any police affidavit or court ruling.

Fast money can make somebody look clever for a very long time, but once the receipts, investigators and court files begin piling up, cleverness suddenly becomes a much more expensive lifestyle to maintain.

Lol No. The Soviet Union (not “Russia”) floated a 1954 note about possibly discussing NATO membership and this was years after NATO was founded in 1949 precisely *because* of Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe, the Berlin Blockade, and the Czech coup. It was a transparent propaganda stunt designed to sabotage West German rearmament and dissolve the alliance’s purpose; the Western powers correctly called it incompatible with NATO’s defensive character and rejected the Soviet offer. 

Secondly, NATO did not “decide Russia was the new threat” out of nowhere and then “park bases” around it for sport. The threat was already Soviet tanks in half of Europe. Post-Cold War expansion happened because former Warsaw Pact and Baltic states BEGGED to join after decades under Moscow’s boot, seeking some insurance against a return of Russian imperialism which later delivered Moldova 1992, Chechnya in the late 90s, Georgia 2008, Crimea and Donbas 2014, and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Most “bases” are in sovereign member states that REQUESTED them.

Thirdly, as for “what had Russia done?” Well, how about installing communist dictatorships across Eastern Europe, crushing Hungary 1956 and the Prague spring in 1968, the gulags, Holodomor, Afghanistan, etc. “Helping Zimbabwe free itself” is a cute whataboutism that doesn’t erase any of that. For what it's worth, Soviet involvement in the Rhodesian Bush war/Liberation struggle had nothing to do with the Soviets having a desire to free anybody. It was all a cold war game between two camps who armed rebel movements in each other's "spheres of influence". Nothing more.

The 4 most important things happening in nuclear this week:

1. Google @Google signed a 20-year deal with Constellation @ConstellationEG to pay for uprates at 11 reactors across six plants in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. An uprate means squeezing more power out of a machine that already runs. The target is about 890 megawatts of new output on the PJM grid, the regional market that covers 13 states. Constellation says that is more than $4.3 billion of its own investment. The first extra watts are expected by 2028. The full 890 megawatts are aimed at before the end of 2032. They also signed a separate 15-year deal covering 2,700 megawatts of Constellation’s existing fleet. No power price was published.

2. The Department of Energy @ENERGY offered Vistra a conditional loan of up to $4.2 billion for uprates and modernization at Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania and Davis-Besse and Perry in Ohio. Vistra is a power company based in Irving, Texas. It owns plants and sells electricity. Its nuclear fleet is Comanche Peak in Texas, plus those three Midwest plants, which came with the Energy Harbor deal. It is not a reactor designer. It runs the machines and sells the watts. The package would add about 433 megawatts and keep nearly 4 gigawatts of existing nuclear on the grid, with an option later for Comanche Peak. Conditional means the money is not wired. Vistra still has to clear technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions. Announced October 5.

3. Fuel loading at Palisades stopped after one used assembly tilted in the core. Holtec @holtecintl says assembly DD41 was placed, released, and leaned over at about 30 degrees. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission @NRCgov says the rods are intact, there was no release, and no one was hurt. Holtec filed an emergency license amendment on September 30 so crews can move that assembly to the spent fuel pool with custom gear. The NRC opened public comment on October 6. Holtec still says the restart is aimed at before March 2027. That date now depends on getting this assembly out.

4. The United States and South Korea outlined Project Power, a framework for eight large reactors in the United States: six Westinghouse @WECNuclear AP1000s and two Korean APR1400s. The Commerce Department fact sheet puts the package at $120 billion, $100 billion for construction and $20 billion held as contingency. Sites are not picked. Schedules and contracts are not signed. Seoul said this week the project is likely to take a real shape around 2028. It is a blueprint, not a pour.

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Adam Grant #4 (on the secrets of strong connections)

Overview
Adam Grant reframes connection as something built through repeated proximity, shared intensity, and thoughtful maintenance rather than spontaneous chemistry. He traces his own path from childhood exclusion and schoolyard cruelty through springboard diving, Wharton teaching, and the study of friendship, arguing that connection quality depends on situation, context, and which version of a person shows up. Grant distinguishes four relationship types, associates, allies, pals, and companions, and shows that most conflict comes from expecting one person to fill roles they never signed up for. He challenges universal likability as a virtue, warns that ambivalent relationships can be worse than enemies, and argues that AI companions cannot replace the mutual need at the center of real relationships.

Key Themes
- Connection is built, not discovered: proximity, repeated contact, and choreographed interaction outperform compatibility matching and stated preferences.
- Relationship roles are distinct: associates, allies, pals, and companions serve different functions, and mismatched expectations cause the deepest frustration.
- Being liked by everyone can be a warning sign; trustworthiness often requires the willingness to disappoint some people.
- Emotional intensity accelerates bonding, but only a debrief afterward turns intensity into closeness.
- Personality is context-dependent; people have "if-then" signatures, and one bad interaction rarely captures who someone is.
- Maintenance is not the same as strengthening; some relationships survive long gaps, while companions require ongoing touch points.
- Ambivalence is its own category, with measurable health costs that can exceed those of outright enemies.
- Small personal gestures, sending a meme or article that reminded you of someone, sustain connection across distance.
- AI companions lack the mutual contribution side of relationship, and early evidence suggests they may deepen loneliness rather than relieve it.

Detailed Summary
Grant has taught at Wharton for roughly eighteen years and says he will never retire. He received a top-rated professor award for seven consecutive years before the award was retired. He argues the award measured being liked more than being good. A newer excellence in teaching award replaced it, going to about twenty or thirty faculty per year, and Grant has not failed to receive it. His teaching centers on students rather than subjects: good teachers care about the material, great teachers care about the people. He memorizes personal details about MBA students so they feel seen, then draws on their backgrounds to choreograph discussions, calling on a military student for culture or a former professional athlete for teamwork. Teaching three sections of about seventy-five students for only a week made real connection difficult.

Grant describes childhood social pain with unusual precision. A friend group dropped him gradually, a death by a thousand cuts, and no one he considered a friend had his back. He transitioned from being bullied to being excluded, and because the bullying stopped, exclusion felt like an improvement. Bullies mocked him for being a nerd, and even friends called him Mr. Fax. In middle school he saved babysitting money for an NBA basketball; it vanished after a game, and a friend later said one of Grant's friends had stolen it and bragged about it. He had two close friends outside that group and later realized they gravitated together partly because neither had other options. His diving coach said he arrived in high school with one friend and seemed unbothered, though Grant says he had two. By graduation he was voted team captain.

Springboard diving taught him a lesson he still uses. When he scored points at junior Olympics, swimmers stopped hating the divers because he helped the team. People wanted him around when he was good at something that served the group. Diving also forced social skill by making him talk with teammates in line during practice. Meeting personality psychologist Brian Little in college changed how he approached conversation: rather than sharing what interested him, he learned to elicit curiosity and spark interest in others. Little illustrated introvert and extrovert differences with an example about lemon juice on the tongue, where introverts salivate more, and there is evidence behind it. Grant also notes he could not instantly vibe with James Hetfield despite being a longtime Metallica fan; no sparks flew, nothing went wrong, and you will not click with everyone.

Harvard brought imposter syndrome into sharp relief. Many students felt either like God's gift or like a mistake who did not belong. Bill Gates was first in math in Washington, then found he was third best at Harvard. A friend named Christine went to the University of Michigan and then Harvard Law, and learned not to drop the H bomb because of the antagonistic reaction it provokes. Grant described feeling defined by being a Harvard student and graduate throughout his twenties as a burden. People are both envious of and mystified by Harvard attendees, he notes, though they are really just people.

A failed connection is not necessarily anyone's fault. Two people can show up authentically and simply not click, and the common response, shame directed either at the other person or at oneself, is unhelpful. Connection quality may depend on which version of a person shows up and what approach might elicit a different response. Grant argues that trustworthiness may be inversely related to universal likability, since vibing with everyone can signal people-pleasing, approval-seeking, or dishonesty. He defines vibe as the quality of connection between two people, created in interaction rather than intrinsic to a person or place. Vibe has measurable physiological signatures: brain waves synchronize and heartbeats share a rhythm. He rejects the framing of vibing as gaming or a hack. It is a skill you build, not a shortcut or manipulation.

The four connection types organize much of the discussion. Associates are people with compatible needs, reliable and trustworthy but not usually meaningful. Allies share your goals. Pals share your interests and hobbies. Companions share your values. Life gets complicated when someone wants one person to be all four. A pal may be ideal for fun but wrong for emotional support, reliability, or shared values. Starting a company with someone you like as a friend can fail if they turn out to be a bad ally. The friend label is too vague to convey importance, reciprocity, goals, or the nature of the connection. Grant describes sliding a disappointing but loved friend into the pal category by adjusting expectations rather than demanding change. Dax is described as skilled at connecting, though there may be deliberate behaviors behind it rather than pure natural charisma.

Proximity, not similarity, drives friendship formation. Children in elementary school and police academy trainees tend to become close with people whose last names sit nearby alphabetically, because they sit next to each other. Grant's friendship with Aaron Weekley formed after being seated together in Mr. Nelson's seventh-grade class, despite an awkward earlier bathroom introduction. Online and similarity-based matching removes proximity, which may undermine how friendships actually form. Paul Eastwick, Eli Finkel, and colleagues found pre-speed-dating questionnaires and machine-learning algorithms had zero predictive utility for who clicked. What people claim they want had no bearing on matches. Swipe-based dating may be problematic because people are poor at predicting matches yet are empowered to select only those they believe are good matches.

NASA deliberately accelerates bonding. Astronauts Cady Coleman and Paolo Nespoli were initially deemed incompatible during training for an ISS robotic-arm mission. Coleman is an American PhD chemist; Nespoli an Italian parachute jumper and engineer. NASA considered re-engineering the mission because the mismatch seemed unworkable. By the end of six months in space, Coleman called Nespoli her space brother. They became allies, pals through shared music, and companions, with Coleman supporting him after his mother's death. During a robotic-arm task they improvised complementary maneuvers without communicating, showing synchrony. NASA uses wilderness expeditions, often in Utah with an outdoor leadership guide, to accelerate bonding by removing masks and forcing the real self to emerge. Trainer John Kaninger had astronauts tell origin stories about when they first knew they wanted to go to space. Emotional intensity, shared arousal, fear, physical exertion, and vulnerability accelerate connection, as seen at summer camp, on film sets, in military service, and in college dorms.

Shared goals and a common enemy can bridge deep divides. Ann Atwater, a Black civil rights leader, and C.P. Ellis, the local KKK Exalted Cyclops in Durham, North Carolina, clashed violently in the late nineteen sixties and early seventies, including threats with a gun and a knife. Mediator Bill Riddick appointed them co-chairs of a committee to desegregate Durham schools, forcing collaboration. They discovered shared goals: both came from poverty, both had suffering children, and both wanted to protect their communities from violence during desegregation. They became close friends, and Atwater's granddaughter called Ellis Uncle C.P. Haunted house data shows going with a friend accelerates closeness, but only if you debrief afterward; shared experience must be processed together. The thin slicing finding shows a thirty-second silent video of a professor's first lecture predicts end-of-semester ratings, but captures only a snapshot, not the whole person. Orna, a relationship therapist, does not subscribe to all-day personality types and sees narcissism and other traits as contextually dependent. People have if-then signatures, agreeable and disagreeable sides, extroverted and introverted sides, and the ifs are triggers that bring out each version. Monica is described as generally more agreeable than Dax, but when family was late leaving for a flight, Dax was angry while Monica stayed agreeable to avoid a fight, noting she would normally be the disagreeable one.

Personality is context-dependent. The same person can behave differently depending on situation, fluctuating on the then when the if changes. First impressions can mislead, and writing someone off after one bad interaction may cost a deep connection. C.S. Lewis and Tolkien initially disliked each other, had different literary tastes, one Christian and one atheist, but bonded over a shared reading of Norse mythology that became a gateway to their fantasy writing. Narnia and The Lord of the Rings might not exist without that connection. Dax identifies a pattern of quickly creating emotional intimacy to determine friend or foe, and recognizes it can mislead in casual relationships. Serena Williams and Maria Sharapova became close after their heated rivalry ended, since the only other person who understands that experience is a fellow competitor. Dax's son is both courageous and timid depending on context, on ski slopes with friends versus at an amusement park with older sisters. Dax told an ex-girlfriend's story during an amends: she said things never really got better for her, which he found heartbreaking and which made him realize the level of intimacy he offered was unique and potentially misleading.

Frequency of interaction is not closeness. A relationship that cannot withstand time may be fragile, and sustaining a connection differs from strengthening one. Ally and pal relationships survive long gaps, but companion relationships are harder because they assume ongoing emotional support and knowledge of each other's lives. Small personal gestures can signal care without constant contact. A daughter coined the term palvator for someone trying to barge into a closer relationship than desired. One host and Aaron were separated during Aaron's active addiction, then resumed as if back in seventh grade once he got sober. Penguin courtship involves presenting smooth shiny stones, and the digital equivalent, pebbling, means sending a specific article, meme, or reel that reminded you of someone, not mass spam. Research cited shows pebbling functions as a memory flex, signaling you paid attention to what someone cares about.

Ambivalent relationships are a distinct category worse than enemies. Unlike consistent enemies, frenemies are unpredictable and drain energy through anticipation, management, and rumination. They carry measurable health costs, including higher blood pressure and greater vulnerability to heart attacks and cardiovascular disease. In-law relationships are a textbook example: loving someone as a grandparent while resenting how they treat your partner. Jared Diamond's book on leadership includes statistics showing CEOs who lose a spouse see profits drop over the next year or two, while losing an in-law shows a not statistically significant increase. The key is accepting emotions while containing behavior, distinguishing tolerable vices from hurtful ones. Joe Dumars traded for Rasheed Wallace, the most volatile player in NBA history, then told him at the airport he understood Rasheed would lose his cool and have meltdowns but could not have technical fouls in the fourth quarter. Rasheed agreed. The principle is: I accept the way you feel, but this is not an okay response to that feeling. One speaker's lateness in marriage was reframed from moral failing to a hard time disengaging from tasks, then contained in specific situations like when dinner will get cold.

Jeff Zazzlo's Zazbash events show strong connection is choreographed, not spontaneous. Zazzlo lived across the street, invited a twelve-year-old Grant to play HORSE at a neighborhood barbecue, was a journalist who took over the Ann Landers advice column, and created Zazbash, inviting single readers to Chicago. People came from multiple states, couples fell in love and married, and over fifteen years Zazbash produced seventy-eight marriages. His approach was not matchmaking profiles but choreographing interactions that bring out a better version of each person, including a Kramer dance during the heyday of Seinfeld. Suggested gathering rules include no phones, do not talk to anyone you know, and no advising, fixing, or solving. To create allies, have people bring a problem and let the group solve it. To create pals, do something silly like playing teleustrations. To create companions, skip small talk and go to deep talk, such as discussing your biggest regret or your relationship with your mother.

AI companions pose a new test. An alarming number of young people say they have an AI companion, and a sizable minority, a quarter to a third, would rather interact with the AI than an actual person, even a friend. Numbers vary by survey and location but are climbing, and elderly people increasingly have them. One empirical claim holds that the most lonely elderly people end up lonelier after interacting with AI companions. A counterargument is that AI can simulate companionship, sympathy, conversation, and pal-like interaction about interests, and for some isolated people it may be that or nothing. A relationship requires two-way exchange, and because an AI does not need help, emotional support, fun, or shared experience, it cannot provide the meaningful contribution side of relationship. Technologies already driving isolation include online jobs, delivered food, and not needing to go to restaurants or movies. Social video games are proposed as a better existing intervention. The marshmallow experiment debate surfaces here: longer waiting for a second marshmallow correlates with better grades and SAT scores years later, but the effect is entangled with socioeconomic status and trust that promised rewards will materialize. Walter Mischel's original studies controlled for SES, reducing but not always eliminating the effect, and Keith Payne synthesized the research. Delayed gratification is a skill built over time through trustworthy relationships and environments. Loneliness is rising across all age groups. The debate over Jonathan Haidt's social media claims continues, with one side seeing moral panic and ignored conflicting data, while phone-out-of-school experiments reportedly show boys bullied less and girls getting better grades and mental health. Social prescribing in England includes gym referrals, clubs, and friendship benches. The Ashley Madison leak study found CEOs, financial advisers, and police officers who cheated on spouses were two to three times more likely to commit job misconduct, though critics note the sample represents a risk-embracing subgroup rather than the general population of people who have affairs.

Our Masks, Their Veils: Robert Jenrick, Dan Wootton and the Grammar of ‘Left Bad, Right Good’

On the evening of 6 October 2026, Robert Jenrick posted a 35-second clip to @X with the caption: “The Islamification of our country is one of the greatest threats to our way of life.”

The clip came from his appearance that day on Dan Wootton’s Outspoken, his first as a representative of Reform UK, the party he joined on 15 January 2026 after Kemi Badenoch sacked him from the Conservative shadow cabinet. The programme introduced him by his new title: Reform UK Shadow Chancellor.

In the clip, Jenrick says: “I don’t want to live in a country, I don’t want my children to grow up in a country, where the rise of radical Islam has been left unchecked. The Islamification of this country is perhaps the greatest threat to our way of life right now.”

Taken alone, it sounds like a warning about extremism. Read alongside the full interview, it becomes something else. Across an interview of around 45 to 50 minutes, Jenrick and Wootton construct a world in which the right is persecuted, patriotic and nearly always correct, while the left, the police, the “mainstream media”, the civil service and the Conservative Party are weak, corrupt or complicit. This essay looks at how that world is built: the misleading claims it rests on, and the rhetorical moves that hold it together.

Some of what Jenrick says is true, and it is worth saying so first. Islamist terrorism is real, and it makes up about three quarters of MI5’s terrorism caseload. Shoplifting has risen and few thefts end in a charge. Asylum hotels are expensive. Some people who crossed the Channel by small boat were later identified as terror suspects. His account of the key Rwanda vote is correct. None of this justifies a false census figure, a rewritten ministerial record, or a fair-trial rule that applies only to Andy Burnham.

Two frameworks and a toolkit help here. The first framework is Teun van Dijk’s ideological square, a model of how group ideologies show up in talk. Speakers tend to do four things at once: emphasise Our good qualities, emphasise Their bad qualities, play down Our bad qualities, and play down Their good ones. The square is useful because it shows that persuasion depends as much on what is left out as on what is said.

Alongside the square, Martin Reisigl and Ruth Wodak’s discourse-historical approach offers a practical toolkit. It looks at nomination (what people are called), predication (what qualities they are given), argumentation (what is said to justify treating them that way), perspectivation (where the speaker places himself) and intensification (how strongly a claim is pushed). Each of these turns up below.

The second framework is the sociology of moral panic, from Stanley Cohen’s Folk Devils and Moral Panics to Stuart Hall and colleagues’ Policing the Crisis. A moral panic needs a folk devil, a threat presented as larger and more urgent than the evidence supports, and moral entrepreneurs who gain authority by naming it. Policing the Crisis added something important: a panic is often a way of telling a story about a society in crisis, in which a strong hand becomes the obvious answer.

All three are visible throughout the Wootton interview. The folk devils change from one segment to the next, from shoplifters and “illegal migrants” to Muslims, “left-wing commentators”, the police and the Tory press. The structure stays the same: decline, betrayal, a persecuted in-group, and a last chance to save the country.

The clip depends on a distinction it never keeps. Its first sentence is about “radical Islam”, meaning violent Islamist extremism. Its second is about “Islamification”, which refers to Islam itself spreading through a country. The first sentence lends credibility to the second without supporting it.

The full interview shows how little Jenrick holds to the distinction. A few minutes before the clipped passage, Wootton reads out, and the programme puts on screen, a Truth Social post Donald Trump had published earlier that day, 6 October, about unrest in France: “This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” He asks: “Do you agree?” Jenrick replies: “Yes, I do.” Only then does he move on to “a willingness to tolerate radical Islam”. The first thing he endorses is a claim about the religion, not its extremist fringe.

His list of remedies tells the same story. To counter “radical Islam” he proposes banning Sharia courts, “complete zero tolerance on hate preachers” and banning the burka. The first two concern extremism or parallel legal authority. The third concerns what some ordinary Muslim women wear. Earlier, explaining Reform’s proposed ban on face coverings, he says of the burka: “I think that is not British and it is threatening.”

The same answer shows which way Reform is moving. Wootton notes that Farage once said Reform needed the Muslim vote, and asks whether he has toughened up. Jenrick replies that Farage has always shared his view that radical Islam “has to be eradicated from our country” and that “we can’t allow the creeping Islamification of the United Kingdom”. He adds: “as far as I’m aware”. The hedge is fair, and nobody should claim to know Farage’s mind. But the policies Jenrick lists, burka ban included, are the ones he says Reform has adopted.

In the broadcast, the images shown over his words make the same shift, from radical Islam to ordinary Muslims, in a sequence that rewards close attention. As Jenrick says “That is the kind of policies”, the screen shows rows of men at prayer in a mosque. As he says “that are needed now”, it cuts to a line of women in light-blue headscarves holding hands on Westminster Bridge, with Parliament behind them. As he says “I don’t want to live in a country... where the rise of radical Islam has been left unchecked”, it cuts again, to two women in niqabs on the same bridge, phones in hand, with Big Ben behind them.

The second image is from a solidarity vigil on Westminster Bridge on 26 March 2017. Four days after Khalid Masood’s attack on Westminster Bridge, almost 100 women, many of them Muslim and wearing blue as a symbol of peace, formed a human chain on the bridge and stood in silence for five minutes as Big Ben struck four. One participant said at the time that an attack on London was an attack on her, and that her faith condemned violence of any kind. In Outspoken’s edit, Muslim women mourning the victims of an Islamist attack illustrate the policies needed to tackle “radical Islam”.

Nobody in these images is doing anything but praying, mourning or standing on a bridge. Together they turn ordinary Muslim life, and even Muslim solidarity against terrorism, into pictures of the threat. In van Dijk’s terms, Their good deeds are not merely played down; they are recruited as evidence against Them. The editing is Outspoken’s, but it fits what Jenrick says in the same interview, and the niqab sequence is in the clip he chose to post.

There is one more small move. On camera Jenrick calls Islamification “perhaps the greatest threat to our way of life right now”. His caption on X softens this to “one of the greatest threats”. The strongest version reaches viewers as sound and image, while the written words he can be quoted on are more cautious.

None of this means Islamist terrorism isn’t real. It is, and it is the largest part of the security services’ terrorism caseload: MI5’s Director General has put it at roughly three quarters, with extreme right-wing terrorism making up about a quarter. Prevent referral figures for the year to March 2025 show 870 referrals for Islamist extremism (10%) against 1,798 for extreme right-wing concerns (21%). Referrals measure where concern is raised, not where the threat is greatest, but they show that extremism is not one-directional.

Two things follow. First, Islamist extremism has not been “left unchecked”. It is the main focus of MI5’s counter-terrorism work. Second, the scale of the religion Jenrick says is taking over is modest. In England and Wales, the 2021 census recorded 3.9 million Muslims, 6.5% of the population, up from 4.9% in 2011. Over the same decade, the share reporting no religion rose by twelve points, from 25.2% to 37.2%, far more than any faith.

This is the folk devil at work. A real but specific security problem is stretched to cover a faith community of nearly four million people. In van Dijk’s terms, Their worst members come to stand for all of Them.

Asked whether his Reform colleague Suella Braverman is English, Jenrick sets out three categories: ethnicity, culture and nationality. He presents the debate as “perfectly normal”, and the three-part structure sounds measured. What it does is make citizenship the least important of the three.

He supports his idea of a stable English ethnicity with history. “Barring some Irish immigration at the end of the 19th century,” he says, “the British population has remained fairly stable really from 1066 until about 1960. In fact, in 1900 I think only 7% of the population of this country was foreign-born.”

Both claims are wrong. Irish migration to Britain peaked around the Famine of the 1840s, not at the end of the century. The “fairly stable” story also leaves out Huguenot refugees, the Jewish migration from Eastern Europe between roughly 1880 and 1914, and the long-standing Black and Asian communities of Britain’s port cities.

The number is wrong by a factor of about seven. The 1901 census of England and Wales counted 339,436 people born in foreign countries, 10.4 per thousand of the population, or about 1%. Of those, 247,758 were foreign nationals: 7.6 per thousand. Jenrick may have read a rate per thousand as a percentage. Oddly, the true figure would have suited his argument better. That suggests a number half-remembered and offered with confidence rather than checked, and the hedge “I think” does nothing to stop it travelling to a large and receptive audience.

The destination of the argument is this: “We’ve ended up in a country where there are millions and millions of people who have a British passport in their bedroom drawer, but who are not culturally British by my standards, are not culturally English either, and are not ethnically English as well.”

Three features stand out. The passport in the drawer reduces citizenship to an object kept out of sight, held but not deserved. The repetition in “millions and millions” is intensification: it conveys scale without offering a figure, and no figure could exist, because nobody can count how many people fail a cultural test of his own devising. And “by my standards” gives the game away: Jenrick sets the cultural test, then reports that millions fail it. Braverman passes, he explains, because she is “certainly culturally English or British”. Who else passes is left for the listener to decide. Braverman is the British-born daughter of a father of Goan heritage who came from Kenya and a mother of Tamil heritage from Mauritius, and she is a practising Buddhist. Jenrick has no difficulty calling her culturally English. Nothing he says explains why the same could not be true of many of the “millions” he places outside the line.

This is the ideological square in its plainest form. Those who are Us by ethnicity need no test. Those who are not must prove themselves culturally, and many of them, Jenrick says, have not. A legal status shared by all citizens is reframed as a hierarchy of belonging, with the speaker as judge.

The interview opens with a montage of Jenrick confronting shoplifters in Brixton market and scenes from the anti-migrant protests in Gosport. His reading sets the tone for everything that follows. The shoplifters are “frankly feral people”, there is “total impunity for scumbags and criminals”, and some communities “are just like the third world right now”. The protesters, by contrast, are people “who just want to display their anger and frustration”, met by the state “like a ton of bricks”.

There is a ritual disclaimer: “of course none of us sanction people breaking the law or threatening people”. It occupies one clause. The rest of the answer explains why the law is unfair to them. The “two-tier policing” frame does a lot of work here. It turns a policing response to large, partly masked crowds outside asylum accommodation into proof that the state favours migrants over the native population.

Wootton then raises Danny Tommo (Daniel Thomas), leader of the Patriot Platform, whose masked supporters mobilised in Dover and Portsmouth. Wootton tells viewers Tommo is “locked up probably for Christmas” for having “burst a boat being used by human traffickers”. Jenrick replies: “I completely understand that.”

Wootton’s summary leaves out what the charge alleges. Thomas is charged with criminal damage for slashing a small boat with a knife on 22 September while a rescue worker was on board, and with refusing to give police the PIN for his phone. He has pleaded not guilty to both. On 29 September he was refused bail at Portsmouth Crown Court, and a provisional trial date has been set for 1 March 2027. “Locked up” means remanded, not convicted.

He then criticises the Prime Minister. Andy Burnham, he says, went on the BBC and condemned Tommo “as a racist, without providing any evidence for that, prejudicing his trial or certainly risking it”. His conclusion is a principle: “You can’t have public figures going around just attacking somebody like Danny Tommo without providing any evidence whatsoever.”

What Burnham actually said was more qualified. Asked whether Tommo is racist, he said it was “hard to conclude that he’s anything other than someone who has racist views”, then added that he hesitated, had not read or followed everything Tommo had said or done, and did not “just throw labels on people”. You can still argue that a Prime Minister shouldn’t comment on a defendant at all. But Jenrick’s account removes the hedge to make the comment sound more reckless than it was.

Later in the same interview, Wootton turns to the killing of Ann Widdecombe. Joshua Kerry has been charged with her murder and, on 2 October, with preparing acts of terrorism, including against Nigel Farage. The CPS has repeatedly warned against commentary that could prejudice the proceedings. Wootton acknowledges this (“you can literally be locked up for reporting the truth about a case which is currently before the court”) and then puts forward a “deep state” cover-up theory based on the timing of police announcements.

Jenrick doesn’t push back. “I don’t know exactly what happened,” he says, “but I think we can say that had the police properly investigated the threat to Nigel Farage, Ann would probably still be alive today.” Asked why the police failed, he wonders whether it was “incompetence, or was it political bias, or was it a bit of both? I have my own theory on that.” He says the timing “does seem very suspicious” and that he has “a strong suspicion” officers did not do their jobs.

Each part of that answer is a problem. It begins by admitting he doesn’t know what happened, then tells viewers what “we can say” anyway. More seriously, the claim only works if the allegations against Kerry are proven: that he plotted against Farage and went on to kill Widdecombe. Those are the questions a jury will decide. To say that a police failure probably cost her life is to treat the prosecution’s case as already established. Jenrick also concedes that why the police failed is “to be discovered in the investigations to come”, then offers his theory regardless, floating “political bias” without any evidence and leaving “my own theory” for the audience to fill in. That is insinuation rather than argument, directed at the police while a prosecution that depends on police evidence is under way.

He then says James O’Brien’s earlier comments casting doubt on Farage’s account of a firebomb attempt were defamatory, “and now provably so”. Nothing has yet been proved. Kerry has been charged, not convicted, and the facts behind those charges are for a court to determine.

Whether any of this risks prejudicing proceedings is a matter for lawyers and the courts, and this essay draws no conclusion on it. The point is simpler, and it starts with Tommo himself. In the same answer in which he condemns Burnham, Jenrick says that a man awaiting trial faces “the full force of the law whilst many, many others get away with it scot free”, and calls it “two-tier Britain”. In one interview, Jenrick holds a Labour Prime Minister to a standard of strict restraint over a defendant’s case, then speculates freely about police bias, cover-ups and causation in a live murder and terrorism case. The rule exists when it protects Us and lapses when it constrains Us.

Wootton’s own contribution goes further still. He tells viewers he was “the first person to report that leftist ideology, and actually there was quite a lot of Russian communist-type stuff” had been found at Kerry’s home. That is exactly the kind of speculation about a defendant’s motive that both sides of politics would be wise to avoid until a jury has heard the evidence.

When Wootton puts it to him that Restore Britain supporters blame him for the state of the country, Jenrick answers with a long account of his own record. It is the clearest example in the interview of positive self-presentation, the corner of van Dijk’s square where Our good deeds are emphasised and Our failures are played down.

Some of it is accurate, and it is worth saying so. Jenrick did resign as immigration minister in December 2023 over the Rwanda bill. At its third reading in January 2024 he was one of 11 Conservative MPs who voted against it, so his claim that “only 10 others” joined him is correct.

The rest needs closer attention.

“A complete bin fire because of the disastrous policies of Boris Johnson and Priti Patel.”

Jenrick served in Johnson’s cabinet as Housing Secretary from 2019 to 2021. The story of inheriting a mess leaves out that he sat at the table where it was made.

“It’s the hotels, the HMOs... I joined the protest outside the Epping Hotel last summer.”

The use of hotels for asylum seekers peaked on his watch: Home Office figures show 56,042 people in hotels at the end of September 2023, while Jenrick was immigration minister. A week into the job, he told Sky News that more hotels had been coming online almost every month. When he joined the Epping protest in August 2025, it was Reform that resurfaced his words: Zia Yusuf pointed to his talk of procuring “even more” hotels, and Nigel Farage called him a “fraud”. Both are now his colleagues. To be fair, Jenrick also said at the time that the country needed to exit hotels altogether, and in October 2023 he announced the first closures. But the minister who presided over the peak now protests outside the hotels and presents them on Outspokenas a scandal done to the country by others.

“I persuaded Rishi belatedly to make the first serious changes.”

Jenrick was immigration minister from October 2022. Under the ONS’s latest revisions, net migration peaked at about 944,000 in the year to March 2023, a few months into his time in the job. The earlier estimate put the peak at 906,000 in the year to June 2023, also on his watch. The visa restrictions that later brought numbers down were announced while he was in office, so he can claim some credit for the fall. But he cannot claim to have inherited a crisis he then fixed, when the record came while he held the brief.

“I was the only person to resign on principle from the last Conservative government.”

This is true only on the narrowest reading. During the same Rwanda rebellion, Lee Anderson resigned as the party’s deputy chairman in protest and abstained at third reading. That was a party post rather than a government one, so Jenrick can defend the words. It is still a claim to unique virtue that survives only on a technicality.

“The Home Office wrote to me saying that I shouldn’t say that... threatening me that there would be legal action.”

Jenrick has said before that terror suspects reached Britain on small boats; in 2024 he wrote that more than a dozen known suspects had crossed in the year before he became immigration minister. In August 2025 the Telegraph reported that, a fortnight after that article, the Home Office’s permanent secretary, Sir Matthew Rycroft, wrote to tell him the information “should not have been made public”, warned him against further disclosures, and reminded him that the ministerial code and the Official Secrets Act still applied to him. The same report noted that it is not unusual for officials to remind current and former ministers of these obligations. The letter has not been published, and the report mentions no threat of legal action.

The account has grown with each telling. In 2025 it was a reprimand. On 27 September 2026, Jenrick posted that the Home Office, “with the support of Yvette Cooper”, had “threatened me” and “sought to cover up a national security emergency”. On Outspoken nine days later, it had become “threatening me that there would be legal action”. This is intensification in Reisigl and Wodak’s sense: a routine reminder of confidentiality rules, sent to a Privy Counsellor, becomes the state trying to silence a whistleblower.

“As we see now... terrorists, foreign agents, have come across on small boats... and are behind some of the terrible incidents that we’re seeing right now.”

The first part has some support: some small-boat arrivals have later been identified as subjects of security interest. The second part, that they are behind current “terrible incidents”, is offered with no example. Coming minutes after he and Wootton have discussed a murder and terrorism case, it invites the audience to make connections he does not make himself.

The pattern is consistent. Where the record is good, Jenrick claims it. Where it is bad, the blame lies with Johnson, Patel or Sunak. Where it can’t be checked, he presents himself as a whistleblower silenced by the state, which puts any doubt about his claims down to the same establishment he says is persecuting him.

Wootton asks why the “mainstream media” are trying to revive “this dead Tory brand”. Jenrick’s answer is the most revealing passage about media in the interview. “I used to think that there was a right-wing press in this country, but it’s the Tory press. And it is utterly corrupt.” His evidence is a list of names: Lord Gove editing The Spectator, and Daniel Finkelstein, William Hague and Charles Moore as Tory peers. “It’s the money they pick up in the House of Lords that they want to defend. These people have got to be swept away.”

The facts in the list are broadly right, but the conclusion does not follow from them. A newspaper’s political alignment, even a cosy one, is not corruption. Calling it corruption turns disagreement into illegitimacy. It is also a sudden conversion. Jenrick spent years writing for those same papers, and it was in The Telegraph in 2024 that he made his claim about terror suspects on small boats. The “Tory press” became corrupt at about the time it stopped being his.

The other half of his claim, that there is no right-wing press, only a Tory one, is hard to take seriously. By any ordinary measure Britain has a right-wing press, and it dominates print.

According to the Media Reform Coalition’s 2025 report, DMG Media, controlled by Jonathan Harmsworth, Viscount Rothermere, accounts for 43% of national newspaper circulation through the Daily Mail, Mail on Sunday, Metro and the i, and Rupert Murdoch’s News UK for about a third through the Sun and The Times. With Reach, which publishes the Express as well as the Mirror, three companies control 90%. Not every title in those groups leans right: Metro is a free sheet and the i sits nearer the centre. But the Mail, Sun, Times, Express
and Telegraph between them account for a clear majority of the papers people pay for.

Relabelling these papers the “Tory press” does something specific. It recasts criticism from the right as the self-interest of a failed establishment, so that a right-wing paper which doubts Reform becomes a Conservative mouthpiece rather than a right-wing critic. The papers have not moved; Jenrick has. And his lead example undercuts the distinction he is drawing.

The Spectator is owned by Sir Paul Marshall, who is also a co-owner of GB News, the channel that has given Nigel Farage and Lee Anderson their own presenting slots, along with other Reform-aligned figures such as former Reform parliamentary candidate Matt Goodwin, former Brexit Party MEP Martin Daubney and former Brexit Party candidate Michelle Dewberry. The ownership of the right-wing media does not divide as neatly as Jenrick’s labels suggest.

The alternative he offers is telling.

“On this annual occasion of painful remembrance,” the Pope stressed, “I ask the Almighty for the gift of a world no longer marked by antisemitism, nor by prejudice, oppression, and persecution against any human being.”

He went on to renew his appeal to the international community, urging vigilance so that “the horror of genocide may never again be inflicted upon any people,” and so that “a society founded on mutual respect and the common good may be built.”

Beltane (/ˈbɛl.teɪn/ BEL-tayn) or Bealtaine (Irish pronunciation: [ˈbʲal̪ˠt̪ˠənʲə])[5][6] is the Gaelic May Day festival, marking the beginning of summer. It is traditionally held on 1 May, or about midway between the spring equinox and summer solstice. Historically, it was widely observed in Ireland, Scotland, and the Isle of Man. In Ireland, the name for the festival in both Irish and English is Lá Bealtaine ([l̪ˠaː ˈbʲal̪ˠt̪ˠənʲə]). In Scottish Gaelic it is Là Bealltainn ([l̪ˠaː ˈpjaul̪ˠt̪ɪɲ]), and in Manx Gaelic Boaltinn or Boaldyn. It is one of the four main Gaelic seasonal festivals—along with Samhain, Imbolc, and Lughnasadh—and is similar to the Welsh Calan Mai.

Pope Leo XIV[a] (born Robert Francis Prevost,[b] pronounced /ˈpriːvoʊst/ PREE-vohst;[3][c] September 14, 1955) is the head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City.

Born in Chicago, United States, Prevost became a friar in the Order of Saint Augustine in 1977 and was ordained as a priest in 1982. He earned a Doctor of Canon Law degree in 1987 from the Pontifical University of St. Thomas Aquinas in Rome. He performed extensive missionary work in Peru in the 1980s and 1990s, working as a parish pastor, diocesan official, seminary teacher, and administrator. Elected prior general of the Order of Saint Augustine, he was based in Rome from 2001 to 2013, though traveled extensively. He then returned to Peru as Bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, and became a Peruvian citizen. In 2023, Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops in Rome, and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America. Upon his return to Rome, Prevost was made a cardinal.

Papacy (2025–present)
Election
In pre-conclave speculation, Prevost was considered a dark horse compared to more prominent papabili,[137][138] although he was noted to be an ally of Pope Francis and a possible compromise candidate.[137][139] His U.S. nationality had been regarded as a potential stumbling block to his candidacy, reflecting unease about enhancing the United States's geopolitical power.[140][141] Prevost was well aware of this, explaining to a friend by text message: "I'm an American, I can't be elected".[51] Supporters argued that he represented a "dignified middle of the road".[142]

Prevost was elected pope on May 8, 2025, the second day of the conclave, on the fourth ballot. As a result, white smoke appeared from the Sistine Chapel at 18:07 CEST (UTC+2), informing the world that a new pope had been chosen.[143] After accepting his election and adopting his papal name, Leo embraced his fellow cardinals upon exiting the Sistine Chapel. Cardinal Dominique Mamberti, the cardinal protodeacon, made the traditional Latin proclamation, Habemus papam, announcing Pope Leo XIV to the public for the first time from the central loggia of St. Peter's Basilica.[144][145] According to Italian law enforcement, by the time of the habemus papam announcement, there were up to 150,000 people in the square.[146]

AI Overview
An October surprise is a deliberate or spontaneous news event occurring late in the month of October that has the potential to influence the outcome of an upcoming November election.

Origin of the Term
• William Casey: The term was coined in 1980 by William Casey, the campaign manager for Ronald Reagan's presidential campaign.
• The 1980 Context: Casey worried that incumbent President Jimmy Carter would pull off a last-minute foreign policy success by securing the release of American hostages held in Iran just before Election Day.

Notable Examples in U.S. History
• 1980 (Iran Hostage Crisis): The ongoing captivity of American hostages in Iran dominated the final stretch of the Carter-Reagan race, highlighting the incumbent's struggles before Reagan's victory.
• 2000 (George W. Bush DUI): Just five days before the election, news broke of George W. Bush's 1976 arrest for driving under the influence, adding late drama to a tight race.
• 2004 (Osama bin Laden Video): A video message from Osama bin Laden surfaced merely four days before voters went to the polls, thrusting national security back into the spotlight.
• 2016 (The Comey Letter): FBI Director James Comey sent a letter to Congress announcing a review of emails related to Hillary Clinton’s private server just days before the election.
• 2020 (Hunter Biden Laptop): Reporting on materials from a laptop attributed to Hunter Biden emerged in the final weeks of the campaign, sparking extensive media and political debate.
